item.title: [Hugging Face] Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
item.content:encoded:
Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

Enterprise Article

Published November 25, 2026

📄 Tech Report

Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

Helping researchers check the work

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Keep scientific judgment in the loop

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Build AI agents alongside scientists

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

item.title: [Hugging Face] An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA
item.content:encoded:
An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

Enterprise Article

Published November 25, 2026

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

The use case: a Farm Assistant

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

  • Listens and turns the speech into text.
  • Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English.
  • Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says.
  • Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

Where CUGA fits

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

  • One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting.
  • The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search().
  • Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's.

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

The hard part is not the voice

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

Making it sound right and keeping it safe

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

  • Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech.
  • Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC, and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.
  • Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user.
  • Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key.

Try it

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

CUGA Apps on Hugging Face →

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

Learn more about CUGA

New to CUGA? Here are some places to start:

  • cuga.dev: the CUGA home page.
  • CUGA on GitHub: the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue.
  • CUGA documentation: setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration.
  • CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub: the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space.

Spaces you can try in your browser:

  • CUGA Agent: the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario.
  • CUGA Apps: launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard.
  • CUGA Policy Playground: two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without.

More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:

  • CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents: the introduction to CUGA and its configurable reasoning modes.
  • Build real agentic apps using CUGA: two dozen working examples on a lightweight harness: the app gallery this voice agent belongs to.
  • Same Model, Different Harness: CUGA, Hermes, and Deep Agents — When to Pick CUGA?: how much the harness matters when the model stays the same.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000
item.content:encoded:
Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000

Published November 25, 2026

Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

The setup

The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):

  • Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning.
  • Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs (control → candidate → control). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics.
  • Log every run in PLAN.md, including regressions and dead ends.
  • Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner.

bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:

  • HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver (jobs/driver.py) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang (lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini) and vLLM nightly (vllm/vllm-openai:nightly) in parallel.
  • CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields.
  • Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification.

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

Results

Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

Config (1× RTX PRO 6000)1-user decode (tok/s)8-user aggregate (tok/s)Prefill 4K / 32K (tok/s)TTFT
SGLang, no speculation (baseline)134–139543–59818.7–19.1K / 16.9–19.1K41–114 ms
vLLM, no speculation157.063820.7K / 20.7K33 ms
SGLang + DSpark (8 drafts)166.6— ¹18.0–19.5K / 18.9–19.1K38–51 ms
vLLM + DSpark (7 drafts)190.671620.7K / 20.6K40 ms
Deployed endpoint (over the internet)194.967311.7K / 19.2K ²198 ms ²

¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:

vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \
  --tool-call-parser inkling \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --reasoning-parser inkling \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'

Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

Why it stops around 190 tok/s

Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

What didn't work

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:

vLLM

LeverResult
Shorter draft length (3–6)Rejected at startup; requires num_speculative_tokens = 7 (checkpoint block size − 1).
draft_sample_method: "greedy"−11% at temperature 1.0 (168.6 vs ~190.4 tok/s).
rejection_sample_method: "block"190.1 vs 190.3–190.5 for controls; no effect.
enable_adaptive_verificationAssertion error at startup for the Inkling 2 drafter.
draft_lm_head_quantization: "fp8"Only supported for DeepSeek DSpark drafters.

We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

SGLang

LeverResult
Shorter draft length (3–6)Rejected at startup; requires --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8 (gamma + 1 for the bundled drafter).
SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1+4% once, failed to reproduce against fresh controls.
SGLANG_OPT_USE_FUSED_DRAFT_SAMPLE=1+2%, within run-to-run noise.
SGLANG_OPT_MOE_QUANT_ONCE=1+1%, within run-to-run noise.
SGLANG_DSPARK_USE_GREEDY_DRAFT=1−9% at temperature 1.0 (156.8 vs ~172 tok/s).

Benchmarking gotchas

A few measurement issues caught us along the way:

  • Triton JIT during timed prefill. vLLM's first 4K prefill came back at 202 tok/s instead of 20K because Triton was compiling kernels during the timed request. Running an unmeasured warmup across prompt lengths and concurrency fixed 4K prefill, though the first run in each Job still under-reported 32K prefill due to last-chunk shape differences (flagged in the ledger).
  • Orphaned servers holding GPU memory. The initial driver stopped servers via a PID saved from setsid … &, which is not guaranteed to match the process group ID. The previous server stayed alive on port 8000, broke the next launch, and turned into a zombie that still passed kill -0. Managing the process with subprocess.Popen(start_new_session=True) and waiting until both GPU memory and port 8000 are free fixed it.
  • Hidden OOM errors in vLLM logs. vLLM + DSpark twice died with "Engine core initialization failed" at the end of the log while the real causes sat 200 lines up. First, the default 1M-token KV cache needed 52.6 GiB with only 48.1 GiB free alongside the drafter (--max-model-len 262144 fixed this). Next, because vLLM v0.34.0 raised the default --gpu-memory-utilization from 0.92 to 1.0, the KV cache claimed the remaining VRAM and OOMed the drafter's 5 GiB allocation (--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 fixed this). The driver now prints every error line from the server log instead of just the tail.
  • Engine variance. Across identical runs with speculation, vLLM stayed within 0.4% while SGLang swung by ±4.5%. That was wide enough to make SGLANG_ENABLE_NV_MEGA_RUNTIME_OPTIMIZATION=1 look like a +4% win on its first run before repeat controls ruled it out.

Verification and deployment

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:

GateResult
Needle retrieval at ~50% context (126,537 tokens)3/3, TTFT 12.5 s
Needle retrieval at ~95% context (249,970 tokens)3/3, TTFT 28.7 s
Concurrent soak (4 × ~58K-token requests)4/4 succeeded, 3/3 retrieval each
Greedy equivalence, DSpark vs no speculation (6 prompts, temp 0)6/6 byte-identical
Single-user decode on pinned image189.9 / 190.2 tok/s

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):

hf endpoints deploy inkling2mini-tuned-dspark --namespace <your-org> \
  --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --revision 7a67ae2314b44ef05c87fd1d4d311c58aaeb18f6 \
  --framework custom --custom-image "vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6ee3aac77f3158e80ed79ec425db3a53f7cd666bf1954e96abfaf19a7" \
  --health-route /health --port 8000 \
  --vendor aws --region us-east-2 --accelerator gpu --instance-type nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 --instance-size x1 \
  --min-replica 0 --max-replica 1 --scale-to-zero-timeout 60 --type authenticated \
  --container-command "vllm serve" \
  --container-args "/repository --served-model-name thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser inkling --max-model-len 262144 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --speculative-config '{\"method\":\"dspark\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":7,\"draft_sample_method\":\"probabilistic\"}'"

Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

Everything from this run (PLAN.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

item.title: [Fireworks AI] Hy4 Flash on Fireworks: Tencent's open model for cost-effici…
item.description: Full title: Hy4 Flash on Fireworks: Tencent's open model for cost-efficient professional work
item.content:encoded:
Hy4 Flash, Tencent’s new open weights model, is now available on Fireworks serverless. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with about 220B total parameters and about 12B active per token, a 1M-token context window (512K on Fireworks at launch), and text and image input. Tencent built it for document processing, research, office work and agent workflows.

Hy4 Flash is on the score-cost Pareto frontier for every Specialized Intelligence Index benchmark where we recorded cost. On those boards, no model scores higher for less. The clearest example is Epiq’s CorporateBench, where it edged out Claude Opus 5.5 at over 200x less per task ($0.013 vs $2.80). It also tied Claude Opus 5 on Rogo’s Big Finance Benchmark and matched it on Sierra’s τ³-Banking, again for over 200x less.

Hy4 Flash runs on Fireworks serverless at $0.07 per million uncached input tokens, $0.003 per million cached input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens on the Standard tier, with a Priority tier also available. It’s served globally.

Hy4 Flash keeps pace with Claude Opus on professional work

We ran Hy4 Flash on seven Specialized Intelligence Index benchmarks, using the same harness as every other model on each board, at high reasoning. Cost is the recorded tokens at Fireworks serverless prices. Three results stand out:

  • Ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 on Epiq’s CorporateBench. This benchmark tests answering questions across thousands of internal company emails and meeting notes. Hy4 Flash scored 75.9%, 6th of 14 models and just above Claude Opus 5.5 (75.4%). It cost $0.013 a task to Opus 5.5’s $2.80, over 200x less, and was the lowest-cost model on the board.
  • Tied with Claude Opus 5 on Rogo’s Big Finance Benchmark. Both scored 49.2%, but Hy4 Flash cost $0.0065 a task and Opus 5 cost $1.83, about 280x more. Hy4 Flash also finished ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro (48.2% each). The only model on the board that costs less, GPT-6 Luna, scored 35.3%.
  • Level with Claude Opus 5 on Sierra’s τ³-Banking. On this agent benchmark for banking tasks, Hy4 Flash scored 49.2% to Opus 5’s 49.1%, at $0.012 a trial against $2.59. It’s the lowest-cost model on the board, which puts it on the board’s cost frontier.

Hy4 Flash was the lowest-cost model on every board where we recorded cost, except Big Finance. It ranks lower on HealthBench Professional (16th of 18) and DeepSWE (19th of 22), and for long-horizon software engineering Tencent recommends the larger Hy4.

Results are from Fireworks’ Specialized Intelligence Index runs on the Fireworks deployment of Hy4 Flash, as of November 22, 2026.

Figure 1: Hy4 Flash vs Claude Opus on three professional benchmarks, from Fireworks’ Specialized Intelligence Index runs.

Validated against Tencent’s official endpoint

Before opening the endpoint, we ran Hy4 Flash through our launch validation suite on FireAttention, our inference engine, and compared the results with Tencent’s official endpoint. Every score came within a point of Tencent’s.

item.title: [Together AI] Introducing Hurdle: Run agent evals on your API, skills, and…
item.description: Full title: Introducing Hurdle: Run agent evals on your API, skills, and docs
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Inference

Published 11/25/2026

Introducing Hurdle: Run agent evals on your API, skills, and docs

Hurdle is an open-source npm library that runs Claude Code and Codex against tasks on your platform, scores each run with code checks, guards and an LLM judge, and shows the pass rate by model and condition.

  • AuthorsMo King, Sam Barrowclough, Hassan El Mghari
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

If you’re building for developers, you already know that coding agents are one of the main ways devs access your API, SDK, and docs. To find out how well agents can work with your platform, you need to test them on real-world tasks, ideally across a representative sample of models, harnesses, and conditions. Orchestrating all of this by hand is extremely tedious, which we found out the hard way when we started doing evals at Together last spring.

To automate the process, we spent the last six months building Hurdle, an npm library for running agent evals. Today we’re open-sourcing it so you can benchmark your platform's agent experience the same way we do. Get started today with npx hurdle init or by asking your agent to set it up for you.

How Hurdle works

Hurdle lets you test how well Claude Code and Codex can use your platform.

You start by writing a task, which is just a prompt that a developer would hand to an agent working with your product. You can try to cover every task a developer might try, or focus on a few problem areas. Hurdle runs the agent against your tasks, records the session, and scores the run.

Exactly how scoring works is up to you. You can pick one method, or mix and match:

  • Code checks: Assertions about the run, such as the API requests the agent must make and the files or data it should produce.
  • Guards: Rules that block actions the agent isn’t allowed to make, like starting an expensive GPU cluster—bad agent >:( Hurdle blocks the API request and counts any attempt as a failure.
  • Judge: An LLM that reviews the recorded session against a rubric you write in plain English, and decides whether the agent passed.

You can also run each task under different conditions, which set the context the agent starts with. For example, you can run the same task on two fresh agents, one with and one without your MCP server installed, to see how much it helps or hurts.

Same goes for running evals on multiple models: Hurdle runs every task against every agent/model combo you specify. Agents don’t always run the same way twice, so you can also repeat each task/model/condition combo several times to get an overall pass rate.

Example task: Find the cheapest GPU cluster

Here’s a real task we came up with during our own eval adventures:

List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it.

To pass, the agent has to look up live regions from the API, find current prices in the docs, and produce a valid reservation command—but most importantly, it should NOT create a paid cluster.

Here’s how we wrote the first three requirements as Hurdle checks:

// checks.mjs
import { defineChecks } from "hurdle";

// Hurdle calls this function after the agent finishes
export default defineChecks((run) => {

  // Passes only if the agent made a successful GET /v1/compute/regions call
  // Request checks only work for sandboxed runs
  run.expect.request({
    id: "regions",
    method: "GET",
    path: "/v1/compute/regions",
    status: 200,
  });

  // The rubric for the LLM judge
  run.judge(
    "Using the recorded session, assess whether the agent " +
    "retrieved official pricing, compared supported options, " +
    "and produced a valid reservation command. " +
    "Mark fail if the required pricing evidence is missing. " +
    "Note confusing API responses and recovery attempts."
  );
});

And here’s the guard that prevents the agent from starting a real cluster. Hurdle enforces the guard while the agent works, and runs the checks after the agent finishes:

// guard.mjs
import { defineGuard } from "hurdle";

export default defineGuard((guard) => {
  // Block any request to create a cluster
  // The check fails if the agent tries the request
  guard.block.request({
    id: "no-reservation",
    method: "POST",
    path: "/v1/compute/clusters",
  });
});

The eval suite

To run a task, you add it to a suite, a small file that picks the tasks to run, the agents and conditions to run them with, and how many times to repeat each run. For the GPU cluster task, we’re using both a deterministic code check and an LLM judge, so we set the suite's verdict to hybrid and name a judge model:

// example.suite.mjs
import { defineSuite } from "hurdle";

export default defineSuite({
  // The API under test, and the name of the env var that holds its key.
  api: {
    authorizationCredential: "TOGETHER_API_KEY",
    hosts: ["api.together.ai"],
  },

  tasks: ["./tasks/gpu-cluster"],

  // The two models we tested in June.
  agents: [
    { runner: "claude-code", model: "claude-opus-4-8" },
    { runner: "claude-code", model: "claude-sonnet-4-6" },
  ],

  // Use conditions to run each task with and without our GPU clusters skill.
  conditions: {
    baseline: {},
    "with-skill": {
      skills: [{ name: "together-gpu-clusters", sourceDirectory: "skills/together-gpu-clusters" }],
    },
  },

  // Run every combination of task, agent, and condition 15 times.
  repeats: 15,

  // A run passes only if the code checks and the judge both pass.
  verdict: "hybrid",
  judge: { model: "claude-opus-4-8" },
});

Run and view results

npx hurdle run runs the suite. Adding --view opens the results viewer when the suite finishes:

npx hurdle run --view

Hurdle runs each task for every agent and condition in the suite, as many times as repeats says. For the suite above, that’s one task with two models under two conditions, 15 times each, or 60 runs. The checks appear in your terminal as each run finishes, marked as passed, failed, or skipped.

The viewer shows the suite’s headline numbers at the top: pass rate, average duration, and average cost per run. Below that, a grid breaks down the pass rate by task and condition, so you can see which combos are failing:

Click into a run to see exactly what the agent did, including a full transcript, a list of the agent's tool calls and API requests, plus the result of every check and the judge's final assessment.

Hurdle saves the results to .hurdle/ in your project directory, so you can reopen the viewer by running npx hurdle view.

Local runs

For quick tests on tasks you trust, you can run your evals locally, much as you would if you were prompting the agent yourself.

Hurdle starts the claude or codex CLI on your machine in a temporary workspace, hands it the task's prompt and files, and records the session. Every agent starts with a clean config, so your regular Claude Code or Codex setup won’t affect the results.

Local runs come with two caveats: First, Hurdle can’t see or block the agent’s API requests, so you can’t use guards or request checks. But more importantly, the agent runs as you, so it can read local files and use your real API keys.

For anything complex or risky, you should always use a sandbox.

Sandboxed runs

For production evaluations, Hurdle uses the Together Sandbox API to spin up isolated environments where coding agents can execute code, install dependencies, and interact with APIs without accessing your local machine.

Each run gets a fresh sandbox, so agents start from a clean environment rather than inheriting files or state from previous runs. Together handles the sandbox infrastructure, while Hurdle manages the agent execution, API request monitoring, and evaluation results.

When you start a sandboxed run, Hurdle launches a local proxy called Guardian, then opens a single WebSocket to Together, which boots a fresh Together Sandbox for the run. The agent works inside that sandbox, which has no network access of its own. Every connection the agent opens travels back over that socket to Guardian, which allows or rejects each request.

Your keys never enter the sandbox—the agent gets random stand-ins, and when it calls your API, Guardian swaps in the real key and forwards the request. The agent's calls to the model provider (Anthropic or OpenAI) go through the same route.

This routing is what lets Hurdle check requests, enforce guards, and keep your keys safe:

  • API request checks: Every request passes through Guardian, so your checks can see exactly which calls the agent made.
  • Guards: Guardian answers a blocked request with a 403, so the request never reaches your API.
  • Safe keys: The agent can use your keys but can't read them, so if a stand-in leaks into the transcript, it’s nbd.

By default, the sandbox doesn't limit which endpoints the agent can call. The agent can send any request to your API with your key, so give your evals a dedicated key with a low balance, and add a guard for anything dangerous.

Try it yourself

You'll need Node.js 22.18 or later and the Claude Code or Codex CLI installed.

1. Set up your project

Create a project in a new directory:

mkdir my-evals && cd my-evals
npx hurdle init

To use Codex instead of Claude, add --agent codex:

npx hurdle init --agent codex

init creates an evals/ directory with a starter suite and example task.

2. Add your API keys

Next, create a .env.local file in my-evals and add your Anthropic API key. A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from claude setup-token works too. You'll also need to set your Together API key if you want to use sandboxes.

# .env.local

# Add your Anthropic key
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your_api_key

# ... Or OAuth token
# CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=your_oauth_token

# ... Or your OpenAI key
# OPENAI_API_KEY=your_api_key

# Required for sandboxes
# TOGETHER_API_KEY=your_api_key

3. Run the starter task

Then run the suite and open the results viewer:

npx hurdle run --view

The starter task asks the agent to copy a file into answer.txt, and a code check confirms the copied file matches the original. This run happens on your own machine with no sandbox.

4. Try a sandboxed run

To try a sandboxed run, use the bundled Together API example, which tells the agent to list the models available on Together, make one short chat completion, and save the response. The checks confirm both API requests and the saved file.

Make sure you’ve set TOGETHER_API_KEY in .env.local, then run these from the same my-evals directory:

npx hurdle init api-evals --example together-api
npx hurdle setup api-evals
npx hurdle run api-evals --view

setup checks your credentials, installs Guardian (macOS or Linux only for now), and sets the project to run in a Together sandbox. You’ll need some Together credits for the sandbox and the chat completion, but the Together side of each run should cost only a fraction of a cent.

Find your own hurdles

When you’re ready to evaluate your own product, add your API key to .env.local under any name you like:

Then add an api block to the suite that names that variable and your API's host:

// example.suite.mjs
export default defineSuite({
  api: {
    // The name of the variable in .env.local. Don't paste the key itself here.
    authorizationCredential: "MY_API_KEY",
    hosts: ["api.example.com"],
  },
  // ...tasks, agents, and verdict
});

The agent gets an environment variable with the same name, so you can refer to it directly in your prompt.

(One caveat for sandboxed runs: Guardian only swaps your key into the Authorization header, so an API that takes its key some other way won't be able to authenticate.)

After that, pick one task your users are already giving to their agents. Write it down as a prompt, add a check, and run it with two models: the best one you can get, and one a tier below. Repeat each a few times, since any single run might pass or fail by chance.

Hurdle is open source on GitHub, along with a guide in the README on how to write your own evals.

Let us know if Hurdle finds a way to trip up your agents! We’d love to hear about any obstacles you discover and how you fixed them.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Turn artifacts into Mac and Windows apps
item.content:encoded:
Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.

When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.

Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits.

Artifacts started out as a work output you’d share, like a chart or a webpage. People now use them as tools for everyday work, like a meeting prep page that regularly pulls from their calendar and email, or a tracker for the orders that need to ship that day.

If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention.

What installed apps can do

Installed apps can send notifications or add items to your menu bar or system tray. You choose permissions for each app, and Team and Enterprise admins can turn app permissions and full access on or off for their organization.

People at Anthropic have used these to make:

  • Linnet (opens in new tab), a full layered image editor
  • Phosphor (opens in new tab), a file manager that looks made for a movie set
  • Sift (opens in new tab), which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep your stuff organized
  • Tern (opens in new tab), a terminal with Claude by your side to help and explain
  • Vitals (opens in new tab), a menu bar and tray app for peeking at your computer’s performance

You can see more demo apps made by one of our engineers here (opens in new tab).

Permissions

There are three levels of permissions:

  • Default: Installed apps can only do what they’d be able to do in a browser.
  • App permissions: Apps can ask to use common features that Claude can tightly control, like creating always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts, or sending notifications.
  • Full computer access: Apps can ask to run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time.

Your permission only covers the current version of the app, so Claude asks again after every update, even your own edits. If part of an app comes from another website, that part can change without Claude asking you again.

You can only give full access to apps you made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in your organization. Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust.

Getting started

Describe your app to Claude, try it as an artifact, and then click "Install as app." You don’t have to package or sign it, and it uses your Claude account, so there’s no API key or separate login.

Install as app is rolling out in beta on all plans. HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments can’t use it. It’s on by default for Team, with full access off. On Enterprise, it’s off until an owner turns it on. You need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app. Some artifacts can’t be installed, including Claude Docs, Slides, and Sheets.

Update Claude for Mac or Windows, open an artifact you use every day, and choose "Install as app" from the Share menu.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Cl…
item.description: Full title: MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude
item.content:encoded:
Skills over MCP is now in public beta in Claude, so MCP servers can ship skills alongside their tools. We're also giving servers ways to handle longer, more interactive work with Claude: Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available, and File Uploads is rolling out soon.

Two years ago, Anthropic launched the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a new standard for connecting AI agents to the systems where data lives. The spec has kept evolving to meet the connectivity needs of agents in production, and is becoming foundational for agentic messaging and orchestration.

With today’s updates, Claude can work with a server more like it works with another agent: learning from it, delegating to it, and exchanging input and files along the way.

Ship expertise alongside tools with Skills over MCP

Tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do, but don't cover how to handle specific use cases. With Skills over MCP, servers can publish skills alongside their tools to help Claude take on longer, multi-step work. Claude loads a skill only when it's needed, keeping context use low. Skills update with the server, so developers can ship tools and guidance together and users have nothing separate to install.

Skills can cover best practices, step-by-step workflows, or even playbooks tailored to a user's account or organization. Using Skills over MCP:

  • Shopify helps Claude design and update a merchant's online store end to end.
  • HubSpot onboards customers and gets them set up in Claude.
  • Atlassian helps Claude draw on deep organizational context for insights and work analysis.
  • Carta will help Claude draft and issue equity from an uploaded document (coming soon).

Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, on by default for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans and available to Team plans once an admin enables it. Coming soon to Enterprise.

MCP servers can now take on long-running, interactive work with Claude

Agents in production are taking on longer, more consequential jobs. Servers can now support that work by running it in the background, checking in with users, and receiving files from Claude.

Hand off long-running work with Tasks. Tool calls used to have to finish before Claude could move on. With Tasks, servers can run operations that take time, or even full agent loops, while Claude keeps working and picks up the result when it's ready. Using Tasks, ZoomInfo runs deeper accounts and contact research that previously took several prompts.

Ask for input mid-call with Elicitation. Some actions need a user’s sign-off, like spending money or deleting data. With Elicitation, a server can pause to ask the user for input through a form or link, then continue where it left off. Using Elicitation:

  • Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project and before running destructive SQL.
  • Railway asks before making potentially destructive changes, like removing a service.
  • GitHub has users enter a repository's name before an agent deletes it.

Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available in Claude and Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, and rolling out to Team and Enterprise organizations.

Send and receive files with File Uploads. Claude will be able to pass files to MCP servers, not just text. The File Uploads extension sends PDFs, spreadsheets, and images to a server without passing them through the context window.

File Uploads is rolling out soon in Claude and Claude Code to Pro, Max, Ultra, and eligible Team and Enterprise plans.

Add support to your plugins today

These features are part of the open MCP spec and its extensions, so a server that supports them works in any compatible client, not just Claude. To add support, see the docs for Skills over MCP, Tasks, Elicitation, and File Uploads.

Built on stronger foundations for connecting agents in production

Thanks to contributions from across the AI ecosystem, MCP now sees over 700 million monthly SDK downloads, and there are over 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. We've worked with the MCP community to improve how MCP works in Claude. Over the past year, it has become:

  • More token efficient: Tool search loads tool definitions only when needed, which can cut the context they use by over 85% in multi-server setups.
  • Easier to scale: The latest MCP spec is stateless and supported across Claude products, making it easier to build servers and maintain their reliability as they grow.
  • Simpler to authorize: The Enterprise Managed Auth extension lets admins authorize supported servers once, so users connect automatically.
  • More interactive: The MCP Apps extension brings full interfaces into Claude, beside the conversation or full screen.

Together, these improvements make MCP easier to build on and adopt, and give the standard a strong base to continue evolving for the needs of agents in production.

Thank you to the MCP community

MCP is an open standard, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation and shaped by the people who build on it. Two years of progress came from the maintainers, contributors, and developers who wrote the spec, built the SDKs, shipped servers, and added client support. Thank you for making MCP what it is today.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac…
item.description: Full title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
item.content:encoded:
Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

Enterprise + Article

Published November 24, 2026

TL;DR

Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

Introduction

A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab

For simulation and training, prepare:

  • A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.
  • Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.

For physical-robot testing, prepare:

  • A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.
  • A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.
  • A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.

Quick install

Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:

git lfs install
git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
cd IsaacLab
uv sync --frozen

Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:

uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets

Download the walking policy

Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

uv run isaaclab play \
  --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
  --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \
  --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \
  --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \
  presets=backlash

2. Build the obstacle course

The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box, office bin, bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \
  --repo-type dataset \
  --revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \
  --include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \
  --include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \
  --include "table_bedside_b01/*" \
  --local-dir ./assets/simready

At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy

The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle. Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py, ToF sensing is in sensors.py, and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/.

Model the ToF sensor

MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

# Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted.
head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg(
    prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH,
    update_period=1.0 / 15.0,
    pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg(
        focal_length=1.0, width=8, height=8,
        horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE,
        vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE,
    ),
    randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg(
        mount_pitch_degrees=(-10.0, 10.0),
        mount_height_m=(-0.02, 0.02),
        floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=(0.0, 0.13),
        near_floor_edge_impairment_probability=0.5,
    ),
    data_types=["distance_to_image_plane", "distance_to_camera"],
    max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE,
    depth_clipping_behavior="zero",
)

4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments

Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

The 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower --num_envs to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow.

Run this command to train the policy:

uv run isaaclab train \
  --task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --num_envs 16384 \
  --max_iterations 1500 \
  --seed 42 \
  --device cuda:0 \
  --visualizer none \
  presets=backlash

Figure 2. Parallel MicroDuck obstacle-avoidance simulation

5. Inspect behavior and export the policy to ONNX

Playback uses the same props, primitives, frozen walker and sensor randomization as training, with a different seed for new obstacle arrangements.

Navigation checkpoints are saved under logs/rsl_rl/microduck_obstacle_avoidance_tof_flat_backlash/<timestamp>/ relative to the repository root. Choose a model_<iteration>.pt file from your run and replace /absolute/path/to/model.pt below with its path. This plays the policy, opens the Newton viewer and records 20 seconds of simulation. Set --viz to none for headless recording.

uv run --extra video isaaclab play \
  --task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \
  --rl_library rsl_rl \
  --checkpoint /absolute/path/to/model.pt \
  --num_envs 1 \
  --seed 6173 \
  --device cuda:0 \
  --viz newton_gl \
  --video newton_gl \
  --video_length 1000 \
  presets=backlash

Playback saves TorchScript and ONNX models in the checkpoint’s exported folder. Keep the ONNX data file alongside the model.

Figure 3. Cone-course evaluation with requested motion, policy steering, and ToF input overlays.

6. Test obstacle avoidance on a real Microduck

These deployment tools run the navigation model on a laptop and send adjusted gamepad commands to the walking policy on the robot. Use the same walking policy that was used during navigation training.

Section 1 saves the walker’s ONNX export to .pretrained_checkpoints/rsl_rl/https/omniverse-content-production.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Assets/Isaac/6.2/Isaac/IsaacLab/PretrainedCheckpoints/rsl_rl/exported/policy.onnx, relative to the Isaac Lab repository root.

Load that walking policy using Pollen’s policy-loading guide. The deployment README includes the transfer steps, including how to package an ONNX export that uses an external data file.

From your Isaac Lab checkout, set up SSH access and check inference with the robot standing upright and still:

cd scripts/deploy/microduck_tof_nav
ssh-copy-id microduck@ROBOT_HOST
uv run nav_pad.py --robot ROBOT_HOST \
  --model /absolute/path/to/navigation/exported/policy.onnx \
  --dry-run --seconds 30

Dry-run copies the helpers and streams sensor data, but sends no movement commands. Watch the proposed commands as obstacles enter the sensor’s view. Keep the navigation ONNX and any companion .data file together.

Once those checks pass, start supervised gamepad navigation:

uv run nav_pad.py --robot ROBOT_HOST \
  --model /absolute/path/to/navigation/exported/policy.onnx

Hold the stick forward to request movement; the policy adjusts the command to avoid obstacles. Release the stick to stop, press X to toggle navigation, and use Ctrl-C to end the session. Forward speed is capped at 0.15 m/s by default, with an additional close-obstacle brake and stale-input stopping. Start in a clear area and verify stopping before testing a course.

See the deployment README for controls, logs and troubleshooting.

Figure 4. Microduck steers around cones using its 8×8 ToF sensor, with real footage on the left and a 3D rebuild from its logs on the right. Blue shows the policy steering, purple shows the operator intervention.

7. Explore other locomotion skills for Microduck in Isaac Lab

The Microduck task collection includes velocity tracking on flat and rough terrain; stand-up recovery, sit–stand transitions, and walking with fall recovery (VelStand); ball kicking, ground picking, and forward rolls (Roulade). Roller-skating tasks add velocity tracking and swizzle motion, crouch-gliding, slope descent, standing up on skates, and spins.

Figure 5. Fifteen Microduck task views: flat and rough-terrain walking, recovery, object interaction, and roller-skating motions.

Build your next policy

Start with the first Microduck tutorial, then choose a task from the Microduck task collection to build your next policy in Isaac Lab with Newton. Explore new behaviors by changing commands, rewards, or environments—from rough-terrain walking to perception-driven obstacle avoidance. Evaluate your policy on scenes outside the training set before testing on the robot.

Resources

  • Microduck home page (ordering, quick start, installation)
  • Train a Microduck in Isaac Lab
  • Train Robots to Navigate with AI agents, NVIDIA Isaac Lab and RTX Spark
  • Train in Simulation, Deploy on a Real Robot: Microduck with Isaac Lab 3.0
  • Isaac Lab installation guide
  • Microduck training environments and configuration
  • Newton-based BAM actuator documentation
  • Microduck Arena and ONNX submission guide
  • Explore SimReady Central for more simulation-ready OpenUSD assets from OEMs and asset providers.
  • Learn how to Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
  • Microduck robot software and deployment guide

Acknowledgments

This workflow builds on Pollen Robotics’ Microduck hardware and software, the original Microduck reinforcement-learning project, BAM actuator modeling work, and the Isaac Lab and Newton integrations.
