item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API, with Ente…
item.description: Full title: Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API, with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls for Claude models
item.content:encoded:
Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API with Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls

Today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock. The API gives you one place to discover, request, and enroll in model provider trusted access programs. We are also announcing the public preview of the first two offerings, Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) and Enterprise Data Controls (EDC). Both are available on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP).

Frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock. For eligible customers, model providers also offer customers more control on how those policies are met, such as where retained data is stored and how it is reviewed. Each offering has its own terms, approvals, and settings.

The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience. Your teams discover offerings, check eligibility, and enroll in the same way for every provider. Your administrators decide who can enroll, using existing IAM policies and service control policies. As more model providers add offerings, those appear in the same place.

EFS and EDC were built in partnership between AWS and Anthropic. They let you access Anthropic’s most capable models safely, from both a model use and a customer data perspective. With both EFS and EDC, when automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for your team to review. With EFS, customers store their data in their own AWS account, and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic or Amazon Bedrock. With EDC, retained data is stored in Amazon-managed storage instead of your account and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic. One application gives access to both programs.

In this post, we explain how the trusted access program API works, then walk through EFS and EDC storage options and setup.

How trusted access programs work

A trusted access program is a named provider program that gives customers more control of safety reviews and access to model capabilities in exchange for accepting the program’s terms. Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API now gives you one place to find the model and use case programs available to your account. EFS and EDC are the first offerings available today. Offerings that providers add later appear in the same place and follow the same steps.

Anyone with access to the trusted access program API can list the offerings and check their status for an account, an organization in AWS Organizations, or an Amazon Bedrock project. The status tells you what to do next. eligible means you’re eligible for the offering and can enroll, requestable means you need approval for eligibility first, and the statusReason field in the response explains how to request it. The model provider (or AWS, as authorized by the model provider) approves your eligibility.

Enrolling is a separate step where you accept the offering’s terms imposed by the provider. You enroll at the scope where you were approved: an account, every account in an organization from the management account, or a single project. You can opt out at any time. Each step is a call to the trusted access program API, so you control who can enroll with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and service control policies (SCPs). More information is available in the trusted access programs documentation.

Enterprise Frontier Safeguards

With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), you can retain your data in your own AWS environment with full control. It is designed with over 100 customers, including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility, like healthcare, financial services, and law.

Automated safety monitoring looks for patterns that only show up across many requests. These include intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm, such as offensive cyber operations. They also include agents that go beyond what a user asked for, such as using a software exploit to reach an internal system.

On Amazon Bedrock, AWS operates EFS and the customer inputs and outputs stay within the customer’s AWS account. Only automated safety monitoring within AWS reads the retained inputs and outputs. AWS human reviewers don’t review content for EFS. Your review stays with you. Neither AWS nor Anthropic humans access your retained inputs or outputs. Your inputs and outputs are never used for training.

How it works

Amazon Bedrock reaches your AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket as a single AWS service principal and only through the key policy and bucket policy that you write. You can remove that access at any time, but Amazon Bedrock stops serving the covered models 24 hours after it loses access to your key or bucket.

Figure 1: EFS workflow on Amazon Bedrock

When you call a covered model including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP):

  • Your application calls the model. Inference works as it does for any Amazon Bedrock model.
  • Amazon Bedrock writes the prompt and response to its retention and key services.
  • These services encrypt the data with your AWS KMS key.
  • Bedrock writes the prompt and response to your bucket, encrypted with your key, or to Amazon-managed storage. When writing to your bucket, Amazon writes the content within minutes. On some failures with your key or bucket, we can retry for up to 72 hours.
  • Automated safety monitoring, which runs in AWS owned and operated accounts, scans the data and looks for misuse across requests.
  • If automated safety monitoring finds a potential risk, a case is created in your bucket for your review.

How your team handles cases

A Case summarizes what automated safety monitoring found and references the related transcripts. Retained records arrive under the transcripts/ prefix in your bucket, and case files arrive under review-cases/. Your team reviews each Case and writes a response file to review-responses/, stating whether it found a violation (violation or no_violation) and, for a violation, the applicable policy category.

Enterprise Data Controls

EDC offers the same automated safety monitoring as EFS and human review of flagged activity stays with your team. Unlike EFS, EDC stores retained data in Amazon managed storage, encrypted with AWS managed keys, so there’s no bucket or key to set up. Eligible customers can access both EFS and EDC through a single enrollment application. If your policy allows retained data to stay in Amazon-managed storage and encrypted with AWS-managed keys, enroll in EDC. If your policy instead requires retained data to be encrypted with your AWS KMS key and stay in your S3 bucket, enroll in EFS. Either way, your team will be able to review flagged activity.

Outside EFS and EDC, you can use Claude Fable models on Amazon Bedrock in two ways today:

  • With the aws_review data retention mode, Amazon Bedrock retains inputs and outputs for up to 30 days, where they are available for review within the AWS boundary.
  • Eligible customers can use current Fable models for internal use with zero data retention (ZDR) through at least June 30, 2027. EFS is the long-term path after ZDR ends.

Choose where retained data is stored

With EFS, retained data is stored only in your own S3 bucket, encrypted with your KMS key. Neither Anthropic nor AWS keeps it in their own storage. The following table compares EFS with the other routes.

Not Eligible for ZDR, EFS, or EDCZDR exception (interim)EFS, your own Amazon S3 bucket (public preview)EDC, Amazon-managed storage (public preview)
Data retentionUp to 30 daysNone, through at least June 30, 2027, for current Fable models and existing Cyber Verification Program models for internal useAmazon Bedrock keeps no copy. Your lifecycle rules apply, 30 days minimum.Up to 30 days, then Amazon Bedrock deletes it
Where the retained data is storedAWS managed storageNot retainedYour Amazon S3 bucketAmazon-managed storage
Encryption keyAWS managedNot applicableYour AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keyAWS managed
Safety monitoringAvailable for review within the AWS boundaryNoneAutomated. Cases arrive in your bucket for your team to review.Automated. Your team reviews flagged Cases. Cases aren’t delivered during the public preview.
What your AWS CloudTrail showsYour Amazon Bedrock API callsYour Amazon Bedrock API callsYour Amazon Bedrock API calls, plus Amazon Bedrock’s use of your key and bucketYour Amazon Bedrock API calls
Storage costNot applicableNot applicableUsual Amazon S3 and AWS KMS chargesNot applicable

Table 1: Routes for Claude Fable models on Amazon Bedrock.

Storage configurations apply to one Region at a time, and a Region without a configuration uses Amazon-managed storage. Save a configuration in every Region where you call covered models.

Getting started

Start by checking your EFS status with the trusted access program API:

aws bedrock list-trusted-access-programs --region us-east-1

If the status is eligible, your account is approved. If it’s requestable, follow the steps in the statusReason field to request access. Joining the preview turns off zero data retention for the accounts you add.

After you’re approved, set up EFS in each Region where you call covered models:

  • Create an AWS KMS key and an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region. The key and bucket policies give Amazon Bedrock access only through its service principal and only for your account’s data.
  • Give your role permission to save the storage configuration.
  • Save your storage configuration. Amazon Bedrock checks your key and bucket settings before it saves, and the error names any check that fails.
  • Set your data retention mode to aws_review.
  • Call a Claude Fable model, then confirm that AWS CloudTrail shows Amazon Bedrock using your key. Retained records usually appear in your bucket within minutes but can take up to 72 hours if Amazon Bedrock has to retry.

The EFS documentation has the complete key policy, bucket policy, IAM policy, and API calls for each step. It also covers organization and project configurations, and troubleshooting. To use enterprise data controls instead, skip steps 1 and 2 and choose Amazon-managed storage in step 3.

Conclusion

The trusted access program API, now generally available, gives you one way to find model provider offerings on Amazon Bedrock, check your status, and enroll, with IAM policies and SCPs controlling who can opt in. EFS and EDC are the first offerings in public preview. They give you control over your data when you use Claude Fable and Cyber Verification Program models. With your own Amazon S3 bucket, Amazon Bedrock keeps no copy of the retained data, your AWS KMS key encrypts it, and every access appears in your own AWS CloudTrail logs.

To get started, check your EFS status with aws bedrock list-trusted-access-programs and enroll in the EFS preview. To learn more, see the trusted access programs documentation and the EFS/EDC documentation.

To enroll in the EFS and EDC public preview, work with your AWS account team to submit a request. Have the AWS account IDs ready (or Amazon Bedrock runtime project ARNs for projects) and note that the preview is for customers already enrolled in EFS ZDR.

item.title: [Together AI] Introducing preemptible compute: the same compute, half the…
item.description: Full title: Introducing preemptible compute: the same compute, half the price
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

GPU Clusters

Published 9/10/2026

Introducing preemptible compute: the same compute, half the price

Now in public preview for Together GPU Clusters: interruptible GPU compute, with a five-minute drain window and automatic refill toward your target.

  • AuthorsPavneet Ahluwalia, Varun Chakravarthy
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

Today we're announcing the public preview of preemptible compute for Together GPU Clusters, available on Kubernetes clusters in all regions. Preemptible nodes give teams a lower-cost way to run interruption-tolerant work — short experiments, inference bursts, batch jobs — on the same GPU infrastructure they already use, billed sub-hourly at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate. You can add preemptible capacity to a new or existing cluster starting today.

How preemptible compute works

Preemptible compute adds a second compute type to Together GPU Clusters. Standard nodes are fulfilled synchronously and are never preempted. Preemptible nodes use the same NVIDIA accelerated compute, draw from un-used capacity, and can be reclaimed when that capacity is needed elsewhere.

Preemptible nodes are billed at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate. The rate remains fixed rather than moving with a spot market.

When a node is reclaimed, the cluster follows a five-minute drain (maximum 5 minutes) sequence:

  • T+0 — the node is cordoned, a TogetherPreempted Kubernetes event fires, and your pods receive SIGTERM.
  • T+0 to T+5:00 — your workload has up to five minutes (terminationGracePeriodSeconds) to checkpoint and exit.
  • T+5:00 — the node is removed.

The cluster retains its preemptible target after the node is removed and automatically refills toward that target as capacity becomes available. You do not need to request replacement capacity.

Billing is sub-hourly, with usage metered every one to two minutes. A node that runs for 12 minutes is billed for approximately 12 minutes.

Preemptible nodes are not a separate cluster type. They join your existing cluster, labeled together.ai/compute-class=preemptible, so interruptible workers run on discounted capacity while coordinators, login pods, and serving replicas stay on standard nodes.

Where preemptible compute fits

The five-minute reclamation sequence makes recovery behavior the deciding factor. Work that can resume, retry, or requeue can use preemptible capacity while critical components should remain on standard nodes.

Short experiments. Ablations, config sweeps, quick fine-tunes, evals, distillation, and batch inference are good candidates when the work can resume from a checkpoint or retry after a worker disappears. Frameworks such as Ray Train and PyTorch Lightning resume from the latest checkpoint without intervention. As a reference point, a full weight model checkpoint for GLM5.3 Flash, 321B parameter model is roughly 3.5TB which would take between 22s to 4mins to write to a parallel filesystem even at degraded performance. Leaving headroom inside the five-minute drain window.

Temporary bursts. When batch or internal inference demand spikes, add cheaper preemptible nodes to absorb the burst and non-critical workloads instead of holding standard capacity sized for your peak or risking burst standard compute availability. Interrupted requests requeue; user-facing replicas remain on standard nodes.

The common thread: work that is chunked, checkpointed, or retryable. Multi-day runs without checkpointing and strict-SLO serving with no fallback are not a fit.

Together has a strong culture dogfooding , several internal research, dev/test and non-critical production workloads at Together are based on our preemptible compute based GPU clusters enabling us to leverage our spare capacity across product teams.

Before you enable it

  • Treat preemptible nodes as ephemeral. There is no minimum node lifetime during the preview, so checkpoint frequently and plan for capacity to disappear at any time.
  • Keep critical components on standard nodes. Coordinators, login pods, and user-facing replicas belong to guaranteed capacity — use the compute-class label to enforce it.
  • Use the drain window. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to as much as 300 seconds, checkpoint when the pod receives SIGTERM, and exit before the node is removed.
  • Clusters require at least one standard node, and nodes can't be converted between compute types in place.

How to use it

After the workload is prepared for preemption, setup has two parts: set the preemptible target and schedule eligible work onto the labeled nodes.

You can set the target when creating a cluster or on a cluster that is already running, using the Together Cloud console, CLI, or API. The API reports both the requested target, desired_preemptible_gpus, and the capacity currently live, allocated_preemptible_gpus. Because preemptible nodes draw from unused capacity, allocated capacity can remain below the desired target when capacity is tight.

On a new cluster

Choose your standard node count, then add a preemptible target on top.

tg beta clusters create \
  --name my-cluster --region us-central-2 --gpu-type RTX_6000_PCI \
  --cluster-type KUBERNETES --num-gpus 8 --billing-type ON_DEMAND \
  --num-preemptible-gpus 8 \
  --project-id <proj_id>

On an existing cluster

Scale up the preemptible target when you need additional worker capacity, then lower it when the work is complete. The cluster remains running throughout.

tg beta clusters update <cluster-id> --num-preemptible-gpus 16

Fig: Adding/Deleting Preemptible nodes to an existing cluster

Fig: Preemptible nodes follow the “gpu-preemptible-xxx” naming convention

Scheduling work on preemptible nodes

Target preemptible nodes explicitly:

nodeSelector:
  together.ai/compute-class: preemptible

Preemption notices are delivered as SIGTERM to the pod, as Kubernetes events (reason=TogetherPreempted), in the console's Event Timeline, and via the Together API's node_lifecycle_events — handling patterns are covered in the docs.

Preemptible compute is now in public preview on Kubernetes clusters. Slurm support, additional regions, and in-place conversion between compute types are planned next.

item.title: [Anyscale] Enabling Mid-Epoch Training Resumption with Ray Train
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Enabling Mid-Epoch Training Resumption with Ray Train

By Jason Li | November 24, 2026

Training failures are increasingly common at scale, and effective training infrastructure is judged by how quickly it recovers from them. Mid-epoch resumption lets Ray Train and Ray Data checkpoint your data loader alongside your model, so your restarted run picks up where its last checkpoint left off without breaking exactly-once training. Here's what it gives you:

  • Less repeated work: a restarted job picks up from its last checkpoint, instead of starting the epoch over.
  • Correct data coverage: every row is still trained on exactly once per epoch, even across failures.
  • Simple adoption: it works with your existing Ray Train checkpoints and requires minimal changes to your training script.

In our benchmark, with mid-epoch resumption, a training job that failed 75% of the way through an epoch achieved 9% faster overall runtime and 9% lower dollar cost than when it skipped batches to resume. The bigger your epochs, the more it saves you on failure.

Mid-epoch resumption will ship with Ray 2.61 and is currently available in the Anyscale Runtime starting with Ray version 2.50.

LinkThe cost of mid-epoch training failures

Mid-epoch training failures can be costly. Picture a run whose latest checkpoint was saved 75% of the way through an epoch, followed by a worker failure at 80%:

Mid-epoch training failures can be costly. Picture a run whose latest checkpoint was saved 75% of the way through an epoch, followed by a worker failure at 80%

The model restores from the 75% checkpoint, but the data loader has no record of where it was. The typical recovery approach is to restart the epoch from the beginning, but that has two costs:

  • Data imbalance: Previously consumed rows are trained on twice in the same epoch while the rest of the dataset is trained on once, which skews what the model learns toward that part of the data.
  • GPU time: Additional GPU time is spent training on rows that were already consumed.

Both of these costs grow with the size of your epoch. On a small dataset, replaying most of an epoch is a minor cost. However, on a dataset that takes a day to get through, a single late failure can cost another day of GPU time.

To avoid these costs, teams often fast-forward to where training failed, iterating past the batches they've already seen after a restart. However, with streaming loaders like Ray Data that process data on the fly and don’t guarantee row order, skipped rows still need to be recomputed, and fast-forwarding can't guarantee each row is trained on exactly once.

Instead, we require a data loader that keeps its own record of which rows have been consumed and saves it alongside model checkpoints so the two never drift apart. The rest of this post shows how Ray Train and Ray Data do that, and what it saves in practice.

LinkHow it works

With mid-epoch resumption, the restart picks up at the 75% checkpoint

The key idea is to track consumed rows rather than a position. Ray Data doesn't hand out rows in a fixed order, so knowing how many batches were consumed isn't enough to find your place again, but knowing which rows were consumed is. To make that work, every row needs a unique ID, each worker records the IDs it trains on, and after a restart Ray Data uses that record to skip those rows as it reads. Let’s walk through how Ray Train and Ray Data do this when saving and restoring progress.

LinkSaving progress

  • Record every yielded batch. Once you turn on data checkpointing for a dataset with a DatasetCheckpointConfig, every batch Ray Data’s data iterator hands to your training loop is recorded: a background thread writes the batch's row IDs to files in shared storage.
  • Commit at checkpoint time. When you checkpoint the model, you also call state_dict() on the data iterator. That call flushes any remaining row IDs, closes out the current set of files, and returns a small dictionary: the epoch, a checkpoint index, the path where the row ID files live, and the ID column name.
  • Save it with the model. You store that dictionary in the same checkpoint as the model and optimizer state, and report it with ray.train.report(). The model and the data loader state are committed together, so they always agree on what has been trained.

Each worker writes its own files, organized by rank, epoch, and checkpoint index:

ray_data_checkpoints/train/
└── rank=0/
    └── epoch=0/
        ├── checkpoint=0/chunk_0.parquet
        ├── checkpoint=1/chunk_0.parquet
        └── checkpoint=2/chunk_0.parquet

By default these files live under your Ray Train storage path and are deleted once an epoch finishes, since there's nothing left to resume within it.

LinkRestoring progress

  • Load the state. When the job restarts, your training function gets the latest checkpoint from ray.train.get_checkpoint(), reads the saved dictionary from it, and passes it to ray.train.get_dataset_shard() through the state_dict argument.
  • Load the consumed row IDs. Ray Data reads the row ID files for that epoch up to the saved checkpoint index, across every rank, and sorts them so lookups are fast.
  • Filter as you read. A filter step right after the read drops any row whose ID is in that set, using a binary search per row. Skipped rows never reach your preprocessing or your training loop.
  • Continue the epoch. Training picks up with the remaining rows. After that epoch ends, later epochs read the full dataset as usual.

Because the filter applies to the dataset as a whole rather than to each worker, the remaining rows are split across whatever workers the restarted run has. Restoring still rereads the input files, but reading and filtering a row costs far less than preprocessing it and running it through a training step.

LinkUsing mid-epoch resumption

All of this bookkeeping happens inside Ray Train and Ray Data. If you already checkpoint with ray.train.report, turning on mid-epoch resumption takes three changes: tell Ray Train which dataset to track, save the data iterator's state with your model, and pass that state back in when you restore.

import ray
from ray.train import DataConfig, DatasetCheckpointConfig, ScalingConfig
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer

def train_func():
    model, data_state = build_model(), None
    if checkpoint := ray.train.get_checkpoint():
        model, data_state = load_checkpoint(checkpoint)  # your restore logic

    # Change 3: resume the data iterator from the saved state.
    shard = ray.train.get_dataset_shard("train", state_dict=data_state)

    for step, batch in enumerate(shard.iter_torch_batches(batch_size=64)):
        ...  # training step
        if step % 100 == 0:
            # Change 2: save the data iterator state with the model.
            checkpoint = save_checkpoint(model, data_state=shard.state_dict())
            ray.train.report({"step": step}, checkpoint=checkpoint)

trainer = TorchTrainer(
    train_func,
    datasets={"train": ray.data.read_parquet("s3://my-bucket/train/")},
    # Change 1: track which rows each worker has consumed.
    dataset_config=DataConfig(
        dataset_checkpoint_configs={
            "train": DatasetCheckpointConfig(id_column="id")
        }
    ),
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=16, use_gpu=True),
)
trainer.fit()

Note: build_model, save_checkpoint, and load_checkpoint stand in for your existing model and checkpoint code.

Here's what each change above does:

  • Turn on data checkpointing for the dataset. Pass a DatasetCheckpointConfig for the dataset through DataConfig(dataset_checkpoint_configs=...). id_column names the column that uniquely identifies each row, here a column called id. If your data doesn't have one, see the requirements below.
  • Save the data iterator's state with every model checkpoint. Call shard.state_dict() on every worker each time you checkpoint. On each worker, the call makes sure every row ID that worker has consumed is written to shared storage. What it returns isn't those IDs but a small, JSON-serializable dictionary that points to where every worker's files are stored, so it's identical on every worker. Store it in the checkpoint directory next to your model before calling ray.train.report.
  • Pass the state back in on restore. Load the dictionary from the checkpoint and pass it to ray.train.get_dataset_shard. Every worker loads the same dictionary, so every worker can pass it in. Ray Train uses rank 0's copy to set up the restored dataset.

For a complete, runnable script, see the mid-epoch resumption docs.

LinkRequirements

To use mid-epoch resumption, there are a few conditions:

  • Every row needs a unique ID. Point id_column at an existing column whose values are unique and survive your preprocessing. If your data doesn't have one, generate_id_column=True creates one for you and removes it from the batches your training loop sees. Generated IDs currently only work with Parquet.
  • Only use row-preserving transformations. Stick to transformations that don't add rows, such as map, map_batches, and filter, and pass the ID column through to the end of the pipeline.
  • Checkpoints need shared storage. Row ID files go to your Ray Train storage path by default, so it must be cloud storage or a network file system that every node can reach.
  • Automatic restarts need fault tolerance. Set FailureConfig(max_failures=...) in your RunConfig so Ray Train restarts the run after a failure and restores the latest checkpoint.
  • Finish consuming a batch before you checkpoint. Ray Data’s iterator counts a batch as consumed once it hands it to your loop. If your framework queues batches before the model trains on them, drain that queue before calling ray.train.report. Otherwise, your data checkpoint will be ahead of what the model has actually trained on.

LinkEvaluating the impact

With the setup covered, how much does mid-epoch resumption actually save when a run fails late in an epoch? We benchmarked it on an image classification job. The setup is as follows:

  • Model and data: ResNet-50 (26M parameters) on a modified ImageNet with images up to 2048x2048, with 1M training rows and 50k validation rows.
  • Cluster: 16 A100 GPUs for training, plus 10 CPU nodes for Ray Data preprocessing.
  • Checkpointing and validation: every 50 steps.
  • Failure: a simulated failure 75% of the way through the epoch.

With this setup, we ran the same job twice: once skipping batches to get back to the restored position after the failure, which is what frameworks like Hugging Face Transformers do by default, and once with mid-epoch resumption:

MetricBaseline (skip batches)Mid-epoch resumption
End-to-end time594 s542 s
Cost$1.45$1.32

Compared to skipping batches, enabling mid-epoch resumption reduced both end-to-end job runtime and dollar cost by 9%. Without mid-epoch resumption, skipping batches still needs to read, preprocess, and transfer every row before the restore point, only to throw it away. Mid-epoch resumption still reads those rows, but drops them right after the read, before any preprocessing or transfer to the training workers. This is also why the savings grow with larger epochs and heavier preprocessing.

LinkSummary

Training runs fail, and the bigger the run, the more each failure costs. Mid-epoch resumption makes the data loader's state part of your checkpoint, so a restarted Ray Train job picks up where its last checkpoint left off, training on each row exactly once. In our benchmark, it cut the job's end-to-end runtime and total cost by 9% compared with skipping batches, and every row is still trained on exactly once per epoch. Mid-epoch resumption ships with open source Ray starting in Ray 2.61 and is available today in the Anyscale Runtime starting with Ray 2.50. For usage details, see the mid-epoch resumption docs. If you run into problems or have ideas for what we should build next, file an issue on GitHub.

We'd like to thank Justin Yu, who led the work on mid-epoch resumption, and our colleagues on the Ray Train and Ray Data teams for their reviews, design feedback, and contributions to this work.

Table of contents

  • The cost of mid-epoch training failures
  • How it works
  • Saving progress
  • Restoring progress
  • Using mid-epoch resumption
  • Requirements
  • Evaluating the impact
  • Summary

item.description: Full title: Zero data retention with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in beta
item.content:encoded:
Over the past few months, we've been developing Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) for our business customers. EFS provides state-of-the-art detection of sophisticated misuse, while remaining compatible with zero data retention (ZDR): neither Anthropic nor any cloud providers retain enterprises' data.

Since we announced EFS in September, we've been developing it further with over 100 of our customers—including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility (like healthcare, financial services, and law). Leading enterprises like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe have been evaluating EFS in private beta.

“As a company that runs critical infrastructure, safety matters as much to us as model capability. We need a solution that gives us strong safeguards while allowing us to keep our data in our own account. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards delivers just that.”

Noopur Davis, EVP, Chief Information Security and Product Privacy Officer

“At Stripe, protecting customer data is foundational to how we operate. Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will enable us to use frontier models with added protection against misuse. It will also let us retain conversation logs in Stripe’s AWS environment, with access and review governed by Stripe’s security controls.”

Matthew Kemelhar, Head of Security

“With EFS, customers can keep sensitive data in their own environments, protected with their own encryption keys, while still preserving the specialized safety mechanisms frontier capabilities require. That balance, keeping enterprises in control of their data without abandoning frontier-model safety, is critical to broader adoption of advanced AI in security-sensitive organizations like Cisco.”

Omar Santos, Distinguished Engineer

“Enterprise Frontier Safeguards gives us exactly what we asked for: our logs stay in a Wells-managed environment under Wells-managed keys. We keep custody of our data while Anthropic operates the detection. That split is what lets our teams put frontier models to work safely and meet our obligations to customers, employees, and regulators. We helped shape these safeguards because our industry needs them.”

Munish Kumar Sharma, Chief Information Security Officer

“Where we have regulated or highly sensitive data, having Enterprise Frontier Safeguards with zero data retention will allow us to confidently accelerate our AI deployment across those highly regulated and sensitive client engagements.”

Todd Lohr, US Vice Chair and Head of Client Technology & Innovation

“As a company that runs critical infrastructure, safety matters as much to us as model capability. We need a solution that gives us strong safeguards while allowing us to keep our data in our own account. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards delivers just that.”

Noopur Davis, EVP, Chief Information Security and Product Privacy Officer

“At Stripe, protecting customer data is foundational to how we operate. Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will enable us to use frontier models with added protection against misuse. It will also let us retain conversation logs in Stripe’s AWS environment, with access and review governed by Stripe’s security controls.”

Matthew Kemelhar, Head of Security

“With EFS, customers can keep sensitive data in their own environments, protected with their own encryption keys, while still preserving the specialized safety mechanisms frontier capabilities require. That balance, keeping enterprises in control of their data without abandoning frontier-model safety, is critical to broader adoption of advanced AI in security-sensitive organizations like Cisco.”

Omar Santos, Distinguished Engineer

“Enterprise Frontier Safeguards gives us exactly what we asked for: our logs stay in a Wells-managed environment under Wells-managed keys. We keep custody of our data while Anthropic operates the detection. That split is what lets our teams put frontier models to work safely and meet our obligations to customers, employees, and regulators. We helped shape these safeguards because our industry needs them.”

Munish Kumar Sharma, Chief Information Security Officer

“Where we have regulated or highly sensitive data, having Enterprise Frontier Safeguards with zero data retention will allow us to confidently accelerate our AI deployment across those highly regulated and sensitive client engagements.”

Todd Lohr, US Vice Chair and Head of Client Technology & Innovation

“As a company that runs critical infrastructure, safety matters as much to us as model capability. We need a solution that gives us strong safeguards while allowing us to keep our data in our own account. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards delivers just that.”

Noopur Davis, EVP, Chief Information Security and Product Privacy Officer

1/5

Now, we're opening up EFS in public beta. In this post, we explain how EFS works in more detail, how it stays compatible with ZDR, and how businesses can join the beta program.

How EFS provides automated safety monitoring with ZDR

Customers who rely on legacy ZDR are protected by Claude's classifiers: our real-time safeguards that screen individual requests to assess whether they might cause harm. But sophisticated attacks generally occur across multiple queries—and any single request might, in isolation, look harmless.

For example, our September threat intelligence report describes an operation against roughly fifty organizations in which an AI agent divided the work of an attack among many other agents running in parallel. It saved the credentials it had harvested between sessions, so that the attackers could easily resume their campaign. Viewed one request at a time, this attack would have appeared as separate, more benign tasks.

To catch attacks like these, we use a second defensive layer, known as automated safety monitoring. This layer looks for patterns of misuse across many requests. Through EFS, Anthropic can provide automated safety monitoring without storing any customer data. Instead, our automated safety monitoring system analyzes data stored entirely on infrastructure controlled by our customers.

When automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for you to review. These cases can be read from your cloud storage or through an API, and can be integrated with security information and event management systems. They do not include inputs and outputs.

Once it's set up, automated safety monitoring can help your team detect intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm (like offensive cyber operations). It can also help detect agents that take actions beyond a user's intentions, such as—in extreme cases—using a software exploit to access an internal database or external system.

Zero data retention and EFS

With EFS, you bring your own storage for storing inputs and outputs. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider keeps a copy of your data once it is delivered to storage you control. This provides you the following guarantees:

  • Zero data retention. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider retains your data. You bring your own storage and store your own data. Inputs and outputs are deleted promptly after they're written to your own storage. You configure your own access policies and audit logging, and encrypt safety data with your own keys.
  • No operator human review. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider personnel access your inputs and outputs. Only automated safety monitoring can access this data.
  • We never train on your data. Inputs and outputs are used only for automated safety monitoring, never for model or classifier training.

You can use EFS through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, or Claude on Google Cloud. When you use EFS through Amazon Bedrock or Claude on Google Cloud (Google Managed), it's operated by your cloud provider, and the end-to-end data flow stays within that cloud's boundary.

You can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage in your own account for your storage, depending on where you use Claude. Your cloud provider bills you for that storage as usual, including reads, writes, and key operations (plus any applicable network transfer).

Get started

EFS is available on the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Claude on Google Cloud. Support for EFS in Microsoft Foundry is coming soon.

Eligible customers will be notified with instructions on how to get started. Read our developer docs to learn how to set it up, and our security whitepaper (opens in new tab) for how the architecture works, or deploy it through consulting partners like Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] KPMG's Todd Lohr on AI when your data is also your clients'…
item.description: Full title: KPMG's Todd Lohr on AI when your data is also your clients' data
item.content:encoded:
KPMG is one of the world's largest professional services firms, with more than 276,000 employees providing audit, tax, and advisory services across 138 countries and territories. Todd Lohr, KPMG US Vice Chair and Head of Client Technology & Innovation, focuses on bringing AI to clients through products and platforms. He has worked on KPMG's AI capabilities for more than a decade.

Much of the data KPMG handles belongs to its clients, often in highly regulated industries. Lohr spoke with us about what that means for adopting frontier AI, how embedding enterprise safeguards can unlock AI capabilities and accelerate responsible deployment, and where Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will fit.

Why did KPMG decide to work with Anthropic?

We’ve followed Anthropic very closely since its founding, and its mission was intriguing from a partnership perspective because we share a lot of the same values.

At KPMG, trust is foundational. It's what clients expect from us across our core business of audit, tax, and advisory, and it's what underpins confidence in the capital markets.

What are frontier models changing about your business right now?

Ten years ago we were focused on using predictive analytics, machine learning, and bringing very bespoke applications of LLMs to our clients. The last three years have been marked by bringing general intelligence to both our clients and KPMG workforce. Now we're at another pivot point, where our strategy is to embed our industry and domain knowledge, like tax and legal, into AI platforms and products. We’re working with partners like Anthropic not only on how we help our clients disrupt their industries but also how we disrupt professional services more broadly.

Our tax business runs on Digital Gateway (opens in new tab), which we see as a market-leading platform for how we deliver services. With Claude now integrated into the platform, we’ve introduced Digital Gateway Powered by Claude (opens in new tab), bringing frontier AI directly into how we work and deliver for clients with greater intelligence, speed, and scale.

More capability means more value, but also more potential for misuse. How do you weigh the two?

I’m optimistic about what AI can bring to humanity and to businesses, from healthcare and longevity to agriculture. We’re already seeing AI create entirely new ways to serve our clients in all industries.

Healthcare is a good example. Emerging capabilities like ambient listening can generate clinician notes directly from patient conversations, and physicians tell us this type of tool could give them back hours each day. Clinicians remain firmly in the loop, and every hour they spend with patients rather than with systems is an hour that can improve care.

With that said, the same technology can create security and safety challenges. There are going to be people who use it for nefarious reasons. It’s critically important that as an industry we understand that, take an honest look at how it’s being used, and create a responsible, safe, and secure framework for how we deploy these technologies.

That’s why our Trusted AI framework (opens in new tab) is foundational to how we innovate at KPMG. As a professional services firm, we take seriously our responsibility to help organizations realize the value of AI safely and securely while preparing for what’s next. That includes rigorous testing, ongoing monitoring, human oversight, and independent assurance to help ensure AI systems remain transparent, reliable, and aligned to their intended purpose.

Additionally, we're using Claude Mythos to identify system vulnerabilities, and cyber AI more broadly to defend against them. This is an area where we’re investing heavily alongside partners like Anthropic.

KPMG had an early look at Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (opens in new tab). What was your reaction?

It was positive to see how much thought and intention Anthropic put into the safeguards and working with partners on the program. Specifically, what stood out was data retention: how we will be able to keep the data within our organization and still have access to frontier models.

That's critically important for a firm like KPMG because we are the trustee of our clients' data in some of the most sensitive, regulated environments. We want our clients and firm to have the benefit of the powerful combination of that data and AI, but we need to do it at all times in view of how our clients want us to use their data, and what we can use it for.

What will Enterprise Frontier Safeguards let you do that you couldn't before?

Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will allow us to move faster, with confidence, in how we're able to use AI and where we can use it. One of the key tenets of the safeguards architecture will be the ability for us to retain data in cloud infrastructure we control.

Where we have regulated or highly sensitive data, having these safeguards built-in will allow us to confidently accelerate our AI deployment across those highly regulated and sensitive client engagements.

How will the automated misuse review in Enterprise Frontier Safeguards fit with KPMG's own Trusted AI program and risk processes?

As AI capabilities become more powerful and autonomous, organizations need the ability to identify potential misuse, emerging risks, and unintended outcomes at a scale that manual processes simply can't support. Automated misuse review helps provide that additional layer of oversight by continuously evaluating how AI systems are being used and flagging signs of serious misuse for our team to review.

We see automated misuse review as a natural extension of our Trusted AI approach and an enhancement to our existing risk management processes. Combining automated monitoring, KPMG human oversight, governance controls, and independent assurance creates a stronger and more resilient framework than any one approach alone.

What do you expect from AI vendors when it comes to safeguards?

Trust is paramount to our brand. It's literally our business model. We’re not going to make a trade-off between AI capability and trust. We expect both.

The more capable AI models become, the more important those safeguards become, and strong guardrails are what give organizations the confidence to put powerful AI to work at scale. We have an expectation with all of our vendors that safety, security, the safeguards around the use of AI, and alignment to our Trusted AI beliefs and programs are central to how we work together.

We have to strongly prioritize safeguards in every aspect of our business, and certainly in our use of AI.

What would you tell other leaders weighing frontier models right now?

You need to use these models. I can't think of a business or an industry that is not going to have some level of disruption from AI. "Wait and see" is not likely a sustainable answer for most organizations.

So, you have to adopt and secure at the same time. Think through the safety and security aspects, define the guardrails, and put them in place so you can move faster through the enterprise. Most organizations aren't going to have the luxury of not deploying these models. But they're going to have to do it in a way that's aligned to their business strategy and goals and done in a safe and secure manner.

What are you building with Claude next?

We've already started to put Claude to work to build AI-native ways of working in our business, specifically in tax and private equity. We've also built frontier AI cybersecurity services, and we’re using Claude Mythos to look at vulnerabilities across the enterprise, and then using AI to quickly patch and secure the enterprise against them.

What you're going to see in the next several months is an acceleration effect. As AI enables organizations to identify vulnerabilities and risks faster, AI will also become increasingly important to responding at that same speed.

Learn more about Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) (opens in new tab), now in public beta. EFS provides state-of-the-art detection of sophisticated misuse, while remaining compatible with zero data retention (ZDR): neither Anthropic nor any cloud providers retain enterprises’ data.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] The enterprise guide to securing coding agents
item.content:encoded:
Shipping fast and secure

Coding agents likely write code and open pull requests at your organization already. For many leading enterprises, they are reviewing, testing, and merging it too.

For example, after standardizing on Claude Code across its engineering organization, Salesforce¹ reported:

79%

more pull requests merged per developer at Salesforce

5%

fewer total incidents at Salesforce

As agents do more, technical and security leaders must mitigate risks like prompt injection and privilege abuse with layered controls such as checked permissions and bounded environments.

The first two chapters focus on scoping the risk. We discuss the requirements every AI provider should meet and four agentic risks to mitigate.

The next three chapters focus on bounding the risk. We highlight the defensive layers you can deploy with Claude Code as well as how to centrally manage and enforce those controls.

This guide aims to provide a helpful agent security framework that can give organizations the confidence and trust to run agents effectively at scale.

The components of defending an AI agent: the model, the environment around it, and external checks on what goes in and what comes out.

This guide is written for organizations on Claude Team and Enterprise plans. If you reach Claude through a cloud provider such as AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure, the same principles and local controls apply.

01 Setting the bar for agent security

Six questions for every coding agent · Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider

“A CISO's responsibility in the age of agentic AI is not to achieve zero risk. Instead, our jobs are to make agentic risk legible and bounded. This way, we can deliberately accept what we can manage, so the business moves on our terms instead of around us.”

Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic

Six questions for every coding agent

Here are six questions leaders can ask when evaluating coding agents to verify they are enterprise ready.

Question to askWhy you should careGood answerWeak answer
Does the model refuse when it should?The model is the first check on a harmful request, making a bad action less likely.Refusal trained into weights, with published rates."Our system prompt instructs the model to decline."
Are actions automatically inspected outside the model before they run?External checks can catch when the model is tricked or using bad judgment.Static analysis of commands and a separate evaluator model. Prompt injection probes."The model is very capable."
Is blast radius bounded by the environment?This bounds the severity, and therefore risk, of an incident.Kernel-level sandboxing that admins can require and set to fail closed, or an isolated VM for each session. Egress allowlisting at the network layer."The agent is instructed not to leave the working directory."
Can policy be locked centrally?Sets minimum standards that can’t be undone by individuals.Managed settings with hard-deny rules a local user can't override.“Per-developer config files, and an honor system policy doc.”
Is the code the agent writes secure?Code volume is scaling and vulnerabilities can ship unless checks scale with the volume.Automated security review with a person approving high-risk changes.“The model is trained to write secure code.”
Can you reconstruct an incident?Compliance. Improving security over time.Session telemetry export, audit API (Enterprise), and named known gaps."Logs are available on request."

Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider

You already have a SaaS provider checklist with controls such as single sign-on, role-based access, data handling terms, and audit logs. Hold AI providers to a similar checklist. For example, Claude Code supports these security expectations through:

  • Single sign-on and role-based access control (Enterprise), managed the way you manage your other enterprise tools.
  • We don’t train generative models on code or prompts under our commercial terms, unless your organization has chosen to share that data with us.
  • Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (rolling out in phases) combines the privacy of zero data retention with state-of-the-art safeguards for detecting misuse across highly capable models. Data can be encrypted with your own keys and kept in storage you control for a limited time. Learn more.
  • On Enterprise, BAA coverage for the Claude Code CLI and the desktop app’s Code tab in local mode, once the HIPAA configuration is applied.
  • Encryption options on cloud platforms: customer-managed keys in AWS KMS on Amazon Bedrock, CMEK on Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry’s Hosted on Azure option.
  • A SOC 2 Type 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate in the Anthropic Trust Center.

02 Identifying AI-specific risks

Leaked credentials and privilege abuse · Unvetted dependencies and extensions · Data exfiltration · Prompt injection

Security and technical leaders are familiar with risks like leaked credentials, abused privileges, compromised dependencies, and insider threats. However the attack surfaces, velocity, and scale all change when it comes to agents. Let’s look at some of the risks.

RiskHow you handle it todayWhat changes with an agent
Leaked credentials and privilege abuseLeast privilege, short-lived tokens, keyless auth through workload identity or OIDC. Regular review of over-privileged accounts.Named accounts for people, per-workload identity for software.Credentials should be short-lived and scoped to the task or job, not the developer’s full access.The agent acts inside a developer’s session and most logs outside Claude Code only show the developer’s name.
Unvetted dependencies and extensionsPinned versions, review gates, two reviewers on manifest changes. Version controlled configuration.Agents add both vetted and unvetted dependencies faster than manual processes. Extensions instruct the agent the moment they connect.
Data exfiltrationEgress allowlisting at the network layer.A compromised agent can send data out through services you already allow. Unlike traditional malware, it can try multiple routes the attacker doesn’t have to proactively define.
Insider riskSocial engineering awareness training, verification, reporting paths.Prompt injection: The check moves to the tool call and the network boundary.

Risk 1: Leaked credentials and privilege abuse

Anything an agent can read, it can leak. That includes credentials like a long-lived AWS access key or GitHub token.

Anything the agent can do, a compromised or overeager agent can misuse. By default, an agent in Claude Code runs under the identity of the developer who oversees it. In the event of an incident, you may need to distinguish between agent and developer actions so you can appropriately respond.

Illustrative example of a pull request conversation. In the pipeline, the agent’s work arrives under its own name.

Risk 2: Unvetted dependencies and extensions

Agentic coding accelerates the rate at which code is generated and reviewed, which includes the speed at which dependencies are added and configuration changes are made.

When you ask an agent to add JSON schema validation, it will find a package, add the latest version, and have working code in minutes. That speed can be a risk if agents aren’t pointed in the right direction.

MCP servers, plugins, skills, subagent definitions, and a repository’s CLAUDE.md file are dependencies too, and they deserve the review you give a package. Unlike a compromised library, which waits to be called, they reach the agent as soon as they load. Their descriptions and instructions enter the context window before the agent has done any work.

On Enterprise plans, skill and plugin scanning checks third-party skills and plugins for malicious content when someone uploads or edits them in your organization.

Illustrative example of what an admin sees when skill and plugin scanning blocks a plugin on an Enterprise plan.

Risk 3: Data exfiltration

Every leak needs a route out. The challenge is a domain allowlist can't tell your account from an attacker's account. For example, if you allow github.com, then the agent can push to a repository the attacker owns.

DNS is a second possible exfiltration route that HTTP allowlists miss as data can be encoded into the names an agent looks up.

And of course once a token has leaked, an attacker doesn't need the agent's network at all. They can use the credential from anywhere, so egress filtering never sees the request.

Risk 4: Prompt injection

OWASP has ranked prompt injection as the top risk in every edition of its Top 10 for LLM Applications since the list began in 2023.

Social engineering and prompt injection work the same way. Social engineering gets past technical controls because the deceived person takes the action and the system sees an authorized request. An injected agent also acts with its own permissions with every log showing a legitimate request.

For a coding agent, that prompt injection can happen multiple ways including via:

  • Issue trackers and pull request comments;
  • Dependency READMEs and changelogs;
  • Web pages the agent fetches;
  • Responses from MCP tool calls;
  • Comments in source files; and more.

What a hidden instruction in a web page has to get past before it can do damage.

03 The judgment layer

Defending in layers · Understanding alignment training · Prompt injection probes · The auto mode classifier

Defending in layers

In Claude Code, a compromised or misaligned agent has to get past multiple controls and two layers of defense before it can do damage.

The first layer is judgment-based. These controls decide whether something looks wrong.

  • Alignment training teaches Claude to refuse malicious requests and favor cautious actions.
  • Prompt injection probes scan incoming tool results in auto mode before Claude acts on them and flag content that looks like an injected instruction.
  • The auto mode classifier checks most proposed tool calls against the intent the user stated.

The second layer enforces fixed boundaries by limiting what any command can do:

  • Permission rules, command analysis, and hooks check each action against the rules you set before it runs.
  • Sandboxing and egress allowlisting limit what a permitted command can touch and where data can go.

This chapter covers the judgment layer and the next will examine the fixed boundary layer.

Understanding alignment training

Claude is trained toward good judgment backed by a list of firm rules like don't write malicious code that can cause significant damage.

In Claude Code testing without production safeguards, current Claude models refused 81% to 85% of malicious requests while completing 98% to 100% of dual-use and benign ones, such as running reconnaissance tools or testing a site for vulnerabilities.

Claude is also trained to prefer cautious actions over irreversible ones, and to raise concerns or ask for guidance rather than improvise. Claude is trained not to act on instructions inside fetched content as if they came from the user.

Keep in mind, model alignment training makes a bad outcome less likely, but it doesn’t limit how bad that outcome can be.

Prompt injection probes

Claude’s prompt injection probe is designed to flag any suspected injected instructions in tool results.

The probe adds a warning beside the injected instruction to tell Claude the content is suspect and that the user’s original request is still the task. Warning and anchoring lets Claude use the content while treating the instructions in it as data rather than commands.

The auto mode classifier

A model that’s been convinced that deleting a directory is a legitimate task will delete it with the same thoroughness and competence it brings to everything else.

This sort of destructive, overeager action is exactly what the auto mode classifier was built to catch. For actions your rules and built-in approvals don’t already decide, the auto mode classifier judges whether the proposed action matches the intent of the developer’s instructions.

How the auto mode classifier decides whether a proposed action runs.

For example, a command that makes sense for "fix the failing test in auth_test.py" looks different from one for "exfiltrate the contents of .env.”

Tool results are stripped from the classifier requests Claude Code sends, so injected text can’t manipulate the classifier directly. If the action fits what the user asked for, it runs. If not, it's blocked or Claude goes back to ask the developer for permission.

Auto mode is now the default starting mode for interactive sessions on every plan. Headless claude -p, Agent SDK, and HIPAA configuration default to manual.

Auto mode is the default because multiple tests showed it catches more dangerous actions than human approval does. For example, in a controlled study Anthropic published in August 2026, 1,053 paid testers caught 13.6% of dangerous commands, and auto mode blocked 89% of the same commands.

Dangerous commands caught by human review and by auto mode. Source: a controlled study of 1,053 paid testers, who were blind to the specific behavior under test.

Configuring auto mode covers tuning the classifier and overriding its block and allow rules.

Approving high-stakes actions

Auto mode relies on classification systems and does not eliminate all risk.

Before rollout, identify high-stakes actions by asking, is this action irreversible, and would a single mistake cost more than having a person review every instance? When the answer is yes to both, require human approval.

For most organizations the list looks like this:

  • Production database migrations
  • Changes to IAM policy, and credential rotation
  • Edits to infrastructure definitions

04 Enforcing fixed boundaries

Setting permission rules · Bash command analysis · Gating actions with hooks · Containing agent actions with sandboxing

The judgment layer is good at catching novel attacks, but its controls are probabilistic, so each one has the chance of being beaten.

The fixed boundary layer can be made deterministic and sets an agent’s blast radius. Permission rules, command analysis, and hooks decide whether an action runs and the sandbox along with egress allowlists limit what can be reached and where data can go.

Their limitation is that they only block what you tell them to block, so they need to be set up with your environment in mind.

Setting permission rules

Permission rules come in three kinds:

  • Allow rules let an action run,
  • Ask rules prompt a person before an action runs, and
  • Deny rules block the action.

Claude Code first checks deny rules, then ask rules, and finally allow rules. This prevents an allow rule from creating an exception to a deny rule. A deny rule defined in managed settings can’t be overridden by any user or project setting. You want to avoid allow rules for any command broad enough to run arbitrary code, such as Bash(python:*).

Claude Code checks deny rules first, then ask rules, then allow rules, so an allow rule can’t create an exception to a deny rule.

Subagents inherit the parent session's permission rules and permission mode, so a broad rule written for the top-level session applies to every agent it delegates to.

Bash command analysis

Claude Code parses every Bash command before it runs. Without parsing, a permission rule allowing git status would also approve git status && curl attacker.example, and wrapping a denied command in a subshell would get it past the rule.

Claude Code splits a command into its parts and checks each one against your rules.

Parsing is deterministic, so the same command gets the same answer every time. Deny and ask rules apply to each part of a command in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.

Gating actions with hooks

A hook is a script, HTTP endpoint, or MCP tool that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed point in a session. Two that are particularly important for security are:

  • PreToolUse runs before a tool call and can block it, approve it, ask a developer, or (in headless runs) defer it for approval later. For example, you may want to block a commit that contains a secret.
  • ConfigChange runs when a settings file changes mid-session and can reject the change. This is how you identify when a repository or developer is trying to loosen a control locally.

Hooks sit inside the fixed boundaries rather than above them. A PreToolUse hook can block a tool call, but a hook returning "allow" can’t approve past a deny rule, an ask rule, or a critical-path deletion.

Hooks defined in managed settings run on every machine and individual developers can’t remove them. allowManagedHooksOnly goes further and prevents user, project, and plugin hooks from running at all, so a hook that reaches the agent is one your platform team put there.

Containing agent actions with sandboxing

Sandboxing is one of the most important ways to contain the severity of an incident because it limits the agent’s scope. But containing agents is easier said than done, as constraint and capability are often inversely correlated.

There are three main Claude Code environments: local, local with sandbox, and cloud.

We’ll discuss the default settings and how to consider which is appropriate for each of the use cases within your organization. The defaults can be modified and locked centrally, which is covered in the next chapter.

Local

Most Claude Code sessions happen locally via the terminal, IDE, or desktop app. By default, the agent can access anything on your computer that you can. In auto mode, the classifier reviews actions your rules and built-in approvals don’t already decide.

This is the least contained environment and appropriate for low-stakes, self-contained work. For most enterprise organizations, we recommend enforcing the sandbox for local sessions.

Local sandbox

The Claude Code sandbox isolates each shell command at the operating system level, so commands can only change files in the project folder and connect to sites on the allowlist unless an exception is approved.

Commands can change the project. Everything else meets a wall or a checkpoint.

By default, the developer or the auto mode classifier can approve agents to operate outside the sandbox or reach sites that aren’t on the allowlist if they deem it safe.

Using managed settings (more on this in the next chapter), admins can make local sandbox use mandatory, contain agent commands to that sandbox, and allow agents to only visit centrally approved sites.

Once you’ve contained an agent to the sandbox, you don’t want it to escape by accessing credentials by reading files outside the project. To combat credential leaks, admins can add Read deny rules for the organization’s credential paths and also set credential masking, which lets a command sign in without ever holding the real value.

Cloud sessions

Claude Code cloud sessions run on an Anthropic managed environment with each task getting its own VM. Not only does this contain where Claude can execute, it also keeps GitHub credentials outside the VM.

Cloud sessions suit work that reads untrusted content or runs unattended. That’s because they are isolated from the developer’s machine and internal networks by default, and VMs can be discarded at any time.

Anatomy of a cloud session: each one runs in a fresh VM, and GitHub credentials stay outside the VM.

When a developer creates a new cloud environment, Claude starts with a limited set of pre-installed tools and allowed domains, although developers can add exceptions. Developers must select what repos will be cloned over every session.

Illustrative example of the settings for a cloud environment.

Organization owners can set a default environment and publish shared environments with settings individual developers can’t change.

Developers can still create new environments and modify those environment settings. Organizations that need to lock this down host their own sessions, running Claude Code on infrastructure they launch and run, so they control the policy for those sessions.

Keep in mind, cloud sessions aren’t available to organizations that use zero data retention, the HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.

05 Enforcing policy

Central settings at a glance · Which settings apply

We covered the default settings in previous chapters. The table below covers two additional configurations.

We’ve labeled one baseline, which you should choose when you want to create alternative defaults–or a starting point that individual developers can add to.

We’ve labeled the other locked, which is how admins can lock in a set of rules that can’t be changed at the developer level. Locking a setting is what turns a written policy into an enforced security control.

This is not an exhaustive list of settings, but rather those that focus on the key dimensions for bounding agent risk.

Central settings at a glance

Local sessionsset in managed settingsCloud sessionsset in claude.ai admin settings
Is it allowed?Can be turned off in the desktop app (disableDesktopLocalSessions), not in the terminalCloud sessions toggle for the organization
How contained is it?Baseline: sandbox on for all local sessions (sandbox.enabled)Locked: no running without it and no unsandboxed retries (failIfUnavailable, allowUnsandboxedCommands: false)Baseline: Owners create shared environments with settings members can't change on the Cloud environments page, and pick one as the organization's default environmentLocked: run Claude Code on infrastructure you operate. On Anthropic-hosted environments, developers can still create personal ones with their own settings
Where can it connect?Baseline: a managed list of approved sites that developers can add to (sandbox.network.allowedDomains)Locked: only your list counts (allowManagedDomainsOnly). The list covers shell commands, so limit the WebFetch tool with its own permission rulesBaseline: Anthropic's trusted list by default (package registries, GitHub, cloud SDKs), or the network access Owners set on each shared environment (connector, GitHub, and Anthropic API traffic isn’t limited by this setting)Locked: use self-hosted environments (public beta), where your own network boundary limits connections. Anthropic-hosted environments have no organization-wide allowlist
What can it read?Baseline: Read deny rules for sensitive paths (permissions.deny)Locked: restrict file-tool reads to the project and block listed paths (permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories, sandbox.filesystem.denyRead)Baseline: the same Read deny rulesLocked: no full lock. Limit the Claude GitHub App to approved repositories to control what sessions can clone and push. Developers can still upload a local repository from the terminal.
What credentials can it use?Block credential files with Read deny rules and set credential masking (sandbox.credentials)Owners store keys as Network secrets on shared environments, never as environment variables.
Which connectors can it use?Baseline: an approved list that developers can add to (allowedMcpServers).Locked: only your list counts (allowManagedMcpServersOnly)Connectors the desktop app delivers skip this list and are limited in organization connector settings.
What can it do without asking?Baseline: managed deny and ask rules, with developers adding their own allow rules.Locked: only your rules and hooks apply, and bypass mode is off (allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, allowManagedHooksOnly, permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode).

Which settings apply

Managed settings can reach a session three ways: server-managed settings from the Claude admin console, an MDM or OS-level policy, and a managed settings file. Only server-managed settings reach Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions.

By default, Claude Code uses the first source that has a policy key. Setting managedSourcesBehavior to “merge” combines the admin sources.

By default, Claude Code applies only the highest-ranked source and ignores the others, in that order, with no warning. If your MDM profile turns on the sandbox and a managed settings file holds the egress allowlist, the allowlist never applies.

06 Getting started

The controls in this guide work as layers, each covering what the others miss. A pilot on one repository shows how the layers hold up in your environment before you widen the rollout.

Pilot checklist

Tier your repositories and run the vendor review. Rank the repositories the agent will touch by sensitivity, then check your provider against the requirements in Chapter 1.

Pick a repository from your lowest tier, such as an internal tool under active development. It should be busy enough to generate real sessions and low-stakes enough that a miss costs little.

Deploy a central policy baseline. Set sandboxing on in strict mode, deny rules on credential paths, credential masking, an egress allowlist, and auto mode. Set and configure a default cloud environment. Add the security-guidance plugin and whatever hooks enforce your non-negotiable rules.

Turn on the record. Enable OpenTelemetry export with tool content (beta), and make sure sandbox and egress logs are being kept.

Run for two weeks without changing the policy, so every result traces back to one configuration.

Review what the layers did. Look at classifier denials, sandbox blocks, unsandboxed retry attempts, and refused egress. Each one is either a control doing its job or a legitimate need the baseline didn’t anticipate. Add the allowlist entries the work needed rather than relaxing deny rules.

Score the pilot against Chapter 1’s five questions before you widen to a second team.

Done right, this secure framework will accelerate rather than slow your team’s ability to run at full speed with coding agents.

¹ Salesforce Ventures is an investor in Anthropic.
