item.description: Full title: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation
item.content:encoded:
RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

Enterprise Article

Published November 23, 2026

🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark

Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes.

One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking. Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions.

Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice.

We introduce RoboTrack, a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces, Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M, a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.

RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos.

Our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks.

Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results.

RoboTrack-Bench: A benchmark for point-tracking in real-world manipulation

RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views.

RoboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold.

Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data.

To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction.

Point trackers struggle on real-world manipulation

We evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better.

RoboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks. Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers.

RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around.

A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos.

These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare.

Note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols.

RoboTrack-15M: Simulation data from MolmoSpaces

Why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric, which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos.

This is where MolmoSpaces comes in—our robotic simulation environment at Ai2. We extend its existing manipulation simulations to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. In each episode, a simulated robot arm picks up an everyday object, such as a cup, a plate, or a block. Two cameras record the interaction: one on the wrist and one at the robot’s base, rendered in MuJoCo. Using the simulator’s geometry, object poses, and camera information, we calculate each point’s position and visibility in every frame without human annotation and filter out static points on the background and the robot’s fixed base.

The pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M for training. RoboTrack-15M has 3,000 videos from 300 simulated homes with 5,000 tracks per video, for 15 million tracks in total.

Data generation pipeline of RoboTrack-15M. Objects, indoor scenes, and robot grasps are obtained from MolmoSpaces. We use the simulator’s geometry and camera information to calculate point positions and visibility.

RoboTracker: Point tracker trained on simulated manipulation

We introduce two models trained on RoboTrack-15M, RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. Each fine-tunes an existing tracker on RoboTrack-15M together with its original training data. RoboTracker builds on AllTracker, a lightweight model with 17 million parameters, and RoboTracker-Warp builds on CoWTracker, a much larger model with about 1 billion parameters.

We’re releasing both model checkpoints so other researchers can inspect and build on this work. RoboTracker-Warp’s weights are for noncommercial use.

Adding RoboTrack-15M improves scores on robotics benchmarks. Compared with the released AllTracker and CoWTracker models, respectively, RoboTracker improves RoboTrack-Bench by 0.8 AJ (62.6 to 63.4) and RoboTracker-Warp by 2.1 AJ (63.9 to 66.0), with gains of up to 1.2 AJ averaged across the three robotics benchmarks. On general video benchmarks, both models perform on par with their base models. Overall, RoboTracker-Warp has the highest AJ of the models we evaluated on four of the five benchmarks. The exception is DAVIS, where BootsTAPNext and CoWTracker score slightly higher.

Improvements from fine-tuning on RoboTrack-15M, for AllTracker (RoboTracker) and CoWTracker (RoboTracker-Warp). The robotics average is taken over RoboTrack-Bench, RoboTAP, and RGB-Stacking.

Results on RoboTrack-Bench by video source.

Breaking the gains down by source shows where they come from. RoboTracker-Warp improves on every source by roughly 1 to 3 AJ, including the human footage from EgoVerse and Ego-Exo4D, even though RoboTrack-15M contains only robot arms. RoboTracker’s gains are smaller and come mostly from robot footage—clearest on DROID Franka and EgoVerse EVA.

What makes good simulation data for point tracking?

RoboTrack-15M is the result of multiple iterations and experiments with our synthetic data. In fact, our first attempt didn’t bring any gain on RoboTrack-Bench. To find out why, we looked at a simple question: how far do the tracked points move compared with real manipulation videos? We plot this as a histogram for each version of our data and measure its distance from RoboTrack-Bench (figure below).

How far points move in each version of our training data compared with RoboTrack-Bench, for third-person (top) and first-person (bottom) views. Distance is the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between the two histograms, with 0 indicating identical histograms. Kubric has one camera type, so the same clips appear in both rows. AJ is measured on the full RoboTrack-Bench.

The histograms made it clear what was going wrong. Our first version picked points anywhere in the frame, including walls, floors, and furniture, so most points seen from the fixed third-person camera never moved. To address this, we next sampled points only on the robot and the objects it handles, which brought the wrist view close to real video and raised the score. Interestingly, we found that Kubric had the same mismatch in the wrist view, which likely explains why it alone isn’t enough for the varied viewpoints of robotic manipulation. Finally, we moved points from the robot’s fixed base and mounting platform onto the moving arm, which brings our third-person view in line with real video as well and raises the ablation score to 63.0 AJ, 1.5 points above the Kubric-only control.

Application: Robotic manipulation using point tracking

Our wet-lab pipeline for guiding the robot with point tracks from a single demonstration.

What does better point tracking mean for robotics? Many robotic systems have found point tracks useful as a compact representation of how objects move that can guide a policy directly. To see this in practice, we built a similar system for a wet-lab task: pipetting liquid from one vial to another.

Here, a robot arm picks up an electronic pipette, draws liquid from the first vial, dispenses it into the second, and returns the pipette to its holder. The task is challenging because the pipette tip has to line up with the vial opening within millimeters, and the robot needs to adjust to different layouts of vials in each trial.

Following RoboTap, the robot learns the task from a single demonstration, which we record by teleoperation and split into steps. At test time, the robot compares what its camera sees with the demonstration and uses RoboTracker to estimate the motion required to align with the vial. Because the following motion runs without further feedback, the task only succeeds if that estimate is accurate.

We compare three ways of estimating where the vial has moved:

  • Optical flow (RAFT) matches pixels directly between the demonstration image and the live camera image.
  • Object masks (SAM3) find the vial in each new image and line up the center of its mask with the demonstration.
  • Point tracking (RoboTracker) follows points on the vial throughout the video, matching points in the demonstration image to the live image.

We ran each method on 20 layouts with the vials in different positions: 10 with a clear view and 10 with partial occlusion. Point tracking completed the full transfer in 17 of 20 trials, compared with 8 for object masks and 5 for optical flow. It succeeded in all 10 clear-view trials and 7 of 10 with occlusion, where the mask-based method succeeded only once.

The other methods fail in different ways. Optical flow breaks down when the vials sit far from where they were in the demonstration, and masks can latch onto a similar-looking object or lose the vial when it’s occluded. Point tracking, on the other hand, follows the same vial object from frame to frame, so it handles both large moves and partial occlusion. These results suggest point tracking is a promising tool for precise robotic manipulation tasks.

Success rate of pipetting trials with each method, with and without occlusion (10 layouts each). A trial counts as a success when the robot completes the full transfer.

Limitations and what’s next

We find the trackers still struggle with long occlusions, finding points when they reappear, and following small objects against busy backgrounds. Training on RoboTrack-15M improves performance, but these failures remain a challenge for real-world use.

Our simulations also focus on picking up everyday objects. They don't yet capture the precise movements involved in tasks such as pipette handling. A next step is to simulate these tasks more closely and test whether training on their trajectories improves tracking during deployment.

RoboTrack gives us a way to measure these failures and generate training data to address them. We hope the benchmarks, simulation pipeline, and released model help others build trackers that robots can rely on.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Can Claude Generate Images? Yes, with a Connector
item.content:encoded:
Can Claude Generate Images? Yes, with a Connector

OpenRouter ·11/23/2026

Claude cannot generate images on its own, because it has no image model. With a connector, it can call an image model and hand you the finished picture.

You give a short request, and Claude writes the detailed prompt and shows it to you before anything is billed. When the picture comes back, Claude can look at the result and check it against what you asked for. This post uses the OpenRouter MCP server as the connector, which reaches 74 image models from different labs as of November 19, 2026.

If you only want the setup, skip to How to make images in Claude with a connector.

Tl;dr

  • Claude has no image model of its own. A connector lets it call one and return a real picture.
  • Add https://mcp.openrouter.ai/mcp as a connector in the Claude app or Claude Code. Nothing is installed on your computer.
  • Name the model you want in your request, or ask Claude to compare models for your job first, which is not billed.
  • Our test images cost between $0.035 and $0.10 each on November 19, 2026, and you approve each one before it is charged.
  • The picture arrives either in the chat or as a link that works for 24 hours.

Can Claude generate images?

Claude cannot generate photos or illustrations on its own. Anthropic’s March 16, 2026 Help Center article says “Claude doesn’t generate photos or illustrations the way image-generation tools do” and notes that it builds diagrams and charts with HTML and SVG. Its vision documentation adds: “Claude is an image understanding model only. It can interpret and analyze images, but it cannot generate, produce, edit, manipulate, or create images.”

A connector is Claude’s word for an MCP server added to the app. The OpenRouter MCP server is one connector, and it reaches every model in the OpenRouter image catalog.

What does Claude do with an image model?

The image model draws, and Claude does the work around the drawing. With an image tool on its own, that surrounding work is the hard part: you write the detailed prompt yourself, and once the picture arrives you check it against your request and carry the file to where it belongs.

In Claude, a short request is enough, because Claude writes the detailed prompt. Name the model you want, for example: “Can you generate an image of a red fox reading a paperback under a streetlamp on a snowy night, in soft watercolor? Use Seedream 5.5.” In our run, Claude expanded that line into a longer prompt. Claude asks for approval before each image, and that approval shows the model and the prompt it wrote, so you can read it before anything is billed.

Claude can also look at the result. When the image came back in our Claude app run, Claude had seen the picture and described it.

In our Claude Code run, Claude opened the saved file and reported that the book was a green hardback where we had asked for a paperback. When that happens, a mismatch gets caught without you comparing the picture to your request yourself. When you ask for a change, Claude can pass the first image back to the model as a reference, and in our run the rest of the scene stayed the same. See Can Claude edit an image it generated? for details.

How to make images in Claude with a connector

Add the OpenRouter MCP server as a custom connector. It is a remote server, so nothing is installed on your computer. You need an OpenRouter account with credits.

In the Claude app:

  • Open Settings > Connectors and add a custom connector.
  • Name it OpenRouter MCP and set the remote MCP server URL to https://mcp.openrouter.ai/mcp. Leave the OAuth fields blank.
  • Add the connector, then connect it. An OpenRouter consent page opens in your browser.
  • Approve the dedicated key for this connection. It expires within 7 days, and you can disconnect at any time.

Some organizations do not allow custom connectors, so this option may be missing on a work account.

In Claude Code, run:

claude mcp add --transport http openrouter https://mcp.openrouter.ai/mcp
claude mcp login openrouter

The OpenRouter MCP server guide has the click-by-click steps for each client.

Which image model should Claude use?

Name the model you want, because no single model fits every job. We sent the same fox prompt to four models, at a 1:1 aspect ratio and the default resolution, to compare look and price.

Each row is a single measurement, as charged on November 19, 2026. Each model’s page has its current price.

ModelSlugTimeCost per imageSize
GPT Image 2.6 Flareopenai/gpt-image-2.6-flare26.4 s$0.0941024×1024
Seedream 5.5bytedance-seed/seedream-5-520.9 s$0.0352048×2048
MAI-Image-2.7microsoft/mai-image-2.734.0 s$0.0351024×1024
Nano Banana 2.1google/gemini-nano-banana-2.113.2 s$0.0401024×1024

The most expensive image cost more than twice the cheapest ($0.094 against $0.035), and Seedream 5.5 was tied for the lowest price while returning the largest image. Three of the four models added text we did not ask for, such as a book title or a hanging sign, so add “no text” to your request. For a wider comparison, read image generation models compared.

You can ask Claude to compare models for your job before spending anything, because looking up models is not billed. When we asked which model to use for product photos on a plain white background, Claude recommended Nano Banana 2.1 from five options, gave a reason and a caveat for each, and said the shortlist came from catalog data and not from test images. It offered to run paid tests on the top three once we agreed.

If you name no model, Claude chooses one itself. In our Claude Code run it picked FLUX 3 Image, and in one Claude app run it picked an older model.

What does it cost?

Each image costs the price of the model that makes it, which was $0.035 to $0.10 in our runs on November 19, 2026. Claude’s own usage is separate.

Aspect ratio and resolution change the price. GPT Image 2.6 Flare cost $0.058 at 16:9 against $0.094 at 1:1, and FLUX 3 Image cost $0.10 at 16:9 and 2K resolution (2736×1536).

The connector’s key starts with a $10 spend cap that you can edit on the consent screen. In our runs Claude also repeated each image’s cost in its reply.

Why does the image sometimes come back as a link?

The generate-image tool returns a link when one can be issued, and the image itself otherwise. A link opens in any browser, without signing in, for 24 hours.

In the Claude app, an image shows in the chat and Claude can see it. A link opens in your browser, and in our run Claude had not seen that picture and could not show it in the chat. In Claude Code, a link is the easier case, because the image downloads straight into your project. An image that comes back directly stays in Claude Code’s own folder until you approve copying it.

Which one you get varied between requests, even for the same model. In our small set of runs on November 19, 2026, Seedream 5.5 returned the image itself 4 of 4 times, GPT Image 2.6 Flare returned a link 3 of 4 times, FLUX 3 Image returned a link 2 of 2 times, and Nano Banana 2.1 returned each once. If you want the picture inside the Claude app, Seedream 5.5 did that every time for us. If you get a link, open it.

Can Claude Code generate images?

Yes. Claude Code generates images with the same connector and puts them straight into your project. Say where to save the file and which page uses it, for example: “This landing page needs a hero illustration. Use OpenRouter to generate one: a red fox reading a paperback under a streetlamp on a snowy night, soft watercolor style. Save it to assets/hero.png and add it to index.html.”

In our run, Claude Code saved a 2736×1536 illustration from FLUX 3 Image at that path and added it to the page. For the full recipe, follow the cookbook Generate and Edit Images from Claude Code.

Can Claude edit an image it generated?

Yes, when the first result came back as a link and the model accepts image input. Claude passes that link back to the model as a reference, along with the changes you asked for.

In our Claude Code session, we asked for a red scarf on the fox and a paperback with a plain red cover, saved over the same file. Claude sent the first image back to FLUX 3 Image, and both changes appeared while the rest of the scene stayed the same.

Without a link, Claude cannot reuse the picture. In the Claude app, after a result that came back as the image itself, asking for a red scarf produced a new picture from a description. The scene changed, and Claude said so.

Frequently asked questions

Can Claude create real images?

Not on its own. Without a connector, Claude builds diagrams and charts in HTML and SVG. With a connector such as the OpenRouter MCP server, it calls an image model and returns a real picture.

Why can’t Claude generate images?

Claude has no image generation model. Anthropic’s documentation describes it as “an image understanding model only”, so it can read the pictures you give it, and drawing one takes a separate image model, which a connector provides.

Does Claude generate images like an image generator does?

No. The image model draws, and Claude writes the prompt from your request and can check the result.

Can Claude generate videos?

We did not test video for this post. The OpenRouter MCP connector also has generate-video, generate-speech and transcribe-audio tools, and they come with the same setup.

Next steps

Connect it to the Claude app or Claude Code and generate your first image:

  • The OpenRouter MCP server guide has the setup for each client and the full tool list.
  • The cookbook Generate and Edit Images from Claude Code is the recipe for project images.
  • The image models on OpenRouter page has current prices.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
item.content:encoded:
Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers

OpenRouter ·11/22/2026

Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them.

These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below.

As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions:

  • Off-boarded three providers from OpenRouter, based on the results of our investigations.
  • Removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility. The removals included providers flagged by researchers, plus additional endpoints that we removed as a precautionary measure.
  • Notified all potentially affected customers.

The following work is underway:

  • We are adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis.
  • We are conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties.
  • We are requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.

We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it.

Provider security announcements

  • Novita: Privacy notice regarding MiniMax requests on Novita
  • Phala: November preliminary incident report
  • Together: Security event: prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026

Not all affected providers have posted publicly. We have notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. We are encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and will keep this list updated.

item.title: [Together AI] Security event: Prompt leakage for requests in June and July…
item.description: Full title: Security event: Prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Company

Published 11/21/2026

Security event: Prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026

  • AuthorsVipul Ved Prakash
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

We are notifying customers about a security incident involving a subset of prompts submitted to Together AI’s serverless inference service in June and July 2026. An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after a credential for a private repository was exposed in a public code repository.

We apologize for this incident. We are reviewing the affected data to determine what information was exposed and which customers require direct notification.

What happened

As part of routine software testing, we collected prompt samples authorized for that use and stored them in a private Hugging Face repository. The samples came from requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.

During development of our public GitHub repository, xorl, an AI coding agent committed a credential that provided access to the private Hugging Face repository. Our automated scanning detected the exposed credential, and we reverted the commit.

During the exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored prompt samples. The party subsequently searched those samples for credentials to other services and tested whether those credentials were valid. Five of the credentials tested were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment.

We have no reason to believe the unauthorized party has leaked this data further and understand that it has now been deleted.

Investigation and scope

We have worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement to investigate the incident.

Based on our review, we have not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident. Our review of the affected prompt contents is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed. We will contact affected customers directly as needed with the findings relevant to them.

Changes we have made

Following the incident, we strengthened controls around development workflows, credentials, and customer data. These changes include:

  • Using scoped or short-lived credentials, and keyless access where supported, to reduce the potential impact of credential exposure.
  • Checking all pull requests for credentials.
  • Making zero data retention (ZDR) the default setting for new accounts.
  • Updating our development processes governing the use of AI coding agents.

What customers can do

Customers handling sensitive prompt data should enable ZDR in their account settings.

If you have questions about this incident or its potential impact on your organization, contact security@together.ai.

Vipul Ved Prakash

CEO and Co-founder, Together AI

item.title: [Together AI] Qwen4 Max is live on Together AI
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Model Library

Published 11/21/2026

Qwen4 Max is live on Together AI

Alibaba's flagship Qwen model is 30% off through November 22, 2026. We gave it a bug report and the whole Tornado repository in one request to see what a 1M-token context window is worth, and what it costs.

  • AuthorsSonny Khan
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articleQwen4 Max in the playgroundQwen4 Max model pageAlibaba's announcement

Summary

  • Qwen4 Max on Together AI: Alibaba's flagship Qwen model is available on Together Serverless Inference with a 1M-token context window.
  • What we tested: Qwen4 Max took a bug report and all 344 files of the Tornado repository in one request, and its patch passes the maintainers' tests.
  • Sale pricing: Through November 22, 2026, it costs \$1.05 per 1M input tokens, \$0.0525 per 1M cached input tokens and \$3.15 per 1M output tokens.
  • Before you call it: Requests have to stream, and thinking is on by default, with thinking tokens counted as output tokens.

We gave Qwen4 Max a bug report and an entire codebase in one request. The codebase was Tornado, the Python web framework: all 344 files, 652,519 tokens. The model had no tools, and we didn't select relevant files or run a retrieval step first. Seventy-two seconds later it returned a patch, and the patch passes the tests Tornado's maintainers wrote for that bug. The request cost 69 cents.

It also found a precedent elsewhere in the repository. The bug report never mentions tornado/iostream.py, but the model pointed to code there that already handles errors the way its patch needed to. Tornado's maintainers cite the same code in their own fix.

Qwen4 Max is Alibaba's flagship Qwen model. It's live on Together AI today, and it's 30% off through November 22, 2026.

The test

Tornado is an open-source Python web framework. Its repository holds about 340 files of code, tests and docs. That fits in Qwen4 Max's context window, and it's far more than anyone would paste into a prompt by hand. We picked a fix the maintainers committed on November 18, 2026, two days after Qwen4 Max was released, and tested against the repository as it was just before that commit.

This is one example, chosen to show what a single call can do and what it costs.

The bug is in Tornado's websocket code. When a connection closed with messages still unsent, every write_message() call that wasn't awaited logged an error, even though awaiting it is optional. We sent every text file in that checkout as one prompt, with a bug report that describes only the symptom:

write_message logs "Task exception was never retrieved" when the connection closesWhen a websocket connection closes while messages are still unsent (for example, the client sends its messages and a FIN, or resets the connection, without reading the replies), every write_message() call whose result was not awaited logs "Task exception was never retrieved" at ERROR level.Awaiting the Future returned by write_message is optional, so an unawaited call should not log anything. A caller that does await it should still get WebSocketClosedError.

We asked for the cause and a patch. This is the request, replayed:

What came back

The first token arrived after 54 seconds, and the reply was complete at 72. Qwen4 Max traced the error to WebSocketProtocol13.write_message in tornado/websocket.py. That method wraps each write in a task. When the connection closes, the task fails with an exception that nobody is required to collect, and Python logs that as "Task exception was never retrieved."

The model's patch marks the exception as retrieved. Nothing is logged, and a caller who does await the write still gets the error:

-        return asyncio.ensure_future(wrapper())
+        task = asyncio.ensure_future(wrapper())
+
+        # Awaiting the returned Future is optional, so an error nobody looks
+        # at must not be reported as "Task exception was never retrieved".
+        # Retrieving it here leaves it in place for callers that do await.
+        def _mark_retrieved(t: "asyncio.Task[None]") -> None:
+            if not t.cancelled():
+                t.exception()
+
+        task.add_done_callback(_mark_retrieved)
+        return task

The precedent is what makes the patch read like it belongs in the project. The model's explanation says the fix should do what BaseIOStream.write already does for its own futures. That method is in tornado/iostream.py, one layer below the websocket code, and it solves the same problem the same way. The maintainers' commit makes the same comparison.

Nobody picked those files for it. All 344 went in, and the model found the two that mattered.

How we checked it

Tornado's maintainers added two regression tests with their fix: one for a write that isn't awaited, and one for a write that is. On the code before the fix, the first one fails. With the model's patch applied, both pass. We then ran Tornado's full suite, 1,673 tests, with the patch in place, and none failed.

What it cost

At the sale price, the request works out to about 69 cents, nearly all of it for the 652,519 input tokens. At list price it would be 98 cents.

Sending the same repository again costs far less. Together AI caches prompt input automatically, and cached input is \$0.0525 per million tokens during the sale. When we repeated a request of about 630,000 tokens, nearly all of it came back cached. The first token arrived in 8 seconds instead of 54, and the input cost about 3 cents instead of 66.

About Qwen4 Max

Alibaba released Qwen4 Max on November 16, 2026, and describes it as the most capable model in the Qwen family to date. It positions the model for long agent work, including coding across large repositories, which is the kind of task we tested.

Qwen4 Max is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 2.4 trillion parameters, of which 71 billion are active for each token. On Work360, Alibaba's own benchmark of industry tasks across 721 specialized fields, Alibaba reports that it outperforms Qwen3.8 Max overall, uses 35% fewer tokens at high reasoning effort, and costs about 60% less per task on average. Those are Alibaba's figures, and its announcement has the details.

Run it on Together AI

Qwen4 Max is on Together Serverless Inference under the model string Qwen/Qwen4-Max. This script sends a whole repository and a bug report in one request, the way our test did. You need the Together Python SDK (pip install together), a TOGETHER_API_KEY, a local clone of the repository and the bug report saved as bug_report.md. It sends every text file git tracks, so check the repository for secrets first.

import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

from together import Together

repo = Path("tornado")
bug_report = Path("bug_report.md").read_text()

# Every file git tracks, skipping the ones that aren't text
names = subprocess.check_output(
    ["git", "-C", str(repo), "ls-files"], text=True
).splitlines()
files = []
for name in names:
    try:
        files.append(f"=== FILE: {name} ===\n{(repo / name).read_text()}\n")
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        continue

client = Together()

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen4-Max",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"This is a complete repository, {len(files)} files.\n\n"
            + "".join(files),
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"Here is a bug report.\n\n{bug_report}\n\n"
            "Explain the cause, then write a patch.",
        },
    ],
    stream=True,
)

for chunk in stream:
    if not chunk.choices:
        continue
    delta = chunk.choices[0].delta
    # delta.reasoning carries the model's thinking, delta.content the answer
    if delta.content:
        print(delta.content, end="", flush=True)

Two things in it are specific to this model. Requests have to set stream=True, because Qwen4 Max on Together AI accepts streaming requests only. And thinking is on by default, so the model's reasoning streams first in delta.reasoning and there's a pause before the answer starts. Thinking tokens count as output tokens. To skip the thinking on a simple request, pass reasoning={"enabled": False}.

To try it without writing code, open it in the playground. The model page has the same details.

Available now

Run Qwen4 Max on Together AI

1M-token context, text and image input and automatic prompt caching, on serverless inference.

Open the playground

FAQs

How much does Qwen4 Max cost on Together AI?

Qwen4 Max on Together AI has a list price of \$1.50 per 1M input tokens, \$4.50 per 1M output tokens and \$0.075 per 1M cached input tokens. Through November 22, 2026, it's 30% off: \$1.05, \$3.15 and \$0.0525. Thinking tokens count as output tokens.

What is the context window of Qwen4 Max on Together AI?

Qwen4 Max has a 1M-token context window on Together AI. In our test, a request with 652,519 input tokens returned its first token after 54 seconds.

Does Qwen4 Max accept images?

Yes, Qwen4 Max accepts text and image input on Together AI and returns text. Send each image as an image_url block in the message content, as described in the vision docs.

Why does my Qwen4 Max request fail without streaming?

Qwen4 Max on Together AI accepts streaming requests only. A request without "stream": true returns a 400 error with the code streaming_required. Set stream=True in the SDK, or "stream": true in the request body, and read the reply from the stream.

How do I turn off thinking on Qwen4 Max?

Pass reasoning={"enabled": False} in the Python SDK, or "reasoning": {"enabled": false} in the request body, to turn off thinking on Qwen4 Max. Thinking is on by default, and it comes back in the reasoning field ahead of the answer. To get more thinking on a hard problem, set reasoning_effort to "max".

Does Qwen4 Max support tool calling?

Yes, Qwen4 Max supports tool calling on Together AI through the standard tools parameter. It can return more than one call in a turn.

Does prompt caching work with Qwen4 Max?

Yes, prompt caching is automatic for Qwen4 Max on Together AI, and cached input tokens cost \$0.075 per 1M at list price. In our test, a repeat of a 630,000-token request came back almost entirely cached, and its first token arrived in 8 seconds instead of 54. Caching is best effort, so not every repeat is cached.

Can I fine-tune Qwen4 Max or run it on a dedicated endpoint?

No, Qwen4 Max is serverless only on Together AI today, and it isn't available for fine-tuning. Alibaba says smaller open-weight models from the Qwen4 series will follow.

item.description: Full title: Anthropic announces closing of initial public offering, including full exercise of underwriters’ option to purchase additional shares, and closing of concurrent private placement
item.content:encoded:
Today Anthropic, PBC announced the closing of its initial public offering of an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at a public offering price of $83.00 per share, including the full exercise by the underwriters of their option to purchase an additional 147,000,000 shares of Class A common stock from Anthropic at the initial public offering price. The offering consisted of 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares sold by certain selling stockholders. The aggregate gross proceeds from the offering, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses, were approximately $93.5 billion, of which approximately $91.6 billion was received by Anthropic. Anthropic did not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders.

Anthropic’s Class A common stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19, 2026 under the symbol “ANT.”

In addition to the shares of Class A common stock sold in the initial public offering, Anthropic closed the concurrent sale of an aggregate of 313,253,007 shares of Class N common stock to Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC, Micron Technology, Inc., Microsoft Corporation, NVIDIA Corporation, and TSMC Partners, Ltd. at the public offering price of $83.00 per share, in a private placement for an aggregate purchase price of approximately $26.0 billion. The sale of these shares of Class N common stock was not registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”). Aggregate gross proceeds from the initial public offering, including the shares sold by the selling stockholders, and the concurrent private placement were approximately $119.5 billion, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses.

Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC and Morgan Stanley acted as lead book-running managers for the offering. J.P. Morgan, Citigroup, Barclays, Wells Fargo Securities, BofA Securities, Deutsche Bank Securities, RBC Capital Markets, and UBS Investment Bank acted as book-running managers for the offering. BMO Capital Markets, BNP Paribas, Credit Agricole CIB, Jefferies, Mizuho, MUFG, and TD Securities acted as additional book-running managers for the offering. BTIG, Cantor, Capital One Securities, Macquarie Capital, and Societe Generale acted as co-managers for the offering.

A registration statement relating to these securities was declared effective by the Securities and Exchange Commission on November 18, 2026, and a related registration statement filed pursuant to Rule 462(b) under the Securities Act became effective upon filing on November 18, 2026. The offering was made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the final prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014, or by email at prospectus@morganstanley.com.

Today’s announcement does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy these securities, nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

item.title: [Meta Llama] Advancing Science Together: Highlights From the Open Source…
item.description: Full title: Advancing Science Together: Highlights From the Open Source AI for Science Summit
item.content:encoded:
Meta

https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Highlights-From-the-Open-Source-AI-For-Science-Summit_Header.mp4

Takeaways

  • Last month, we brought researchers from universities, hospitals, and industry together for the Open Source AI for Science Summit, an event built around using open source AI to accelerate scientific discovery.
  • Researchers at the summit shared how they’re using AI to better understand neurology, make chemistry more accessible, advance drug discovery, and more.

From studying the brain to discovering new materials, open source AI is giving scientists new ways to tackle difficult problems. Last month, Meta’s Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) team brought researchers from universities, hospitals, and industry together at our Menlo Park, California, headquarters for the Open Source AI for Science Summit.

Over two days, attendees explored how openly shared AI models, tools, and data can advance healthcare, neuroscience, chemistry, materials science, and mathematics. Hands-on workshops also gave attendees a chance to collaborate directly with the scientists behind Meta’s models.

Here are a few highlights.

Advancing Medical Research and Real-World Applications

We announced an expansion of the Digital Brain Project, launched with the Rothschild Hospital Foundation and the University of Montreal. The project funds researchers to collect de-identified brain data and share it openly. We’re increasing the project’s data target from 15,000 hours of brain data to 25,000, to help researchers understand human intelligence and explore ways to improve neurological health.

Researchers are also exploring how AI can support greater independence for people with disabilities.The University of Pittsburgh presented an assistive-robotics system built on DINOv3 and SAM 3. The team plans to demonstrate a robot that can help a person eat and is experimenting with letting users give instructions in their own words.

Accelerating Chemistry and Bringing It Into Classrooms

Scientists use computer simulations to identify promising materials and medicines before testing them in a lab. At the summit, we released UMA Nitro, a faster version of Meta’s Universal Model for Atoms.

In a study with Carnegie Mellon and UC Riverside, UMA models identified many crystal forms of drug molecules without additional training data. Knowing a drug’s crystal form helps researchers understand how a pill dissolves. With the University of Chicago, we also showed how UMA can simulate entire enzymes, atom by atom, potentially helping scientists understand how they work and engineer better ones for medicine, sustainability and energy.

The same technology can make chemistry more accessible to students. UMA Playground transforms how we visualize chemistry, letting users build molecules, watch bonds break and form, and explore chemical reactions. Discovery Education announced that the tool is now available to high school chemistry teachers, with classroom guides. RealChem, a college chemistry course from Arizona State and Carnegie Mellon, plans to integrate it into student activities. Discovery Education reaches more than 4 million educators and 45 million students, while RealChem is used by nearly 100 institutions.

Making Math a Community-Driven Science

Checking a new mathematical proof can take experts months or even years. Lean, an open source language for writing mathematics, lets computers verify each logical step. That makes it easier for mathematicians to build on one another’s work, whether a result comes from a colleague, a student, or an AI assistant, without checking the same proof again.

This approach could enable larger, more open collaborations, like those that drive discoveries in physics and genomics. Through it all, we work hand-in-hand with the mathematics community to keep their research questions and priorities at the center. Mathematicians guide the work — they choose the questions and make sure the statements written in Lean reflect what they mean.

At the summit, FAIR researchers shared open source projects designed to support this work, including ATLAS, an open library that formalizes 26 open-access textbooks and more than 45,000 computer-checked definitions and results, giving researchers a shared foundation to build on.

By sharing models, code and research openly, we’re helping scientists and educators build on one another’s work. The summit showed how partnerships like these can extend AI’s impact beyond Meta — and create more opportunities for discovery.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Lo…
item.description: Full title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
item.content:encoded:
Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

Published November 20, 2026

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

What is new with Inkling 2 Mini?

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 312 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical* ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384. The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Each six-layer block has five sliding-window layers and one full-attention layer. The local window holds up to 1,024 tokens.
Attention uses 24 query heads and eight KV heads. It uses learned relative position logits, a learned sink, and an output gate. Full-attention layers use dynamic key and value convolutions.
The router selects eight of 128 SwiGLU experts for each token. It normalizes the selected scores and scales the weights by 8.
During passes 2 and 3, each core layer attends over two residual blocks from the previous pass. Four rank-64 gates mix separate messages into the query, key, value, and MoE inputs.
Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Benchmark Results

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

Inference Support

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

Transformers

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

Fixed loop with Inkling 2 Mini

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

Variable loop

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    text_config={"loop_num_passes": 2},
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

Images and text

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "/path/to/image.jpg"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?"},
        ],
    }
]

Reasoning Effort

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

Tool calling

Let’s get our model to call some tools.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")


def get_current_temperature(location: str, unit: str):
    """
    Get the current temperature at a location.

    Args:
        location: The location to get the temperature for, in the format "City, Country"
        unit: The unit to return the temperature in. (choices: ["celsius", "fahrenheit"])
    """
    return 22.0  # A real function would call a weather API here


def ask(messages):
    inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tools=[get_current_temperature], reasoning_effort="low", tokenize=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt"
    ).to(model.device)
    output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] :]
    parsed = processor.parse_response(output, prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0])
    return parsed


messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Hey, what's the temperature in Paris right now?"}]

reply = ask(messages)
call = reply["tool_calls"][0]["function"]
print("Model calls:", call["name"], call["arguments"])  # the model fills in the arguments itself

temperature = get_current_temperature(**call["arguments"])
messages += [reply, {"role": "tool", "name": call["name"], "content": str(temperature)}]
print(ask(messages)["content"])

# Model calls: get_current_temperature {'location': 'Paris, France', 'unit': 'celsius'}
# Right now in Paris it’s about **22°C** (roughly **71.6°F**).

Llama App and Llama.cpp

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

If you’re on Linux or you want to serve the model from the CLI, you can run the following command for the fixed-loop model:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF:IQ4_NL

To run the variable-loop model, you can run

llama serve -hf ggml-org/TML-d24-varloop-research-GGUF:IQ4_NL

To load the 8-bit weights, change the suffix to :Q8_0.

Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

SGLang

Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

export MODEL="thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path $MODEL \
  --served-model-name inkling \
  --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tp 1 --page-size 128 --grammar-backend xgrammar \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so

curl -s localhost:30000/health_generate && echo OK
curl -s localhost:30000/v1/models | python -m json.tool

curl -s localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "model": "inkling",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 24?"}],
        "max_tokens": 512,
        "reasoning_effort": "low"
      }' | python -m json.tool

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

Speculative decoding

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

Show SGLang benchmarking script

MODEL=thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini

for TAG in base mtp; do
  EXTRA=""; [ $TAG = mtp ] && EXTRA="--speculative-algorithm DSPARK"

  # Start the server (with or without MTP)
  python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path $MODEL \
    --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
    --tp 1 --page-size 128 --context-length 131072 --max-running-requests 64 \
    --port 30000 $EXTRA > $TAG.log 2>&1 &
  until curl -sf localhost:30000/health_generate > /dev/null; do sleep 10; done

  # Benchmark at increasing concurrency
  for C in 1 4 16 64; do
    python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --port 30000 --model $MODEL \
      --dataset-name random --apply-chat-template \
      --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
      --num-prompts $(( C*4 < 32 ? 32 : C*4 )) --max-concurrency $C \
      --output-file results_$TAG.jsonl
  done

  kill %1; wait
done

MLX

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

Here’s an example CLI invocation:

mlx_lm generate --model thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --image image.jpg --prompt "Describe this image.<|end_message|><|message_user|><|content_image|><|unused_200054|>" -m 1000

Demos and Vibe Tests

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

3D shader flythroughs

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Sunset Ridge (Inkling 2 Mini)

Over the Still Sea (Qwen 3.8 27B)

Show shared flythrough prompt

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Starry Night, Alive

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

Inkling 2 Mini recreation

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

Show prompt

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

Napkin to App

Input napkin sketch

Generated Trip Split app

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

Show prompt

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

4-bit Model

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

“Make yourself into a browser agent"

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

Wrapping Up

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!
