item.description: Full title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
item.content:encoded:
Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

Published November 20, 2026

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

TL;DR

  • We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself.
  • Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv and harbor.
  • Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency.
  • The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode.
  • All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection.

Table of Contents

  • Training inside agent harnesses
  • Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face
  • Testing the filters with short training runs
  • AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training
  • Training setup
  • Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one
  • Final results
  • Open question: What did the model really learn to do?
  • Closing words and future directions

Training inside agent harnesses

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Three sources

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

  • SWE-smith (Python, Go) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume.
  • SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove, turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs.
  • Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail.

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

Validation with openenv validate

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

  • The reference solution earns the maximum reward (semantic.oracle_max).
  • Doing nothing scores clearly lower (semantic.floor_gap).
  • No canary scores more than doing nothing (semantic.canary_floor).
  • A replay of the reference gives the same reward (runtime.episode_determinism).

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

Difficulty check with the base model

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

Testing the filters with short training runs

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

  • Unvalidated: 24 accepted tasks plus 8 that failed validation.
  • Validated: 32 accepted tasks, chosen without regard to difficulty.
  • Unqualified: 32 accepted tasks that the base model always or never solves.
  • Qualified: 32 accepted tasks that the base model solves on some attempts.

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

The dataset

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

SourceTask typeTasksQualified
SWE-smithInjected bugs in Python and Go717144
SWE-Gym (TaskTrove)Real GitHub issues13027
TasksmithGenerated from merged pull requests2422
Total871171

AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

Training setup

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Training infrastructure

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

Final mixture

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

safeagents in the loop

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

  • ⅓ (the average): each harness keeps only a third of its own update.
  • ½: each update at half strength.
  • 1 (the plain sum): every update applied in full.
WeightpihermesopencodeAll three harnessesTool calls per task
base model39.1%46.0%44.8%43.3%49.2
⅓ (average)49.4%51.2%47.1%49.2%35.6
½48.8%53.5%55.2%52.5%25.9
1 (sum)40.2%62.8%47.1%50.0%13.4

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Adapter merging evaluation results

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

HarnessBenchmarkQwen3.8-27BQwen3.8-27B-<harness>-adaptedQwen3.8-27B-super-adapterQwen3.8-27B, thinkingQwen3.8-27B-super-adapter, thinking
piSWE-bench Pro (hard 51)40.0%64.0% (−60%)46.0% (−73%)74.0%74.0% (−48%)
hermesSWE-bench Pro (hard 51)29.4%43.1% (−56%)47.1% (−60%)45.1%60.8% (−36%)
opencodeSWE-bench Pro (hard 51)35.3%51.0% (−72%)45.1% (−63%)47.1%66.7% (−31%)
piTerminal-Bench 2.140.0%56.5% (−56%)48.2% (−56%)52.9%57.6% (−25%)
hermesTerminal-Bench 2.144.7%58.8% (−70%)55.3% (−53%)58.8%63.5% (−19%)
opencodeTerminal-Bench 2.147.6%52.4% (−53%)52.4% (−68%)54.9%58.5% (−22%)

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

Final results

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training results

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

Evaluation results

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

Evaluation setup

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

Final evaluation results

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

Does the efficiency and performance ability transfer across harnesses?

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

Evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks and setup

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

Modelpass@1 (all assertions met)vs basePartial credit (share of assertions met)vs base
base23.0%62.2%
pi 16027.0%+4.066.2%+4.0
opencode 15025.3%+2.365.2%+3.0
merged23.7%+0.760.6%−1.6
hermes 16017.7%−5.356.6%−5.6

Open question: What did the model really learn to do?

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Closing words and future directions

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock

Kimi Code CLI is an open source coding agent from Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi series of open-weight foundation models. Previously, using Kimi Code with models on Amazon Bedrock meant configuring a generic connection “provider” with an Amazon Bedrock API key. For many AWS customers, this meant introducing an extra credential to obtain and protect.

With v2.7.0, Moonshot AI adds a native bedrock provider to the CLI. You can now configure the agent to use your standard AWS credential chain, including named profiles and single sign-on (SSO), instead of creating and managing a separate API key.

In this post, we show you how to connect Kimi Code CLI to models on Amazon Bedrock using your existing AWS credentials. We use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example, which supports streaming, configurable reasoning, image input, and client-side tool calling.

What’s new

Amazon Bedrock provides pay-per-token inference for a range of open and proprietary models from leading providers, available through standard APIs. Processing stays within the AWS data boundary, as detailed in the Data protection section of the User Guide. The model cards detail which APIs and features are supported for each model.

In older versions of the Kimi Code CLI, you could connect to Amazon Bedrock through a provider with type = "openai" or type = "openai_responses". These use the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions or Responses APIs, respectively. This approach required you to set the regional base_url and provide an Amazon Bedrock API key. The key could be short-term or long-term, but it was a separate credential for you to obtain and manage.

The native provider changes that setup:

  • Use your existing AWS authentication workflow. The bedrock provider can resolve temporary credentials through the standard AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) credential chain. You can use the default chain or select a named profile, including a profile backed by SSO.
  • Override the protocol for each model, if needed. The provider infers an API format and regional endpoint from the model ID, but you can change them as detailed in the “Override endpoint URL and protocol” section of this post.

AWS recommends short-term credentials over long-term credentials. This new path reduces reliance on manually managed API keys, but it doesn’t change your responsibility to protect AWS credentials and scope permissions appropriately.

How it works

The native provider handles authentication and request routing in four steps:

  • Resolve AWS credentials. Unless you configure an Amazon Bedrock API key, the bedrock provider uses the standard AWS credential chain in your environment. You can set AWS_PROFILE to select a specific named profile.
  • Generate a short-lived bearer token. The provider uses @aws/bedrock-token-generator to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, and renews it when necessary. You don’t need to place any AWS access key or manually generated Amazon Bedrock key in the Kimi Code config.toml. However, an explicit key given through api_key or api_key_env takes precedence if you provide it.
  • Build the regional endpoint. The provider resolves AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION and constructs the appropriate bedrock-runtime endpoint for the model’s inferred API. For Kimi models, this resolves to the recommended OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions path.
  • Call the selected inference profile. The model alias maps to an Amazon Bedrock model or inference profile ID. This example uses the global inference profile global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1. The global. prefix selects the profile, while AWS_REGION determines the regional endpoint that receives your request.

The CLI then streams the model response and can use the model’s client-side tool-calling support during coding tasks. Authentication, authorization, model access, and network connectivity must all succeed for a request to complete. The ephemeral API keys generated by the provider are valid for up to 12 hours or your AWS session length, whichever is shorter.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, we use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example model, accessed through global cross-Region inference for broadest availability and lowest cost. Review the Amazon Bedrock pricing to understand expected costs before using the model.

To follow along, you need:

  • An AWS account with access to the target model and inference profile in a supported source AWS Region. Check the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model card for current Region and inference-profile support.
  • Kimi Code CLI v2.7.0 or later. Follow the Kimi Code CLI installation guide and run kimi --version to check your installation.
  • The AWS CLI, to follow the profile and identity-check commands in this post. The optional aws login workflow requires AWS CLI v2.32.0 or later.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity (user or assumed role) with permissions to invoke the target model and inference profile in your chosen AWS Region.

The following example IAM policy grants the permissions used by this walkthrough, for the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model and global inference profile only. Replace ${AWS_REGION} with your source Region (for example, us-west-2 for US West Oregon) and ${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID} with your 12-digit AWS account ID:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "BedrockShortTermBearerToken",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "bedrock:CallWithBearerToken",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "bedrock:bearerTokenType": "SHORT_TERM"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "BedrockReadKimiK31InferenceProfile",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "bedrock:GetInferenceProfile",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock:${AWS_REGION}:${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}:inference-profile/global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "BedrockInvokeKimiK31GlobalProfile",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "bedrock:InvokeModel",
        "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock:${AWS_REGION}:${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}:inference-profile/global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "BedrockInvokeKimiK31ModelsThroughGlobalProfile",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "bedrock:InvokeModel",
        "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:bedrock:${AWS_REGION}::foundation-model/moonshotai.kimi-k3.1",
        "arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:${AWS_REGION}:${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}:inference-profile/global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "BedrockInvokeKimiK31DefaultProject",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "bedrock:InvokeModel"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock:${AWS_REGION}:${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}:project/default",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "bedrock:ModelArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:${AWS_REGION}:${AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}:inference-profile/global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

The foundation-model ARN without a Region or account ID is intentional and required for global cross-Region routing. The BedrockInvokeKimiK31DefaultProject statement is only required if using the openai_responses protocol, not with the default openai (Chat Completions).

Security of your AWS environment is a shared responsibility. Review and grant IAM permissions according to the principle of least privilege, particularly for production environments. Consider using a dedicated IAM role for Kimi Code CLI, separate from your regular AWS activities.

Get started with the bedrock provider

After your prerequisites are ready, follow these steps to configure AWS authentication, add the provider and model, and send a test request.

Step 1: Configure AWS credentials

There are different ways to authenticate with the AWS CLI, depending on your organization’s setup. With Named profiles, you can configure multiple AWS contexts and switch between them.

For example:

  • If you use SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center, run aws configure sso --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME to set up a profile, then run aws sso login --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME to authenticate.
  • To use AWS Management Console credentials with AWS CLI v2.32.0 or later, run aws login --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME. The console-credential login guide also describes a credential_process configuration for tools that don’t support the cached login session directly.
  • Omit the --profile arguments to use your default AWS profile instead of a named one.

Whichever approach you choose, your session resolves to an IAM identity (user or role) that needs the Amazon Bedrock permissions from the prerequisites. A Region configured in an AWS CLI profile applies to AWS CLI commands, but you must still set the Region explicitly for Kimi Code in Step 2.

Verify that the AWS CLI resolves your intended identity. Omit --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME if you use the default profile:

aws sts get-caller-identity --profile YOUR_PROFILE_NAME

Step 2: Add the provider and model

  • Open or create ~/.kimi-code/config.toml in a text editor. If you set KIMI_CODE_HOME, use $KIMI_CODE_HOME/config.toml instead. If you have an existing file, back it up and merge these entries with your current settings rather than overwriting unrelated providers or models.
  • Replace YOUR_SOURCE_REGION with your supported source Region (for example, us-west-2). To use a named profile, replace YOUR_PROFILE_NAME and uncomment the AWS_PROFILE line: default_model = "bedrock-kimi-k3-1" [providers.bedrock] type = "bedrock" [providers.bedrock.env] AWS_REGION = "YOUR_SOURCE_REGION" # AWS_PROFILE = "YOUR_PROFILE_NAME" [models.bedrock-kimi-k3-1] provider = "bedrock" model = "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1" max_context_size = 1000000 capabilities = ["always_thinking", "thinking", "image_in", "tool_use"] The model alias bedrock-kimi-k3-1 is a local name used by Kimi Code CLI. The model value is the Amazon Bedrock global inference-profile ID. The example declares a 1-million-token context window and explicit reasoning, image-input, and tool-use capabilities. It omits api_key, api_key_env, and AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK, so the provider uses ambient AWS credentials. A configured Amazon Bedrock key would take precedence.
  • Save the file. The [providers.bedrock.env] table supplies configuration to the provider. It doesn’t export variables into your shell.

Step 3: Send a request and start a coding session

  • Run a small non-interactive coding request: kimi --model bedrock-kimi-k3-1 --prompt "Write a Python function that checks whether a string is a palindrome. Include a short usage example."
  • Confirm that the CLI streams a response without an authentication, authorization, Region, model-access, or network error. This request provides a more meaningful connectivity check than a provider status indicator.
  • Start an interactive session in a project directory: cd /path/to/your/project kimi Because you set default_model, the session selects bedrock-kimi-k3-1 automatically. Ask the agent to explain the repository or propose a small change. Review its proposed file modifications and shell commands before approving them.

Configuration best practices

At the time of writing, the native bedrock provider has several configuration considerations. These practices help you avoid ambiguous status information and mismatched settings.

Use the configuration file to set up the provider

At the time of writing, Kimi Code’s desktop and web provider-creation interfaces don’t expose all the provider environment fields used by this credential-chain setup. Edit config.toml directly to set up the Amazon Bedrock provider. For further details, refer to Model providers in the Kimi Code documentation.

Declare model capabilities explicitly

Kimi Code doesn’t auto-detect the capabilities of most models on Amazon Bedrock, including Kimi models. Check the Amazon Bedrock model card for each target model and explicitly declare its capabilities to let Kimi Code make use of them.

For example, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports always_thinking, thinking, image_in, and tool_use, but not audio_in or video_in, as reflected in the config.toml example shown earlier.

These declarations describe client behavior. You should only include capabilities that are supported for each target model and Amazon Bedrock API endpoint. Validate tool and image workflows for your application rather than relying on the capability labels alone.

Keep Region settings consistent and prefer cross-Region inference where possible

The bedrock provider requires an explicit AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION in Kimi Code’s config.toml or the shell environment. It can’t infer a Region configured only in ~/.aws/config or through aws configure.

When you use cross-Region inference profiles (with prefixes such as global., us., or in.), the configured Kimi Code Region controls the source Region that receives your requests. For more information, refer to cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

For workloads without data-residency requirements, start with the global inference profile. This model, like many others, is priced 10% lower for global inference than through geographic profiles. Review Amazon Bedrock pricing for current rates and geographic alternatives.

Override endpoint URL and protocol where needed

In some cases, the provider’s auto-detection might mistake the API protocol or target URL you want to use for a particular model. For example, you will need to set a different URL to use Amazon Bedrock through a VPC endpoint or the Mantle endpoints.

In the Kimi Code config.toml, you can:

  • Set the protocol field to openai (Chat Completions), openai_responses, or anthropic (Messages) to configure a model to use a particular supported wire protocol. See the model cards for which models support which APIs.
  • Set the base_url field to change the target URL, which must include any attached API path like /openai/v1 or /anthropic.

In the following example, we show a configuration to connect to the same model but using the OpenAI Responses API through an Amazon Bedrock VPC endpoint you’ve set up:

[models.bedrock-kimi-k3-1]
provider = "bedrock"
model = "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
max_context_size = 1000000
capabilities = ["always_thinking", "thinking", "image_in", "tool_use"]
protocol = "openai_responses"
base_url = "https://vpce-EXAMPLE-VPCEID.bedrock-runtime.us-west-2.vpce.amazonaws.com/openai/v1"

Treat connectivity status as a configuration indicator

In the Kimi Code desktop and web apps, the provider list can show connected for a bedrock provider. That status doesn’t validate the configured AWS credentials, IAM permissions, Region, model access, or network path. Don’t treat it as proof of a successful model request. Use the non-interactive prompt to test the complete path, and diagnose the actual response if it fails.

Cleanup

If you created a new AWS IAM identity or assigned new permissions to experiment with Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock, remember to delete them when you’re finished testing.

You might also want to revert any local Kimi Code CLI provider configurations or AWS CLI profiles you set up. You can even uninstall the CLIs altogether if they’re no longer required. See the uninstall guides for Kimi Code and AWS CLI for details. Remember that deleting the local AWS configuration or CLI doesn’t by itself revoke IAM permissions or an active AWS session.

Amazon Bedrock inference for the models we showed is charged on a per-token basis, so there’s no persistent cloud infrastructure deployment to clean up.

Conclusion

We showed how Moonshot AI’s native bedrock provider in Kimi Code CLI v2.7.0 connects to Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock through the standard AWS credential chain. You no longer need a separately managed Amazon Bedrock API key.

Amazon Bedrock gives you access to open and proprietary AI models from leading providers, through standard APIs. Its governance controls and compliance validation programs can support even strictly regulated workloads.

If you’re already using Kimi Code CLI and want to run inference on AWS, upgrade today and give the new streamlined authentication a try.

For more information about Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock, see our launch blog post and the Moonshot AI on AWS samples repository. To explore supported APIs and features by model, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To discuss your use case with the Amazon Bedrock team, connect with us.

About the authors

item.title: [Together AI] Qwen3 TTS is now available on Together AI
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Model Library

Published 11/20/2026

Qwen3 TTS is now available on Together AI

Keep one voice across your product, change its tone with a plain-language instruction and move it between 10 languages, with first audio in as little as 97ms.

  • AuthorsAnthony Ji, Charles Duong, Sebastien Beurnier, Sahil Yadav, Sonny Khan
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articleCompare voices in VoiceFinderQwen3 TTS model pageText-to-speech docsQwen's model card on Hugging Face

Summary

  • Qwen3 TTS on Together AI: Qwen's open text-to-speech model, on Together Serverless Inference and dedicated endpoints at \$20 per 1M characters.
  • One voice, many deliveries: nine preset voices that change tone and emotion from a plain-language instruction such as "excited and upbeat."
  • 10 languages per voice: every preset speaks Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Russian, Portuguese, Spanish and Italian.
  • Built for real-time voice: first audio in as little as 97ms, with HTTP streaming and a WebSocket API for text that arrives in pieces.

Starting today, developers can run Qwen3 TTS on Together AI, with first audio in as little as 97ms.

Qwen3 TTS is an open text-to-speech model that separates who is speaking from how they speak. You choose one of nine preset voices, and that voice stays the same while you change its delivery with a plain-language instruction, such as "excited and upbeat," or move it between 10 languages.

Together AI's inference team tuned the serving stack for Qwen3 TTS so that speech starts streaming quickly enough for real-time conversation. The model is available now on Together Serverless Inference and on dedicated endpoints.

Tell it how to say the line

The same sentence can land as good news or bad news depending on how it's said, and with Qwen3 TTS you decide which by describing the delivery in a few words. Here the voice aiden reads one line three times. The voice and the words don't change between clips, only the instruction.

aiden · excited and upbeat

0:02

"Well, that changes everything."

aiden · angry and impatient

0:02

"Well, that changes everything."

aiden · sad and disappointed

0:02

"Well, that changes everything."

The instruction controls the delivery, and the voice stays the one you chose. You can keep that same voice when you change languages too.

Keep one voice across 10 languages

Every preset voice speaks all 10 supported languages: Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Russian, Portuguese, Spanish and Italian. That lets a product keep the same voice when it moves into a new market. Here aiden, an English voice, reads the same order update in four languages.

aiden · English (en)

0:03

"Your order has shipped and should arrive on Thursday."

aiden · Spanish (es)

0:03

"Tu pedido ha sido enviado y debería llegar el jueves."

aiden · German (de)

0:04

"Ihre Bestellung wurde versandt und sollte am Donnerstag ankommen."

aiden · Japanese (ja)

0:05

"ご注文の商品は発送済みで、木曜日に到着する予定です。"

Supply the text in the language you select; the four clips above use separately translated text. Each voice also has a native language, and Qwen recommends using a voice in its native language for the best quality, so listen to the languages your application needs before you settle on a preset.

Choose a voice in VoiceFinder

The quickest way to choose a preset is to hear each one say your own lines. VoiceFinder lists the Qwen3 TTS voices, plays a sample of each and reads the text you enter in any of them.

  • Open voicefinder.together.ai, select Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B in the model menu and select Find voices.
  • Select Preview to play a sample of a voice.
  • Select Try custom text, enter up to 500 characters and select Generate to hear that voice read your text. Repeat with another voice to compare them on the same text.
  • Select Show code to get the request for that voice in Python, TypeScript or cURL.

The nine preset voices, with each one's native language and Qwen's description:

VoiceNative languageDescription
aidenEnglishSunny American male voice with a clear midrange
ryanEnglishDynamic male voice with strong rhythmic drive
vivianChineseBright, slightly edgy young female voice
serenaChineseWarm, gentle young female voice
uncle_fuChineseSeasoned male voice with a low, mellow timbre
dylanChinese, Beijing dialectYouthful Beijing male voice with a clear, natural timbre
ericChinese, Sichuan dialectLively Chengdu male voice with a slightly husky brightness
ono_annaJapanesePlayful Japanese female voice with a light, nimble timbre
soheeKoreanWarm Korean female voice with rich emotion

Generate speech

You need the Together Python SDK (pip install together) and a TOGETHER_API_KEY. This request sets the voice, the language and the instruction together, and produces the excited reading of the line above.

from together import Together

client = Together()

response = client.audio.speech.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B",
    input="Well, that changes everything.",
    voice="aiden",  # who speaks
    language="en",  # the language of the text
    extra_body={"instructions": "excited and upbeat"},  # how to say it
    response_format="mp3",
)

response.write_to_file("excited.mp3")

The Python SDK passes instructions through extra_body. If an instruction doesn't seem to change the delivery, check that the field is spelled instructions, since a misspelled field is skipped without an error.

Parameters for this model:

ParameterWhat to send
voiceOne of the nine voice names, lowercase
instructionsA short description of the delivery, such as excited and upbeat. Optional
languageISO 639-1 code for the input text, such as en, zh, ja or ko
response_formatwav, mp3, raw or mulaw. opus, aac and flac aren't supported
sample_rate24000 (default) or 8000

Word timestamps (alignment=word) aren't supported for Qwen3 TTS.

Stream audio for a voice agent

In a voice agent, speech has to start before the whole reply has been synthesized. On Together AI, Qwen3 TTS returns first audio in as little as 97ms, and it streams in two ways. The right one depends on whether you have the full text when you make the request.

When you have the full text: streaming over HTTP

With stream=True and response_format="raw", the speech API returns server-sent events as the audio is generated. Each conversation.item.audio_output.delta event carries a base64-encoded chunk of audio. This script receives the stream, decodes each chunk and saves the audio to a file.

import base64
import json

from together import Together

client = Together()

with client.audio.speech.with_streaming_response.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B",
    input="Your order has shipped and should arrive on Thursday.",
    voice="aiden",
    language="en",
    extra_body={"instructions": "excited and upbeat"},
    stream=True,
    response_format="raw",
    response_encoding="pcm_s16le",
) as response, open("order-update.pcm", "wb") as audio:
    for line in response.iter_lines():
        if not line.startswith("data: {"):
            continue
        event = json.loads(line[len("data: "):])
        if event.get("type") == "conversation.item.audio_output.delta":
            # Each event carries a base64 chunk of 16-bit PCM at 24 kHz
            audio.write(base64.b64decode(event["delta"]))

The output is 16-bit mono PCM at 24 kHz, and the instruction applies to a streamed request the same way it does to a complete one. To play speech as it arrives, send each decoded chunk to your audio output instead of a file.

When the text is still being written: WebSocket

If the text comes from a language model token by token, the WebSocket endpoint lets you send it in pieces. You open one connection, append text as it becomes available and commit when the input is complete, and the server synthesizes each sentence once it has the whole sentence. This script sends an order update in two pieces and saves the audio that comes back. It needs the websockets package, version 14 or later (pip install websockets).

import asyncio
import base64
import json
import os

import websockets

URL = (
    "wss://api.together.ai/v1/audio/speech/websocket"
    "?model=Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B&voice=aiden&language=en"
    "&response_format=pcm&sample_rate=24000"
)


async def main():
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['TOGETHER_API_KEY']}"}
    async with websockets.connect(URL, additional_headers=headers) as ws:
        # Append text as it becomes available, then commit once the input is complete
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "input_text_buffer.append", "text": "Your order has shipped. "}))
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "input_text_buffer.append", "text": "It should arrive on Thursday."}))
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "input_text_buffer.commit"}))

        with open("order-update.pcm", "wb") as audio:
            async for message in ws:
                event = json.loads(message)
                if event["type"] == "conversation.item.audio_output.delta":
                    # Each event carries a base64 chunk of 16-bit PCM at 24 kHz
                    audio.write(base64.b64decode(event["delta"]))
                elif event["type"] == "conversation.item.audio_output.done":
                    break
                elif event["type"] == "conversation.item.tts.failed":
                    raise RuntimeError(event["error"])


asyncio.run(main())

The connection URL carries the model, voice, language and audio settings (the WebSocket endpoint names raw PCM pcm), and the audio arrives in the same base64 events as the HTTP stream. The WebSocket guide lists every message type.

Get started

  • Compare the voices in VoiceFinder
  • Read the text-to-speech docs, the streaming guide and the WebSocket guide
  • View the Qwen3 TTS model page
  • Read Qwen's model card on Hugging Face

Available now

Run Qwen3 TTS on Together AI

Nine preset voices · 10 languages · \$20 per 1M characters

Compare the voices

FAQs

How much does Qwen3 TTS cost on Together AI?

Qwen3 TTS costs \$20 per 1M characters on Together Serverless Inference. The model is also available on dedicated endpoints.

How fast is Qwen3 TTS on Together AI?

Qwen3 TTS returns first audio in as little as 97ms on Together AI when you stream the response, on a serving stack our inference team tuned for real-time voice.

How do I control the tone of a Qwen3 TTS voice?

Send a plain-language description of the delivery in the instructions field of the speech request, such as excited and upbeat. In the Python SDK, pass it through extra_body. An instruction changes the emotion and tone of the voice and doesn't change who it sounds like.

Can one Qwen3 TTS voice speak more than one language?

Yes, each of the nine Qwen3 TTS preset voices can speak all 10 supported languages. Set voice to the voice name and language to the language of the text, and send the text in that language. Qwen recommends using each voice in its native language for the best quality.

Does Qwen3 TTS support streaming on Together AI?

Yes, Qwen3 TTS supports streaming on Together AI in two ways. Over HTTP, set stream to true and response_format to raw to receive server-sent events with base64-encoded PCM audio. Over WebSocket, send text in pieces and receive audio as it's generated.

What audio formats does Qwen3 TTS return?

Qwen3 TTS returns wav, mp3, raw (PCM) or mulaw audio on Together AI, at a sample rate of 24000 (the default) or 8000. It doesn't return opus, aac or flac.

How do I compare Qwen3 TTS voices before choosing one?

Open VoiceFinder and select Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B in the model menu. You can preview each voice and generate up to 500 characters of your own text with it.

Is Qwen3 TTS open source?

Yes, Qwen released Qwen3 TTS 12Hz 1.7B under the Apache 2.0 license. The weights are on Hugging Face.

Related articles

View All

item.title: [Inference.net] We made vLLM tokenization 120x faster with Elixir
item.content:encoded:
We’ve spent months investing in our inference routing stack, doubling down on a custom request router built in Elixir. This is the first in a series of blog posts discussing our progress and learnings in scaling to trillions of tokens a day. This post focuses on tokenizers and how we’ve managed to make SGLang 33x faster and vLLM 12x faster with tokenization alone.

#Why does tokenization even matter?

When processing an inference request there are 4 main stages before you get the first output token: Tokenization, Routing, Prefill & Decode.

Our routing layer makes decisions based on input context length. Knowing the length of the input requires you to tokenize it, or use a rough estimate (like one token per four characters of input). Once we’ve routed the request, we prefill and decode using one of the popular open source inference engines. All of those engines have the option to either: accept a chat completion or accept raw token IDs. Historically, we would depend on the open-source inference engines to handle tokenization, prefill and then finally start decoding.

How we used to route requests, sending the full JSON payload to the engines

Our routing layer tokenizes the request to get an estimate of how many tokens this request will take. Inference engines can process requests faster when you limit the input context length, and so knowing the length of a request allows you to route short requests to “short pools” that will provide performance gains, as compared to pools that are configured for a models full context length. The tokenizer we used for our production hot path is Toks (from Actual, Inc.) with the caveat that it doesn’t render chat templates and is written in C which isn’t natively in our routing stack and required work to integrate.

As we have scaled demand over the past few months we’ve pushed the open-source inference engines to their limits and now have internal forks of both vLLM and SGLang patching them for efficiency. We still run up against fundamental limits because their frontends are currently written in Python, a single-threaded interpreted language, meaning slow downs, GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) contention and more which all affects your TTFT (time to first token). Instead of sending raw JSON requests, you can cut down on the overhead incurred by tokenization being executed in a Python process by sending the engines raw token IDs!

#Tokenization Library Benchmarking

With that all in-mind we built ChatTokenizer to see how much better we could do!

~158K-token prompt with 8 vCPUs

Req/s by Prompt Size for Deepseek v4.1 Flash with 8 vCPUs

The graphs here come from our own internal benchmark of open-source tokenization libraries and seeing how they perform across different payloads and compute resources. Our methodology is in the appendix at the bottom of this post.

Our goal with the benchmarks was to see:

  • How does tokenization change with payload size? Does it back up the hypothesis we had that large context conversations cause significant slowdowns?
  • What is the best off-the-shelf option?

From the graphs you can see that vLLM and SGLang themselves are by no means the most efficient tokenizers. SGLang ships their own gateway, written in Rust, which is one of the best options (caveat: that it doesn’t tokenize images). Once we realized the gaps and poor performance of the open source options, it was clear that it was time to raise the bar

#What makes ours faster?

We’ve been advocates of Elixir and BEAM and have been using it in production since last December for our Router. Ericsson’s Open Telecom Platform (OTP) has been a fundamental reason of how we’ve managed to scale up to 100s of millions of daily requests. However, it is nowhere near fast enough to beat the other tokenizers here, so we decided to lean into Native Implemented Functions (NIFs) allowing us to use Rust, C & Assembly as part of the BEAM supervision tree.

The core of our tokenizer is still Actual’s toks which uses optimized assembly to produce token IDs that are 1-1 with Hugging Face’s tokenizers but at 13-151x the speed! Toks however doesn’t yet support rendering chat templates and images, among other features we needed internally. This led us to build a supporting Rust and Elixir library around it to handle those features and more.

elixir

{:ok, tok} =
  ChatTokenizer.load("moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro", revision: "6d0a0202956796543364d666ab19c6ad1a494ee1")

compiled =
  ChatTokenizer.compile(tok,
    # varies by model
    engine: :sglang,

    # usually passed to the engines
    default_chat_template_kwargs: %{"reasoning_effort" => "high"},
  )

#Headline Improvements

Each of the improvements below is explained in more detail later in the post but to prevent this from being super-lengthy here are the tl;dr’s for some of the big improvements we have made.

  • Deepseek v4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro chat templates were ported to native Rust with the Jinja/Python kept as references and validated with unit tests
  • A quadratic loop in the Deepseek encoders was removed and Kimi's repeated template pieces were memoized within a request
  • Token IDs are passed from C/Rust to Elixir as a binary of little-endian u32s rather than a list to avoid the overhead of passing around lists
  • Inline base64 images are found with a SIMD byte scan and handed to Rust as sub-binaries pointing into the original request rather than copying them
  • We avoid parsing the whole JSON body multiple times and instead extract only the fields that the engine needs

#Reading image metadata instead of the full image

Agent traffic is full of images. A single 1M token request with 8 inline images is ~30MB of JSON and almost all of that is base64. The naive path (which we originally took) is to parse the whole body, copy every image string out, base64 decode it and open the image just to find out how big it is, because that's all the engine actually needs to know to work out how many image placeholder tokens to insert.

So we stopped doing that:

  • Before we parse anything we do a SIMD byte scan (memchr) over the raw request looking for "data: strings over 4KiB.
  • Each image crosses into Rust as a sub-binary, which is the BEAM's way of pointing into the original request binary rather than copying it. In the JSON we swap the image out for a tiny marker (data:x-chat-tokenizer-ref,0) so the 30MB request parses as the few MB of text it actually is.
  • We read the width and height straight out of the PNG/GIF/WebP/JPEG header while it's still base64, never decoding a single pixel (and apply EXIF orientation where the engine does).
  • The model's own resize rules (Deepseek v4.1, Kimi K3, Qwen-VL, etc.) turn that size into the exact number of image tokens the engine would have produced.

Deepseek v4.1, ~1M tokens + 8 inline images, req/s with 8 vCPUs. Before vs after zero-copy images, against the SGLang gateway and vLLM and SGLang's own preprocessing. The SGLang gateway skips image expansion so its IDs don't match the engine.

That took us from 22.5 to 167 req/s on million token requests, and a single request on one core dropped from 240ms to 28ms. For comparison, vLLM and SGLang’s own preprocessing does 1.3 and 1.6 req/s on the same requests, roughly 2-3 seconds each.

#Only parse the JSON you need

The other thing that surprised us was how much time went into just reading a request to then throw most of it away;

  • serde_json checks UTF-8 on every string with a scalar loop, which was about a tenth of a whole chat request. We do one SIMD UTF-8 check over the entire body up front and then parse it as an already validated string.
  • Chat requests are mostly tiny objects (a message, a content part, a tool call) with a handful of keys. Hashing every key is overkill so for anything with 8 or fewer keys we just scan them.
  • We only pull out the fields the engine reads, and apply the engine's own request rules (like how vLLM pre-parses tool call arguments) in Rust, so the body is never parsed twice or re-serialized.
  • Text going into toks gets the same SIMD UTF-8 check. The standard library ran at ~3GB/s on CJK heavy prompts which was a fifth of toks' entire encode time.

Not everything worked. We tried parallel JSON parsing and parallel template rendering and ripped both out. Waking up threads cost more than the work they saved.

#While Under load

Benchmarking throughput is nice, and you can always make your numbers look many multiples higher than they will actually be in production. As part of building our library we tested how the long tail grew when under load asking ourselves, as a serving instance gets busier how slow are the slow requests?

Latency per request with all 8 vCPUs busy, ours vs the SGLang gateway. The dot is p50 and the cap is p99. Each prompt size has its own axis. Lower is better.

From 8K to 160K token prompts, on both models, our p99 is lower than the SGLang gateway's median. On Deepseek at ~37K tokens our p99 is 2.6ms while their p50 is 2.9ms (and their p99 is 15.9ms). This is thanks to NIFs being run on dirty CPU schedulers, a million token request never stalls the rest of the BEAM, and the router can keep routing while the tokenizer is chewing through large or many requests.

#How does this compare to the engines?

We took vLLM and SGLang's own request preprocessing (applying the chat template, parsing the body and then producing tokens), and benchmarked it in-process against ours.

Req/s by prompt size for ChatTokenizer vs vLLM and SGLang's own preprocessing, in-process with 8 vCPUs. Each prompt size has its own axis. Higher is better.

We're 53-181x faster across every size on both models. Now that we’re sending raw token IDs instead of raw JSON to the inference engines, we wanted to evaluate the impact this has on the inference engines.

Kimi K3.1 with ~37K token prompts, engine HTTP server throughput as concurrency goes up, with 4 API processes. Raw chat vs our token IDs. Each engine has its own axis. Higher is better.

Sending IDs takes SGLang from 31 to 1,031 req/s (33x) and vLLM from 43 to 505 req/s (12x). With raw chat each API server process flattens out at about one core, because tokenization runs in Python under that process's GIL. Running 4 processes only takes vLLM from 13 to 43 req/s on an 8 vCPU box, while sending our ids gets the same 4 processes to 505. This is the hot path change from the start of the post, we tokenize once in the router and then inference engine never has to do it again.

#Tokenization Accuracy

A core requirement for our tokenizer is identical output with engines. If the token IDs we send don't exactly match what the engine would have produced from the raw chat, the model is seeing a different prompt to the one the customer sent which could cause the model to behave in strange ways - when we dug into this most tokenizers outside of the engines themselves aren’t!

The tricky part is that tokenization isn't just running text through a tokenizer. Each engine renders the chat template and applies its own request rules first; each engine has its own weird quirks which produce slightly different tokens. vLLM for example parses tool call arguments and re-serializes them, so the JSON the model sees isn't byte for byte what the client sent. This is why we tokenize differently based on the engine we’re sending the request to ensuring that the tokens are correct for the engine.

What we mean by accurate. vLLM parses tool call arguments and the chat template re-serializes them with a space after the colon, so the prompt the model sees is not the string the client sent. A tokenizer that renders the raw argument string produces different token IDs. We only count a request as a match if every ID is the same, in the same order. Illustrative example.

Deepseek v4.1 with ~8K token prompts and 8 vCPUs. Share of requests whose token IDs exactly match vLLM's, against req/s. Up and to the right is better.

On every benchmark we also compared the tokens against vLLM's and on 100% of requests, at every prompt size, on both models our outputs matched 1-1. The others perform well on short chats but drift once requests have tool calls and longer conversations in them. At ~8K tokens the SGLang gateway only matched 16% of requests (which was expected as SGLang renders the template differently from vLLM), NVIDIA Dynamo 73% and HF transformers 96%. At ~1M tokens with images every other library matched 0%, and on Kimi K3.1 HF transformers renders the wrong prompt entirely because it ignores reasoning_effort.

#Additional Tokenizer Comparisons

Baseten wrote a blog post on how they sped up Kimi tokenization with their library, basetenkenizer, so we wanted to compare both libraries on Kimi K3.1. Their Rust tokenizer can't render Kimi chat templates so their production path renders in Python and then encodes in Rust. To keep it fair we compared just the encode step on their own API, with both libraries encoding the exact same pre-rendered Kimi K3.1 segments.

Encode only, Kimi K3.1. Req/s for ChatTokenizer vs basetenkenizer's encode_segments on identical pre-rendered segments, 8 workers on 8 vCPUs. basetenkenizer shown pinned to 1 core per worker (its faster setting) and with its default thread pools. Each prompt size has its own axis.

With 8 workers we're 1.9-5.7x faster than their fastest setting from ~200 to ~1.1M tokens.

#Agentic workloads and caching

A large percentage of our traffic is agentic, which resend the whole conversation every turn. So we replayed 8 agent conversations of 213 turns each, anywhere from 2K to 160K tokens per turn.

Multi-turn agent replay, req/s with 8 vCPUs. Solid is cold, outlined is with our segment cache on.

The segment cache is content addressed and shared across every BEAM process, so once a chunk of conversation has been encoded it never gets encoded again. After about turn 30, 98-99% of tokens come straight from the cache. The gain is "only" 1.2-1.8x because even a fully cached turn still has to parse the request and render the whole conversation, and that grows every single turn which is still a bottleneck we want to solve!

#What’s next?

Sending token IDs took SGLang from 31 to 1,031 req/s and vLLM from 43 to 505 req/s on long prompts, and ChatTokenizer is 53-181x faster than the engines' own preprocessing while still matching their IDs exactly.

This is the first post in a series, and next we want to write about running 10,000+ concurrent websockets to our GPU workers from a handful of Elixir nodes, how we route inference requests across engines and pools, and what we've learned about getting more prefix cache hits.

If this kind of work sounds fun, we're hiring across engineering. Come work with us! (if there isn’t a perfect fit please email or DM me)

#Appendix 1: Benchmark Methodology

All the benchmarks ran on CoreWeave, one Xeon 8562Y+ node with 8 exclusive vCPUs per run. Every library ran on the same node one after the other with cold caches, and each number is the median of two 10 second runs after a 3 second warm-up. The requests come from WildChat, glaive function-calling and SWE-agent trajectories at pinned commits, bucketed by prompt size (XS ~140 tokens, S ~1.4K, M ~8K, L ~37K, XL ~160K, XXL ~1M plus 8 images).

Versions: vLLM 21d9da46b3, SGLang 31e55a5120, basetenkenizer 0.2.9, dynamo-llm 1.6.2, Kimi K3.1 Pro at 6d0a020.

  • Each graph is Deepseek v4.1 or Kimi K3.1 as labelled, with 8 vCPUs.
  • ChatTokenizer, the SGLang gateway, Baseten (basetenkenizer 0.2.9), NVIDIA Dynamo and HF transformers ran one after another on the same machine.
  • vLLM and SGLang were measured on their own in-process request preprocessing in a separate session on a different CoreWeave region.
  • vllm-rs has no in-process mode so it was measured over HTTP at 256 concurrent clients, which includes HTTP overhead the others don't pay.
  • Ours matched vLLM's IDs on 100% of requests. Exceptions for the others: the SGLang gateway matched 98% at ~140 tokens, 87% at ~1.4K, 16% at ~8K and 0% at ~1M (it skips image expansion); Baseten and HF transformers 96% at ~8K; NVIDIA Dynamo 73% at ~8K. Everything else matched 100%. Mismatched requests still count towards their throughput.
  • On Kimi K3.1, "Baseten" is their production K3 path (the model's Python renderer plus basetenkenizer's encoder) since the Rust library alone can't render Kimi chats. NVIDIA Dynamo can't load Kimi K3.1 and HF transformers renders the wrong prompt for it (it ignores reasoning_effort).
  • HF transformers means Python apply_chat_template followed by tokenization.
  • All graphs use linear scales. Where values span several orders of magnitude, each prompt size (or engine) gets its own axis, so compare bar heights within a panel and not across panels.

#Appendix 2: vLLM and SGLang tokenization speedups

The 120x in the title is Deepseek v4.1 at ~1M tokens with 8 inline images, where our tokenizer does 162 req/s compared to vLLM's own preprocessing does 1.35 req/s. Below is every prompt size on both models so you can see the full range. All numbers are req/s with 8 vCPUs, in-process, using vLLM and SGLang's own request preprocessing (chat template rendering plus tokenization) at the versions listed above. Across every size we're 61-181x faster than vLLM and 53-112x faster than SGLang, with most sizes landing around 90-120x.

Back to the blog

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products wi…
item.description: Full title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
item.content:encoded:
Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments

When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace, so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys.

Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the new AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace

Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect.

The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them:

Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them.
That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale.
This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like.

— Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily

What’s launching today

Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill.

When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill.

To set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID.

An agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace, agents can only buy the products it allows.

In addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request.

In this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account.

Sample walkthrough

Suppose a financial analyst asks the agent what was announced about agentic payments this week. The model wasn’t trained on this week’s news, so the agent looks for a search tool. Through AgentCore Gateway, it searches AWS Marketplace, reads the listing from Tavily, an AWS Marketplace seller, and requests the listing’s x402 endpoints.

The agent calls the endpoint and receives an x402 payload with price details. The agent then forwards the x402 payload to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks it against the remaining session budget and returns a payment token. Once these checks are passed, the agent sends the request again with the token attached, and gets the search results. Its answer includes sources and states what it bought and what it cost.

In this workflow, agents can apply their reasoning to decide which AWS Marketplace tool to use.

How it works

Figure 2: End-to-end flow of the sample solution using a Strands agent

1. Discover. The agent calls three read-only gateway tools in order: search listings, get a listing, and list its fulfillment options. Search listings tool only returns endpoints that accept x402. The last call returns the seller’s endpoint URL and the payment protocols it accepts.

2. Get a quote. The agent calls the endpoint with no payment attached. The seller answers with HTTP 402 and puts a signed quote in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header. AWS Marketplace checks the signature against the seller’s registered key, which means a quote with an altered price gets rejected.

3. Pay. The agent passes the quote to the ProcessPayment API with the payment type AWS_BILLING_X402. If budget remains in the session, AgentCore payments issues a payment token. If not, the call fails and the developer is not charged.

4. Redeem. The agent sends the request again, this time with the token in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header, and the seller returns the content. Payment tokens are valid for about five minutes, so the agent completes steps 2 through 4 in a single pass.

5. Settle. On the developer’s first purchase from a seller, AWS Marketplace creates the agreement with that seller. After that it meters each charge to their AWS bill. Settlement runs asynchronously and shows up in their AWS bill monthly.

Prerequisites

To create an AWS Billing connector, developers’ AWS accounts must have the AWS Marketplace service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForMarketplaceAgenticCommerce. AWS Marketplace uses this role to bill AWS Marketplace purchases that their agents make to their AWS account. Refer to the documentation for more details.
