item.title: [DeepInfra] 9 Best Open-Source Models for Coding (November 2026)
item.content:encoded:
9 Best Open-Source Models for Coding (November 2026)

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) coding tools now analyze repositories, fix bugs, edit several files, run tests, and execute autonomous development loops. These agentic workflows generate millions of input and output tokens through continuous model calls, and that makes proprietary APIs costly at scale.

Open-source coding models offer a cost-effective alternative. You can run them on private infrastructure, choose your serving hardware, pin a specific model version, adjust inference settings, and reduce dependence on a single API provider. Hosted inference services like DeepInfra also let you use these models without managing GPUs yourself, at per-token prices that start under $0.10 per million input tokens for the top-scoring model in this guide.

In this guide, we compare the leading open-source models for coding as of November 2026. We evaluate them on coding benchmarks, context window size, license terms, and API cost, and we cover self-hosting options at the end. Scores and prices are as of November 17, 2026.

How to Evaluate Coding Models: Benchmarks That Matter

Watch the following benchmarks to judge how well a model will perform on the tasks you plan to automate.

  • HumanEval and MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems) measure function-level code generation. A model receives a short natural-language problem and must produce Python code that passes unit tests. They offer a quick measure of basic programming ability, but they do not test repository navigation, tool use, or multi-file changes, and current models have largely saturated them.
  • SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro assess how well a model resolves real GitHub issues within agentic coding workflows. The model has to work through an entire codebase, locate the source of a bug, write a patch across multiple files, and pass execution tests.
  • DeepSWE is the long-horizon software engineering benchmark that most of this year’s model cards report. Because DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi, Z.ai, and Qwen all publish a DeepSWE v1.1 score, it is the closest thing to a common yardstick across vendors, with the caveat that each vendor runs its own harness.
  • Terminal-Bench compares model performance on tasks related to shell commands, command-line interfaces (CLI), and DevOps. Vendors now report versions 2.1 and 4.0, and results change a lot with the agent harness used, so compare scores only within the same model card.
  • LiveBench is independent and regularly refreshed to limit training-data contamination. LiveBench moved to version 2.0 on November 6, 2026. The new version grades long-horizon work (bug fixes, apps that run for hours, research reports), and its scores are not comparable to the LiveBench figures published before that date.

Apart from the leaderboard, check the context window and license. A model that looks good on function-level completion can still be a poor choice for whole-repo refactors or private on-prem use.

  • Context window defines how much code, documentation, terminal output, and conversation history the model can process in a single request. A larger context window helps with repository analysis and long-running agent sessions.
  • License determines whether you can use the weights commercially, modify them, redistribute the model, or provide the model through a hosted service. “Open-source” is used loosely in this field. Several models below ship open weights under custom licenses with commercial conditions, and we note each one. Our guide to open-weight model licenses covers what to check.

Top 9 Open-Source Models for Coding: Comparison

Here is how the current top open-source models for coding compare on size, license, context window, and what they are best at:

ModelDeveloperParameters (total / active)LicenseContext windowBest for
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017)DeepSeek763B totalMIT1MBest coding score per dollar
Mistral Large 4Mistral AI1T / 49BMistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License1MEuropean-built generalist with near-top coding scores
GLM-5.3Z.ai753B totalGLM-5.3 License (custom)1MLong-horizon coding and security work
Qwen3.8-27BAlibaba Qwen27B denseApache 2.0262KSmall deployments and local use
MiniMax M3.1 FlashMiniMax428B / 23BMiniMax Community License1MAgentic coding with image and video input
Kimi K3.1 ProMoonshot AI2.8T / 104BKimi K3.1-Pro License (custom)1MThe hardest long-horizon agent tasks
MiMo-V2.6-ProXiaomi1.02T / 42BMIT1MLong tool-use sessions on an MIT license
DeepSeek V4 Pro (0813)DeepSeek1.65T totalMIT1MDeep reasoning on large codebases
Muse Glimmer 30BMeta29.6B denseApache 2.0131KLocal coding agents on consumer hardware

1. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 is the October update to DeepSeek’s Flash line, and it is the strongest open-weight model on the current independent leaderboard. On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 80.4 in the coding category, the highest of any open-weight model and ahead of several proprietary ones.

DeepSeek’s own model card reports 77.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, both up from the original V4.1 Flash (74.2 and 31.2). The update also reduces task execution time and output length, which matters for agents that pay per output token. The model is MIT-licensed, multimodal, and supports a 1M-token context window.

It is also the cheapest serious coding model in this guide. On DeepInfra it is priced at $0.098 per million input tokens and $0.294 per million output tokens during a 51% launch promotion (list price $0.20 and $0.60), and it supports the Flex tier at 0.8× for work that can wait.

2. Mistral Large 4

Mistral Large 4 is Mistral AI’s largest model: about 1 trillion parameters with 49 billion active per token, natively multimodal, with a 1M-token context window. Mistral released the weights on October 29, 2026, and says the model was trained in its own data centers in Europe. It replaces Devstral as the Mistral model to consider for coding.

On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 79.4 in coding, one point behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 and well clear of the rest of the open-weight field. Its long-horizon agentic score is 24.7, which puts it mid-table on unattended work. (LiveBench lists two Mistral Large 4 entries; these figures are for the October 29 entry, which matches the open-weight release. The earlier entry scores 44.4 in coding.)

The Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License is a modified MIT license that allows commercial and internal use, with one condition: a company operating a model-as-a-service business needs a separate commercial license from Mistral. DeepInfra does not serve Mistral Large 4 at the time of writing, so the routes are Mistral’s own API or self-hosting, which at this size means a multi-GPU cluster.

3. GLM-5.3

GLM-5.3 uses the same base model as GLM-5.2, with all of the gains coming from post-training. Z.ai’s model card reports large jumps on long-horizon work: DeepSWE v1.1 rises from 46.2 to 66.9, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 81.0 to 88.2, and SWE-Marathon v1.1 from 19.4 to 42.5. It also reports the top CyberGym score in its comparison (84.5), which makes it a candidate for security-review agents.

The full GLM-5.3 is not yet listed on LiveBench 2.0. Its smaller sibling, GLM-5.3-Flash, is, and scores 70.9 in coding, third among open-weight models.

Check the license before you build a product on it. GLM-5.3 ships under a custom GLM-5.3 License that reads like MIT with one added condition: companies that run a model-as-a-service business with more than $10 billion in annual revenue must pass a Z.ai security review before commercial use. GLM-5.3-Flash is plain MIT. On DeepInfra, GLM-5.3 costs $0.563 input and $2.50 output per million tokens on a 38% promotion (list $0.90 and $4.00), with Flex available.

4. Qwen3.8-27B

Qwen3.8-27B is a dense 27-billion-parameter model under Apache 2.0, and it is the small model to beat. Its hybrid architecture combines Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention layers, supports a 262K-token context natively, and includes a vision encoder.

On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 69.3 in coding, within two points of GLM-5.3-Flash despite being a fraction of the size. Qwen’s model card reports 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro, 73.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and 90.3 on LiveCodeBench v6. Its DeepSWE v1.1 score is 42.2, well below the large models in this guide, which is the honest picture of a 27B model: strong on contained tasks, weaker on multi-hour ones. LiveBench shows the same thing, with a long-horizon agentic score of 15.9.

On DeepInfra it costs $0.15 input and $1.875 output per million tokens on a 25% promotion (list $0.20 and $2.50), with Flex and Priority tiers.

5. MiniMax M3.1 Flash

MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a native multimodal mixture-of-experts model for coding, agentic workflows, and computer use. It has about 428 billion total parameters with 23 billion active per token, accepts text, image, and video, and supports up to 1M tokens of context. It scores 68.8 in LiveBench 2.0 coding.

MiniMax reports 73.7 on DeepSWE v1.1, 38.1 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and 61.2 on NL2Repo-Bench. Its card also publishes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017’s numbers alongside its own, and DeepSeek leads on all three.

Two things to know. First, the MiniMax Community License grants non-commercial use by default; commercial use requires displaying “Built with MiniMax M3.1-Flash”, notifying MiniMax, and getting written authorization once the product earns more than $20 million a year. Second, DeepInfra does not serve M3.1 Flash at the time of writing. It serves the earlier MiniMax-M3 at $0.28 input and $1.10 output per million tokens, with Flex.

6. Kimi K3.1 Pro

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the largest model here: 2.8 trillion total parameters with 104 billion active. It is post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale reinforcement learning, and it replaces K3’s full-attention layers with sparse attention for more efficient long-context work.

Its profile is the reverse of Qwen’s. On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 67.8 in coding, mid-pack, but 38.7 on the long-horizon agentic category, level with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 at the top of the open-weight field. Moonshot’s card reports 75.5 on DeepSWE v1.1, 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and 51.7 on SWE Marathon v1.1. It improves on Kimi K3 in LiveBench coding by almost 15 points (67.8 against 53.1).

It is also the most expensive open-weight option: $1.90 input and $9.50 output per million tokens on DeepInfra (5% off a $2.00 and $10.00 list price), with Flex at 0.8×. The Kimi K3.1-Pro License is MIT-style with conditions: model-as-a-service operators above $20 million in annual revenue need a separate agreement with Moonshot, and very large consumer products must display the model name. Internal use, and use through Moonshot’s certified inference partners, is exempt.

7. MiMo-V2.6-Pro

MiMo-V2.6-Pro is Xiaomi’s trillion-parameter reasoning model: 1.02 trillion total parameters, 42 billion active, a 1M-token context window, and text, image, video, and audio input. It carries a plain MIT license, which makes it the simplest large model in this guide to adopt commercially.

The jump from the previous version is the largest in this guide. Xiaomi’s card reports DeepSWE v1.1 rising from 19.0 on MiMo-V2.5 Pro to 71.9, and Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 65.2 to 89.9. On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 64.5 in coding and 36.4 on long-horizon agentic work, third among open-weight models on the latter.

On DeepInfra it costs $0.387 input and $0.783 output per million tokens (10% off a $0.43 and $0.87 list price). The low output price stands out: it is less than a tenth of Kimi K3.1 Pro’s for a model that sits close to it on agentic work.

8. DeepSeek V4 Pro (0813)

DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813 is the August production release of DeepSeek’s flagship, at 1.65 trillion parameters with a 1M-token context window and an MIT license. It is not yet listed on LiveBench 2.0, so the evidence here is vendor-reported.

DeepSeek’s card shows how far it moved from the preview: Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 72.1 to 87.9, DeepSWE from 12.8 to 62.7, and NL2Repo from 38.5 to 61.5. Note that the newer and much cheaper V4.1 Flash-1017 reports a higher DeepSWE v1.1 score (77.0). Choose V4 Pro when you want the larger model’s reasoning on hard, single-shot problems, and V4.1 Flash for agent loops.

On DeepInfra it costs $1.30 input, $0.10 cached input, and $2.60 output per million tokens, with Flex at $1.04 and $2.08. The cached-input rate is worth attention for coding agents, which resend the same repository context on every step.

9. Muse Glimmer 30B

Muse Glimmer 30B is Meta’s open model for agents that run on local or consumer hardware. It is a dense 29.6-billion-parameter model under Apache 2.0, released in August 2026, with image input and a 131K-token context window.

Meta reports 76.0 on SWE-bench Verified, 51.2 on SWE-bench Pro, and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. What sets it apart is the packaging. Meta ships two roughly 4-bit variants aimed at 32GB and 24GB of VRAM, reporting 0.2% and 1.0% average degradation, plus a speculative-decoding drafter that it says lifts generation on an RTX 5090 from 74.9 to 233.4 tokens per second. Qwen3.8-27B posts higher coding scores on Qwen’s own card (61.7 against 51.2 on SWE-bench Pro), so Glimmer is the pick when local speed and a ready-made quantized build matter more than the last few points.

If you would rather not run it yourself, DeepInfra serves it at $0.30 input and $1.20 output per million tokens.

Where the Open-Source Coding Models Stand Against Proprietary Models

To set the context, it’s worth understanding where open source stands relative to proprietary options.

Proprietary models provide reliable tool calling, polished IDE integrations, managed infrastructure, and consistent performance across coding tasks. The trade-off is control: usage-based pricing can be unpredictable, and closed APIs limit your choices on data handling and serving infrastructure.

Open-weight models give you more flexibility in deployment, fine-tuning, and provider choice. The trade-off is that self-hosting can require more infrastructure and engineering work to optimize, monitor, and maintain the model.

Here are the LiveBench 2.0 results for the open-weight models it lists, from the November 6, 2026 release. GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813, and Muse Glimmer 30B are not on the leaderboard yet, so they do not appear. The top proprietary score in each category is included as a reference line.

LiveBench 2.0 Coding

ModelOrganizationTypeCoding
Gemini 4 Carbon (reference)GoogleProprietary91.0
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017DeepSeekOpen weights80.4
Mistral Large 4Mistral AIOpen weights79.4
GLM-5.3-FlashZ.aiOpen weights70.9
Qwen3.8-27BAlibabaOpen weights69.3
MiniMax M3.1 FlashMiniMaxOpen weights68.8
Kimi K3.1 ProMoonshot AIOpen weights67.8
MiMo-V2.6-ProXiaomiOpen weights64.5
Muse Spark OpenMetaOpen weights55.1
Nemotron 3.5 Super VLNVIDIAOpen weights54.1
Kimi K3Moonshot AIOpen weights53.1

LiveBench 2.0 Long-Horizon Agentic

ModelOrganizationTypeLong-horizon agentic
Claude Fable 5.2 (reference)AnthropicProprietary82.9
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017DeepSeekOpen weights38.8
Kimi K3.1 ProMoonshot AIOpen weights38.7
MiMo-V2.6-ProXiaomiOpen weights36.4
Kimi K3Moonshot AIOpen weights36.0
MiniMax M3.1 FlashMiniMaxOpen weights25.7
Mistral Large 4Mistral AIOpen weights24.7
GLM-5.3-FlashZ.aiOpen weights20.7
Qwen3.8-27BAlibabaOpen weights15.9
Muse Spark OpenMetaOpen weights12.1
Nemotron 3.5 Super VLNVIDIAOpen weights12.0

The two tables tell different stories. On coding, the best open-weight model is about ten points behind the best proprietary one. On long-horizon agentic work, the kind that runs unattended for hours, the gap is more than forty points. The practical reading: open-weight models are ready for the bulk of coding work, including bug fixes, refactors, test writing, and supervised agent loops. For fully autonomous multi-hour tasks, a proprietary model still earns its price, and a common setup is to route between the two.

Are Open-Source Coding Models Really Free?

Free access to model weights does not mean zero cost. You still need GPUs, storage, networking, inference software, monitoring, security controls, upgrades, and engineering time. Large mixture-of-experts models may activate only a small share of their parameters for each token, but a serving system still needs the full set of weights in memory.

Open weights also come with license terms. MIT and Apache 2.0 grant broad rights to use, modify, and redistribute. Four of the nine models here use custom licenses with commercial conditions: Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and MiniMax M3.1 Flash.

Self-hosting is usually economical when you have steady, high usage, strict source-code privacy requirements, existing GPU capacity, or predictable workloads that keep the hardware busy. A hosted open-model API often makes more sense when usage remains uncertain, or you want to test several models before committing to infrastructure.

You can compare the two options with a simple calculation:

  • Hosted monthly cost = input-token cost + output-token cost, less any cached-input and Flex savings
  • Self-hosted monthly cost = GPU hours + storage + networking + monitoring + engineering operations

Where Do Open-Source Coding Models Deliver the Most Value?

Open-source coding models provide several operational advantages across different scenarios.

  • Private codebases: You can run the model inside controlled infrastructure when source code, credentials, customer data, or internal documentation cannot leave your environment.
  • High-volume agentic workflows: Self-hosting or low-cost open-model APIs give more predictable costs for repeated repository analysis, test execution, debugging, and tool calls.
  • Model customization: You can fine-tune the model, adjust its inference settings, add domain-specific tools, or train adapters for internal frameworks and programming languages.
  • Deployment control: Your team can pin a tested model version, choose the hardware, control latency, and decide when to apply upgrades. Hosted model IDs still get retired, so plan for deprecation either way.
  • Hardware-specific workloads: You can select a dense or MoE architecture based on available VRAM, throughput targets, quantization support, and expected context length.
  • Reduced provider dependence: Open weights make it easier to move between a hosted API, a private endpoint, and self-managed infrastructure without rebuilding the coding application.

Running Open-Source Coding Models Locally or Self-Hosted

Several serving frameworks support open coding models:

  • vLLM focuses on high-throughput GPU serving and production APIs.
  • SGLang provides efficient structured generation and agent-oriented serving. Our vLLM vs SGLang comparison covers how to choose between the two.
  • llama.cpp runs quantized models across CPUs, consumer GPUs, and Apple Silicon.
  • Ollama simplifies local model installation and API access.
  • LM Studio provides a desktop interface and a local OpenAI-compatible server.

When running a model locally, consider its size, precision, and context window. Two models in this guide are sized for it. Muse Glimmer 30B ships with quantized builds that Meta targets at 24GB and 32GB of VRAM. Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B dense model, so a four-bit build needs roughly 14GB for the weights alone, and a 24GB GPU is a practical starting point once you add runtime overhead and context.

Everything else here is a data-center model. The other seven (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro) run from 428 billion to 2.8 trillion parameters and need multi-GPU servers.

Local or hosted, these models connect to any coding tool that accepts an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including open agents such as OpenCode.

Running These Models on DeepInfra

If you want the model without building the serving layer yourself, the simplest approach is DeepInfra’s OpenAI-compatible API: the same request format and client as the OpenAI API, with the model chosen by name. Seven of the nine models above are available, and prices are per token with no minimum.

ModelInput ($/1M)Output ($/1M)Flex tier (0.8×)Est. monthly cost*
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017$0.098$0.294Yes$15.68
Qwen3.8-27B$0.15$1.875Yes$52.50
Muse Glimmer 30B$0.30$1.20No$54.00
MiMo-V2.6-Pro$0.387$0.783No$54.36
GLM-5.3$0.563$2.50Yes$106.30
DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813$1.30$2.60Yes$182.00
Kimi K3.1 Pro$1.90$9.50Yes$380.00

**Estimate for 100M input tokens and 20M output tokens a month at the standard tier, before cached-input savings. Prices are from DeepInfra’s model pages on November 17, 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, Qwen3.8-27B, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, GLM-5.3, and Kimi K3.1 Pro are at promotional rates; list prices are given in each model’s section above. MiniMax M3.1 Flash and Mistral Large 4 are not served; the earlier MiniMax-M3 is, at $0.28 and $1.10.*

The spread is the point. The same workload costs $15.68 on the model with the highest LiveBench coding score and $380 on the largest one, a 24-fold difference. Three settings bring the bill down further:

  • Flex tier. Models with the Flex tag run at 0.8× the standard price in exchange for slower responses and occasional unavailability. That fits batch refactors, test generation, and overnight agent runs. The DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 estimate above drops to about $12.54.
  • Cached input. Coding agents resend the same system prompt, tool definitions, and repository context on every step. Those repeated tokens bill at the cached-input rate: $0.10 instead of $1.30 per million on DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813, for example. Our guide to prompt hygiene covers how to structure prompts so the cache hits.
  • Reasoning effort. Several of these models accept a reasoning_effort setting. GLM-5.3 defaults to max; dropping to high or low for routine edits cuts output tokens.

For high-volume supporting work around a coding agent, such as reading build logs or triaging issues with screenshots, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a low-cost multimodal option at $0.15 input and $0.50 output per million tokens. It scores 54.1 in LiveBench 2.0 coding, so use it for the simple steps.

If response speed is the product, as in inline autocomplete, test providers built on speed-specialized hardware as well. For agents, batch work, and anything billed by volume, the per-token gap compounds.

Here is how to call one of these models with the Python client:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a coding assistant. Return only the refactored code."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Refactor this function for readability:\n\ndef f(a,b):\n    return [x for x in a if x not in b]"},
    ],
    temperature=0.2,
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)copy

To try a different model, change the model name.

The Bottom Line

The best open-source model for coding depends on the work.

For most teams, start with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017: it has the highest independent coding score among open-weight models, an MIT license, and the lowest price in this guide. If your agents run long, unattended tasks, test Kimi K3.1 Pro and MiMo-V2.6-Pro against it; they score close to it on long-horizon work, and MiMo does so on an MIT license at a low output price. For long-horizon coding with a security angle, GLM-5.3 is the one to evaluate, license permitting. If you need a small model you can run yourself, choose Qwen3.8-27B for scores or Muse Glimmer 30B for a ready-made local build. Mistral Large 4 nearly matches DeepSeek on coding and is the choice if a European-built model matters to you, as long as you can use Mistral’s API or host a trillion-parameter model yourself.

Whichever you shortlist, measure it on your own repositories before you commit. Vendor benchmarks use different harnesses, and the independent leaderboard does not yet cover every model here.

Visit the DeepInfra models page to compare open-source models across context window and pricing. For any questions or feedback, reach out to us at feedback@deepinfra.com. You can also join the community on Discord, or find us on X at @DeepInfra.

Kimi K2.5 is positioned as Moonshot AI’s “do-it-all” model for modern product workflows: native multimodality (text + vision/video), Instant vs. Thinking modes, and support for agentic / multi-agent (“swarm”) execution patterns. In real applications, though, model capability is only half the story. The provider’s inference stack determines the things your users actually […]</p>

item.title: [DeepInfra] Prompt Hygiene: Cheaper, Faster LLM API Calls
item.content:encoded:
Prompt Hygiene: Cheaper, Faster LLM API Calls

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Prompt hygiene is the habit of writing prompts that are clean, minimal, and unambiguous. It sounds like a writing tip, but in production it behaves like an infrastructure optimization: it reduces token spend, improves latency, and lowers the retry rate by making model outputs more predictable.

When teams complain that LLM calls are “too expensive” or “too slow,” the root cause is often not the model. It’s the prompt. Bloated inputs, unclear instructions, and unbounded outputs quietly inflate cost and turn reliability into a gamble.

This article explains what prompt hygiene is, why it matters, and how to apply it in a way that makes your calls cheaper and faster without reducing quality.

Why prompt hygiene matters in production

In production, every LLM call has two things that show up on your bill: the tokens you send in and the tokens the model sends back. (If the arithmetic is new to you, Pricing 101 walks through it.) A long prompt costs more up front and usually takes longer to process. A vague prompt often costs even more on the way out, because the model fills the gaps by generating extra text you didn’t actually need, and output tokens are priced higher than input tokens on most models. Both add latency.

The real budget killer, though, isn’t a response that’s a bit wordy. It’s a response that comes back in the wrong shape—missing fields, wrong structure, impossible to parse—and forces you to run the call again. A retry doubles the cost of that call, and it also creates the kind of “random slow” tail latency that users notice right away. It is one of the quieter reasons an API bill can double without anyone changing the model.

Prompt hygiene is simply the easiest way to keep that variability under control.

What “dirty prompts” look like

Messy prompts tend to fail in the same few ways. First, they include too much context “just in case.” People paste whole documents, send full chat histories, or repeat the same instruction three different ways. That inflates token usage, but it rarely improves the answer.

Second, they contain unclear or conflicting constraints. Asking for something “detailed but concise” sounds reasonable to a human, but it forces the model to choose which instruction to prioritize. Sometimes it picks “detailed.” Sometimes it picks “concise.” That inconsistency is exactly what makes production behavior unpredictable.

And finally, dirty prompts often don’t define the output contract. If you want bullets but don’t say so, you’ll sometimes get paragraphs. If you want JSON but don’t specify the schema, you’ll get something that looks like JSON—until one day it doesn’t, and your parser breaks.

The goal: reduce ambiguity and bound the output

The core idea behind prompt hygiene is simple: reduce the number of decisions the model has to make.

When you specify a clear task, clear constraints, and a clear output format, you reduce “entropy” in the generation. Less entropy means the model is less likely to drift, ramble, or invent structure.

And when you bound the output length, you control cost directly. A good prompt could follow this outline:

  • Task: State the task in one sentence, early and explicitly.
  • Constraints: Add the rules that matter: length, tone if needed, allowed sources, and what to do when something is missing.
  • Output format: Describe the exact structure you want the model to return.
  • Input: Provide only the data necessary for this call.

This is not about being rigid for the sake of it. It is about giving the model a well-defined lane so you get consistent results cheaply.

The hygiene rules that save the most money

Rule 1: Put the task in the first two lines

Models respond best when the goal is front-loaded. If the task is buried after a long preamble, you increase the chance of misalignment.

A prompt that starts with “Summarize this…” gives the model less to misread than one that starts with “You are a helpful assistant…” followed by several paragraphs of scene-setting.

Rule 2: Remove anything that doesn’t change the answer

Every token has a cost. If a sentence does not improve correctness, formatting, or compliance, delete it. In practice, this means cutting motivational fluff, duplicate instructions, and “nice-to-have” background that does not affect output.

Rule 3: Cap output length with measurable limits

“Be concise” is subjective, and subjective constraints are ignored more often than teams expect. Hard limits work because they are measurable. You can constrain output with word count, bullet count, character count, or strict JSON keys. Even simple limits like “max 120 words” can cut spending dramatically, because output verbosity is where much of the bill hides.

Rule 4: Always specify an output format

If your downstream system parses the result, formatting is not a preference. It is a contract. Tell the model exactly what the output should look like. If you need JSON, provide the schema (our guide to JSON-only responses shows how to enforce it at the API level). If you need bullets, specify the number and style. If you need headings, specify the headings.

Add a line that prevents extra text, such as “Output only the result. Do not add explanations.”

Rule 5: Eliminate conflicting constraints

Prompts that contain contradictory instructions lead to inconsistent results. Instead of “be detailed but short,” define what “detailed” means. For example, require “exactly three risks” or “include two edge cases.” Then separately cap length. This turns a vague goal into a deterministic target.

Rule 6: Define what to do when information is missing

If you do not define missing-data behavior, the model will often guess. One sentence can prevent hallucinations and retries: “If the answer is not in the input, write ‘Not stated in source.’” Or: “If a field is missing, return null.” This improves reliability and reduces rework.

Production hygiene: what changes at scale

Once you’re calling a model repeatedly—especially behind an API—the biggest waste isn’t a single verbose prompt. It’s paying full price for the same tokens over and over again. Two habits make a huge difference here: separating stable instructions from per-request input, and being intentional about how you feed context.

  • Separate stable instructions from per-request input If you find yourself pasting the same policy, tone guide, or output format rules into every request, you’re paying a “tax” on every call. In production, it’s cleaner to split your prompt into two layers. The first layer is a stable, versioned wrapper that contains the rules that should always apply—things like output format, safety constraints, and how to handle missing data. The second layer is the per-request prompt, which stays short and contains only the actual user input and task-specific details. The API is stateless, so the wrapper still travels with every request, but a wrapper that is identical from call to call can be served from the prompt cache at a fraction of the input price (see the next section). It also makes behavior consistent across endpoints, because you’re not relying on copy-pasted instructions that slowly drift over time.
  • Prefer retrieval and trimming over dumping context Another common cost trap is sending an entire document because the answer is “somewhere in there.” You pay for that whole block of text every single time, even if the model only needs a small paragraph. A better pattern is to retrieve or pre-trim the relevant parts and pass only those into the prompt. Even without a full RAG pipeline, you can often cut token usage dramatically by selecting a specific section, pulling the few paragraphs around a keyword, or providing the top snippets that actually contain the answer. Smaller, more relevant context usually improves quality too, because it reduces noise and keeps the model focused.

Prompt caching: pay less for the part that never changes

A stable prefix is also a cacheable one. On DeepInfra, prompt caching is automatic on supported models: when the beginning of a prompt matches a prefix from a recent request on the same model, the cached state is reused, the model skips reprocessing that portion, and those tokens are billed at the model’s cached-input rate instead of the standard input rate.

Two hygiene rules follow directly from how the cache matches:

  • Put stable content first. The cache matches from the start of the prompt, so the system prompt, format rules, and few-shot examples go before the user’s input.
  • Keep the prefix byte-identical. A single changed character invalidates the match. Keep timestamps, user IDs, and anything else that varies out of the prefix.

Here is what that is worth. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 lists standard input at $1.30 per 1M tokens and cached input at $0.10 per 1M. Take a 3,000-token stable wrapper sent on 200,000 requests a month, which is 600M prefix tokens:

Rate per 1M tokensMonthly cost of the prefix
Standard input$1.30$780
Cached input$0.10$60

That is an estimate with a generous assumption: every request hits the cache. Cache entries expire after a period of inactivity, so real hit rates depend on how steady your traffic is. You can measure yours from the prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens field in each response’s usage object. If you need a prefix to stay warm for a guaranteed window, prompt cache retention holds it for 5 minutes or an hour in exchange for a write premium on the first request.

A concrete before-and-after example

If you’re running prompts through DeepInfra, you feel the cost of messy prompts immediately: more input tokens, longer completions, and higher latency—especially when you’re calling models at scale or powering user-facing endpoints. The quickest win is to tighten the prompt so the model spends tokens only on the work that matters.

Before: a “messy” prompt that wastes tokens

This kind of prompt is common in prototypes:

“You are an expert assistant. Read the following carefully and provide a professional answer. Make sure it includes all relevant details and context. Be thorough but also concise.”

It sounds reasonable, but it’s expensive and unreliable in production:

  • It doesn’t state the task (what is the model actually supposed to do?)
  • It encourages verbosity (“relevant details and context,” “thorough”)
  • It contains conflicting instructions (“thorough but concise”)
  • It has no output contract, so formatting varies and parsers break

In practice, this typically means longer responses, more variance, and more retries—exactly the combination that increases spend and tail latency.

After: a “hygienic” prompt you can ship behind an API

Here’s a production-ready rewrite that is cheaper, faster, and easier to validate:

Task: Answer the question using only the provided text.
Constraints:
Use at most 6 bullet points
Each bullet must be ≤ 18 words
If the text does not contain the answer, write: Not stated in source.
Output format: Return only the bullet list (no intro, no closing line).
Text: …
Question: …

Why this works better:

  • Lower output tokens: the hard cap prevents runaway completions.
  • Lower latency: shorter generations generally complete faster and reduce tail latency.
  • Fewer retries: strict format + clear missing-info behavior makes responses easier to parse and validate.
  • Better caching opportunities: the instruction block is now a fixed prefix the prompt cache can reuse, and when outputs are consistent, you can also cache whole responses by (model, prompt version, input hash).

What the rewrite saves

Here is an estimate at DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813’s standard rates ($1.30 input, $2.60 output per 1M tokens). The assumptions: both prompts carry the same 1,500-token source text; the messy instructions are about 40 tokens and the rewritten ones about 75; the uncapped answer averages 400 tokens; and the capped answer tops out near 145 tokens (6 bullets × 18 words, at roughly 0.75 words per token).

Per 1M callsInput tokensOutput tokensInput costOutput costTotal
Before1,540M400M$2,002$1,040$3,042
After1,575M145M$2,048$377$2,425

The rewritten prompt is slightly longer on the way in and still comes out about 20% cheaper overall, because output cost falls by roughly 64%. Retries widen the gap: if one in ten of the “before” responses had to be re-run because it would not parse, that adds about $304 per million calls. And with the 75-token instruction block cached, the “after” row drops a little further.

Your numbers will differ with your model, your inputs, and how long your uncapped answers run. The method carries over: count tokens in and out, before and after, and price them at the rates on the model page.

A quick pre-launch checklist

Before you ship a prompt, run it through a small checklist:

  • Is the task stated clearly at the top?
  • Can you delete at least 20% of tokens without changing results?
  • Is the output length capped with a measurable rule?
  • Is the output format explicit and parseable?
  • Are there any conflicting instructions?
  • Is missing-data behavior defined?
  • Is only necessary context included?
  • Does the stable part of the prompt come first, unchanged from call to call, so it can be cached?

Prompts that pass this checklist tend to be cheaper, faster, and significantly easier to maintain.

Conclusion

Prompt hygiene is not about making prompts short. It is about making them disciplined.

When you remove unnecessary tokens, constrain output, define clear formats, and keep the stable part of the prompt cacheable, you reduce the model’s guesswork and stop paying full price for repeated text. That lowers cost, reduces latency, and—most importantly—cuts retries. In production, that reliability is often worth more than any single model upgrade.

On June 15, 2026, claude-sonnet-4-20250514 and claude-opus-4-20250514 stopped answering requests. Anthropic had posted the notice 62 days earlier. Teams with either string in a call site learned about it from an error rate, not an email. […]</p>

item.title: [Anyscale] Ray Train: Diagnosing GPU Starvation in Model Training with…
item.description: Full title: Ray Train: Diagnosing GPU Starvation in Model Training with Data Ingest Observability
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Ray Train: Diagnosing GPU Starvation in Model Training with Data Ingest Observability

By Jason Li | November 17, 2026

Part 3 of our KubeRay series. This blog stands on its own, so you don't need the earlier posts to follow along. Part 2: KubeRay in production: best practices from the field covers how teams run KubeRay in production and how Anyscale KubeRay Connect fits on top of it.

The Anyscale platform has built-in observability for Ray workloads, and KubeRay Connect, introduced at the end of Part 2, brings it to the KubeRay clusters you already run. This post covers one of those features, built specifically for training workloads: Ray Train's data ingest observability.

LinkWhy GPU starvation is hard to catch

Model training is capital-intensive, so training teams need to pay close attention to GPU utilization. At the scale of hundreds or thousands of GPUs, even a small slowdown adds up to a lot of lost GPU-hours.

To keep GPUs busy, the next batch of data needs to be ready the moment the model finishes the current one. When it isn't, the GPUs sit and wait. That's GPU starvation, and it's one of the most common reasons utilization drops. It's also one of the quietest: nothing crashes, nothing alerts, and the job just keeps running a little slower than it should.

Teams usually notice one of two symptoms: GPU utilization that swings up and down instead of holding steady, or training runs that take longer than expected. In the run below, for example, SM activity on every GPU keeps rising and falling instead of reaching a plateau:

GPU SM Activity

That pattern is a typical sign of GPU starvation. Data loading and training run in parallel: while the GPU trains on one batch, the next batch is being prepared. When preparing a batch takes longer than training on it, the training step finishes first and the GPU sits idle until the next batch arrives:

Training steps

Each idle gap is one of the dips in the utilization graph above. The symptom is easy to spot. The cause is not. A batch can arrive late for a variety of reasons: a slow upstream data pipeline, data traveling over the network from another node, heavy preprocessing on the training worker such as an expensive collate_fn, or the host-to-device copy. Each cause has a different fix, so the first step is finding which stage is the bottleneck.

The rest of this post walks through the tools for doing that:

  • Data ingest metrics in open source Ray: how Ray Train and Ray Data time each stage of data loading, and how to read the Grafana graphs to see whether training is stalling on data, which stage is responsible, and what to change.
  • Data ingest observability on Anyscale: the same graphs with no setup, plus a live data ingest panel on the Ray Train dashboard that summarizes ingest health for every running dataset. KubeRay Connect brings both to KubeRay clusters you manage yourself.

LinkData ingest metrics in open source Ray

Starting in Ray 2.58, Ray Train and Ray Data record how long each batch spends in every stage of data loading, so you can see which stage is holding training back. If your Ray Train code already reads from Ray Data, no code changes are needed.

A typical setup looks like this. The driver defines a Ray Dataset, here Parquet files read from S3, and passes it to the trainer. Ray Train gives each of the eight training workers its own shard of the dataset. Each worker reads its shard with iter_torch_batches, which applies your collate_fn and returns batches of 64 rows as PyTorch tensors:

import ray
import ray.train
from ray.train import ScalingConfig
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer

train_ds = ray.data.read_parquet("s3://my-bucket/train/")

def train_func():
    shard = ray.train.get_dataset_shard("train")
    for batch in shard.iter_torch_batches(batch_size=64, collate_fn=my_collate):
        ...  # your training step

trainer = TorchTrainer(
    train_func,
    datasets={"train": train_ds},
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=8, use_gpu=True),
)
trainer.fit()

That single iter_torch_batches call is where all of the data loading happens. Like every other Ray Data iterator, including iter_batches, iter_rows, and to_tf, it moves each batch through the same pipeline before handing it to your training loop.

Inside that call, each batch passes through six stages on its way from the Ray Data pipeline to your GPU. Any of them can be the bottleneck:

StageWhat it measures
Production waitWaiting for the upstream Ray Data pipeline to produce the next block
Data transferFetching blocks to the training worker, including from another node's object store
BatchingSlicing and combining blocks into batches, including any local shuffle buffer
FormatConverting each batch to the requested format, such as NumPy or pandas
CollateRunning your own per-batch preprocessing on the training worker, such as tokenizing text or padding sequences to a common length, passed in as collate_fn
FinalizeCopying the batch to the GPU (host-to-device transfer) in iter_torch_batches

These stages don't run one after another on your training thread. Instead, a pool of background threads runs them concurrently to prepare the next batch while your training step runs. As long as the next batch is ready before your training step finishes, all of this work is hidden and doesn’t cost you any wall-clock time. When the next batch isn't ready in time, the training loop waits and the GPU sits idle. That wait is the exposed data loading time. Ray records it on every training worker, along with the time spent in each stage.

In open source Ray, these metrics appear in the Data Ingestion section of the Train Dashboard in Grafana once you set up Prometheus and Grafana for your cluster. The graphs answer three questions in order, shown here for a run that's stalling on an expensive collate_fn:

  • Is training stalling on data? Max Exposed Data Loading Time shows how long the training loop waits for each batch on the slowest rank. If it's zero, data loading keeps up, and tuning the pipeline won't help. If it isn't, that time is GPU idle time on every step.

Max Exposed Data Loading Time

  • Which stage is responsible? Percentage Data Loading Breakdown by Stage shows each stage's share of data loading time, pooled across all ranks. A large production wait share means the upstream Ray Data pipeline can't produce data fast enough. A large share in any other stage points to work on the training worker itself.

Percentage Data Loading Breakdown by Stage

  • Is it every rank or just one? Each stage has its own graph broken down by rank. If one rank sits well above the rest, it's a straggler, and because ranks synchronize on every step, a single slow rank can hold back the entire run.

Production wait time by rank

Two throughput graphs round out the view. Data Ingest Throughput by Rank shows the rows per second each rank consumes, and Data Production Throughput shows the rows per second the Ray Data pipeline delivers to training. Together they show a healthy run's steady-state rate, so drops and imbalance across ranks stand out.

Data Ingest Throughput by Rank & Data Production Throughput

Knowing which stage is responsible is what makes the problem actionable, because each one points to specific things to check or change:

BottleneckWhat to try
Production waitCheck the Ray Data dashboard for the slowest operator in your upstream pipeline and tune its configuration. You can also add CPU-only nodes so Ray Data can scale out preprocessing, or cache the preprocessed dataset in memory with materialize() if it fits.
Data transferIncrease prefetch_batches so blocks start transferring ahead of the training step. Higher values hold more batches in memory, so watch memory usage on the training nodes.
BatchingIf you use local_shuffle_buffer_size, reduce it or shuffle upstream instead, such as with a map_batches shuffle or by shuffling file order at read time.
FormatIncrease prefetch_batches so more batches are converted ahead of the training step.
CollateMove heavy preprocessing out of collate_fn and into the Ray Data pipeline with map_batches, where it scales out across the cluster instead of running on the training worker. For lighter collate work, increasing prefetch_batches can also help by preparing more batches ahead of the training step.
One straggling rankCheck what's different about that rank's node. Common causes are Ray Data tasks competing with the training worker for CPU or memory, and blocks that are repeatedly fetched from remote nodes. If Ray Data tasks are competing for resources, keep them off the training nodes by pinning the dataset to CPU-only nodes with a label_selector.

LinkData ingest observability on Anyscale

On Anyscale, you get all of these Grafana graphs with no setup. Anyscale collects the metrics for every training run and shows the graphs on the Ray Train dashboard, so there's no Prometheus or Grafana to host.

On top of the Grafana graphs, the Ray Train dashboard on Anyscale includes a live data ingest panel. Instead of reading through a dozen graphs, you get one live view of data ingest health across your whole cluster. The sped-up recording below shows it on a run that's stalling on collate:

Live data ingestion health

For each Ray Data dataset that's currently executing, the panel shows the following. Per-batch metrics are for the rank you select; the recording shows the slowest rank.

  • Ingestion progress: how far training has gotten through the dataset, as rows ingested out of the total.
  • Throughput: rows per second produced by the upstream data pipeline and ingested by training in total.
  • Exposed data loading stall: how long the training loop waits on data for each batch.
  • Training compute time: how long the training step takes for each batch.
  • Batch cycle: each batch's total time, split between training compute and the exposed stall.
  • Stage breakdown: time per batch in each of the six data loading stages, so the bottleneck stands out. In the recording, collate takes almost all of it, which points straight at the collate_fn.
  • Link to Grafana: one click to the full Data Ingestion graphs, for historical metrics and more detail.

Everything in this section is part of the observability built into the Anyscale platform. If you run your own KubeRay clusters, KubeRay Connect brings it to them without migrating workloads.

With these metrics, unstable GPU utilization becomes something you can trace to a single bottleneck, instead of something you guess at. Fix that stage and your GPUs stay fed: utilization rises and holds steady, and the same run finishes sooner on the same hardware.

To go deeper, see these guides in the Ray docs:

  • Debug data loading bottlenecks covers the full drill-down and the fix for each result.
  • How does Ray Data iterate over data? covers the threading model behind the six stages.

LinkSummary

Unstable GPU utilization tells you that something is wrong without telling you what. Starting in Ray 2.58, per-stage data loading metrics in Ray Train and Ray Data close that gap. They tell you whether data loading is what's holding training back and, if it is, where the bottleneck is, so you know where to look next. In open source Ray, the metrics show up in the Train Dashboard in Grafana. On Anyscale, you get the same graphs with no setup, plus a live data ingest panel that summarizes every running dataset.

LinkNext steps

GPU starvation is one of several issues that make production training hard to debug, and the Ray team is continuing to build observability into Ray Train for the most common ones. Here's what we're working on next:

  • Automatic hang detection and stack trace capture. Ray Train will detect when training stops making progress and automatically capture stack traces from every worker, so you can see where each one is stuck without reproducing the hang.
  • Health monitoring. More extensive monitoring of training health, including hardware health checks, to surface the problems that slow down or stop production training runs.

If you run into a data ingest issue these tools don't cover, or have ideas for what we should build next, file an issue on GitHub.

Table of contents

  • Why GPU starvation is hard to catch
  • Data ingest metrics in open source Ray
  • Data ingest observability on Anyscale
  • Summary
  • Next steps

Sharing

Tags

item.title: [xAI Grok] Building an accounting team with Grok Bot
item.content:encoded:
Back to newsNov 16, 2026

Building an accounting team with Grok Bot

By Annay (Paul) Bains, Will Smerdon, and Erin Jenks

Five Grok Bots at SpaceXSI each own an accounting job end to end, from provisioning a customer account to collecting payment. They only involve a person when the work needs judgment.

Download for macOSContact sales

Most accounting teams organize their work around a set of well-defined jobs, from managing customer accounts to billing and collecting payments.

At SpaceXSI, we're starting to assign those jobs to Grok Bots. Each Bot takes responsibility for an entire process, working independently and involving us when it encounters something that requires human judgment or approval. They're allowing us to handle more work without increasing headcount at the same rate.

We've built five Team Bots, each with a carefully scoped responsibility:

  • Provisioning Bot checks contracts and sets up or closes customer accounts.
  • Billing Bot verifies contract details and generates invoices.
  • Billing Support Bot answers billing questions and takes action on requests from our go-to-market team, such as updating customer records or retrieving invoices.
  • Cash Applications Bot applies incoming payments, investigates discrepancies, writes off bank fees, and flags short payments for collections.
  • Collections Bot handles customer billing inquiries and coordinates requests such as refunds.

Setting them up has taught us a lot about what it takes to make Bots reliable enough to own important business processes. Here's how we've approached building our team and what each Bot does.

How we build and manage our accounting Bots

Our initial experiments with Grok Bot involved some trial and error as we figured out how best to organize the work. We eventually settled on assigning each Bot an existing well defined and scoped accounting process to own from beginning to end. Rather than asking a Bot to help with various tasks, we give it a specific job that a person on our team would otherwise perform.

One common misconception about AI agents is that they should be able to do a job as soon as you give them access to the right systems. In practice, we've found that Bots need the same investment in documentation, onboarding, and ongoing coaching as new employees.

That takes time upfront, but once trained, they can work around the clock and handle far more volume with greater accuracy than a person doing the same job. When we teach a Bot a new skill, it's like uploading a new capability that it can immediately put to work.

Build reliable processes before assigning them to Bots

A Bot will struggle to run a process that people haven't already figured out how to perform reliably. If the workflow is poorly defined or depends on undocumented knowledge, giving it to a Bot won't solve those problems.

For that reason, we've invested in building applications that make our accounting processes more structured. We use Grok Build to create applications with interfaces that define how a process works and what actions are permitted. This gives the Bot a controlled environment to work in, rather than leaving it to figure out how to perform each task from scratch.

For example, we built an internal provisioning application that provides a defined way to enable customer accounts, with controls on what actions can be taken. Our Provisioning Bot now operates that application. This gives us a reliable process with a logged audit trail of actions taken that both people and Bots can use.

Document each job as if you're onboarding an employee

We maintain a Notion document that serves as each Bot's operating manual. It contains the knowledge and instructions the Bot needs to do its job, from how to verify contract details before issuing an invoice to which billing adjustments require human approval.

Each night, the Bots consult these documents to refresh their knowledge and flag any discrepancies with their existing instructions. They cannot edit the documents themselves. Only the people responsible for each process have that permission.

When we change a policy or discover a better way to handle a transaction, we update the documentation and teach the Bot the new procedure. The people who know the job best remain responsible for defining how it gets done.

Give Bots clear permissions and approval requirements

Accounting processes require careful controls because they affect financial reporting and may be subject to audit requirements or control frameworks. Our Bots can read the information they need, but their ability to change records is more restricted.

Grok Bot can also connect securely to internal systems through integrations such as Tailscale. This allows Bots to access private tools and data without exposing those systems to the public internet. Companies can control which resources a Bot can access, with access policies tied to the identity of the person who authorized the connection.

We allow them to execute lower-risk tasks independently and require approval for sensitive actions such as issuing credits or refunds. We also control who can authorize those actions. For example, anyone with appropriate access can ask Billing Support Bot to explain an invoice, but only designated people can authorize changes to billing records.

Train Bots before letting them work independently

We train new Bots the same way we train new employees. We start by teaching them how the job works, then have them observe us performing the work before gradually giving them responsibility for completing tasks on their own. This gives us time to identify gaps in their knowledge and correct mistakes before they start working independently. Our typical onboarding process now takes about three weeks:

  • Week one: Build the Bot's knowledge base and have it observe how we perform the job.
  • Week two: Let the Bot propose actions and explain what it intends to do, with a person approving its work.
  • Week three: Allow the Bot to execute routine work independently and escalate exceptions.

Our first Bots took longer to develop. Billing Support Bot, for example, took four to five weeks to roll out. As we've learned how to structure the work, we've been able to build subsequent Bots much faster. We continue to coach them after launch, correcting mistakes and updating their instructions, while they handle work that would otherwise require several full-time employees.

Provisioning Bot sets up and closes customer accounts

Provisioning Bot makes sure customers receive the correct access to our products when they sign a contract, and that access is removed when their contract ends. It uses an internal application we built with Cursor to manage this process, which previously required someone on our team to handle manually.

When a deal closes, Provisioning Bot compares the executed contract against the corresponding CRM records. It checks that the order details match, then uses our provisioning application to enable the customer's account. Afterward, it verifies the entitlements against the contract and notifies the sales rep in Slack that provisioning is complete.

When a customer churns or a contract ends, the Bot also removes the corresponding entitlements. This helps us avoid provisioning errors that could leave customers without the access they've purchased or allow access to continue after a contract ends.

Billing Bot generates invoices and checks for errors

Billing Bot takes over once a customer account has been provisioned. It checks that the information in our billing system matches the terms of the executed contract before generating, and sending an invoice.

To do this, the Bot compares the contract against the customer records that flow from the CRM into our Billing System. If it finds a discrepancy, it corrects the information in the Billing System so invoicing can proceed and alerts the appropriate team to fix the underlying CRM record(s). It then sends the invoice and notifies the sales rep.

This has reduced the time required to issue an invoice from roughly 24 hours to minutes.

Billing Bot also checks for missing tax information. For example, if a customer hasn't provided a VAT or GST identification number, the Bot notifies the sales rep of the tax that will be assessed and gives them 24 hours to provide the missing information. Previously, we might have sent the invoice and resolved the issue only after the customer raised a question. Now we can address it before the invoice goes out.

The Bot can also handle credits and rebilling, subject to additional permissions and approvals.

Billing Support Bot answers questions from our go-to-market team

Billing Support Bot handles requests from our go-to-market team about customer billing. It connects to our core accounting systems, allowing sales reps to get answers and make routine updates without involving someone on our accounting team.

For example, a customer might notice that the usage shown on an invoice doesn't match their dashboard. Billing Support Bot can investigate the underlying records to explain why the two amounts differ.

The Bot can also take action directly. If a rep needs to update a customer's billing email or add additional recipients, they can ask the Bot in Slack. It verifies that the new addresses match the customer's domain, then updates the billing records automatically.

Previously, our team handled these requests one at a time, even when the underlying work was straightforward. Now the Bot can resolve many of them from start to finish. We estimate that Billing Support Bot has freed up approximately eight hours a day across our accounting team's work.

Cash Applications Bot reconciles customer payments

Cash Applications Bot reconciles incoming customer payments against outstanding invoices. Beyond matching payments automatically, it investigates discrepancies and handles routine adjustments that would otherwise require an accountant to intervene.

The Bot checks our payment feed twice daily and automatically applies payments that match outstanding invoices exactly. When a payment doesn't match, it searches our customer support system for remittance advice that can help identify which invoices the payment covers.

The Bot also automatically writes off bank fees that cause discrepancies between payment and invoice amounts. If a customer has paid less than they owe, it flags the short payment to our collections team for follow-up.

This process ordinarily takes an accountant three to four hours. The Bot completes it in roughly 30 minutes.

Collections Bot handles customer-facing billing inquiries

Collections Bot is our first accounting Bot to communicate directly with customers. It monitors our accounts receivable inbox, answers billing questions, and coordinates requests that require action from other Bots.

For example, if a customer requests a refund, Collections Bot works with Billing Bot and Cash Applications Bot to investigate the request and prepare the necessary actions. The Bots must obtain approval from an authorized person before processing the refund.

We spent approximately three months training Collections Bot because customer-facing communication introduces additional security requirements. In particular, the Bot must verify that someone requesting account information is authorized to receive it.

It does this by checking the sender's email address against approved contact information in the CRM and our billing system. A similar-looking email domain isn't sufficient. If the information doesn't match, the Bot escalates the inquiry to a person rather than release sensitive information.

Building toward an SI accounting team

Without Grok Bot, we estimate that the work we're assigning to these five Bots would require more than doubling the headcount on our team. Instead, we're building a team in which Bots handle routine processes and our accountants focus on managing the work, improving the systems, and resolving exceptions.

The biggest lesson from our experience is that building an effective AI team requires the same attention we'd give to building a human one. We need to define jobs clearly, document how they're performed, and invest in training. Once we've done that, we can give Bots responsibility for work that previously depended on people being available to do it.

Try Grok Bot today

item.title: [Cohere] Video intelligence: Make every moment in your video library…
item.description: Full title: Video intelligence: Make every moment in your video library searchableIntroducing precise, timestamped video retrieval for enterprise search and AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
Nov 16, 2026

4 minute read

Video intelligence: Make every moment in your video library searchable

Introducing precise, timestamped video retrieval for enterprise search and AI agents.

Enterprises have vast amounts of valuable information locked inside recorded meetings, training videos and media archives. But unlike documents, video remains difficult for AI applications to search and use.

Today, we're introducing Video Intelligence in Compass, enabling AI applications and agents to search across video collections, find relevant moments and retrieve timestamped evidence alongside documents.

Compass understands both what's said and what's shown on screen. Instead of returning an hour-long recording, it retrieves the exact moment that answers a question, with a timestamped clip, transcript and visual description.

We're now recruiting design partners. Register your interest.

Search for moments, not just files

Consider the questions people actually ask of video:

  • When did the team agree to move the launch to Q3?
  • Where does the presenter explain revenue trends on the whiteboard?
  • When did a particular player get sent off during the game?

Answering them takes more than matching keywords in a transcript or scanning individual frames. It takes an understanding of what's said, what's shown and how events unfold over time. A single frame can show a player leaving the pitch, but only the sequence shows they were sent off. A presenter can describe improving KPIs while the chart on screen tells a different story.

Timing matters too. A clip that begins two minutes early, or cuts off before the answer, still leaves someone scrubbing through the footage.

Compass makes video searchable by meaning, context and precise moments in time.

From raw footage to discoverable intelligence

A single search returns the exact moment in a recording alongside the matching page, slide and sheet from related documents, all drawn from one index that respects what each user is allowed to see.

Finding the right moment in a video is only part of the challenge. AI applications also need to retrieve that information, verify its source and use it alongside other enterprise knowledge.

Compass brings video into the same retrieval system as documents, with the precision and controls needed for enterprise AI applications.

  • Precise moments, not predefined clips: Rather than relying on fixed video segments, Compass determines the relevant start and end times at search time, returning the moment that answers the question.
  • Video and documents in one search: Applications and AI agents can retrieve relevant footage alongside documents, bringing video into enterprise search, RAG and agentic workflows.
  • Evidence you can verify: Every result links back to the original footage, with timestamps, transcripts and visual descriptions so users can check the source.
  • Built for enterprise requirements: Permission-aware retrieval ensures users only access authorized content, while configurable fields, model choices and deployment options let organizations adapt the solution to their needs.

Connect your agent to the Compass MCP server so it can reason over what's shown on screen, such as slides, charts and demonstrations, not just what's said.

Unlock new applications for your video data

Compass makes video accessible to AI applications, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic search. By making spoken and visual content searchable alongside documents, Compass gives your applications and AI agents eyes and ears to reason over new modalities and use information that was previously difficult to access.

Meetings and enterprise knowledge: Build AI assistants that surface decisions, forecasts and commitments from recorded meetings, research presentations, earnings calls and analyst briefings. Find exactly when something was discussed and retrieve the relevant clip, rather than searching through hours of recordings.

Education and training: Help employees and learners find answers across recorded lectures, onboarding sessions and training libraries. Retrieve the precise explanation relevant to a question, making educational content easier to discover, reference and reuse.

Sports and media archives: Search large video libraries for specific plays, players, events, camera angles or visible brands. Accelerate highlight creation, footage discovery, content licensing and sponsor reporting without manually reviewing recordings.

Legal and compliance: Find statements, disclosures and other relevant moments across recorded footage. Retrieve timestamped clips with supporting transcripts and visual context, enabling reviewers to locate and verify information against the original source.

Video Intelligence turns recorded meetings into a searchable record of decisions, returning just the minute where something was agreed so anyone can check it against the source.

Strong retrieval performance across enterprise video

Good moment retrieval means finding the most relevant moments and identifying precisely where they start and end. We evaluated Compass against seven video embedding models across 11 datasets, including six public benchmarks and five internal enterprise video datasets.

Compass ranks first on average, with an nDCG@10 (how accurately the top ten search results are ranked) 4.4 points ahead of the strongest alternative. The lead holds up across all three domains, even as the strongest competitor rotates from one domain to the next:

  • Public benchmarks: 2.4 points ahead of Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, averaged across six widely used open-source moment and video retrieval benchmarks.
  • Sports: 5.1 points ahead of Gemini Embedding 2 on soccer broadcast footage, where queries look for specific players, teams, and plays.
  • Enterprise knowledge: 2.0 points ahead of Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B on business meetings, lectures, and workplace-safety training.

Cohere Video Intelligence ranks first across our evaluation suite. Scores are nDCG@10 over 11,133 queries across 11 datasets, including open-source public benchmarks (six datasets), enterprise knowledge (meetings, lectures and safety training; three datasets) and sports (two soccer broadcast datasets).

Build with Video Intelligence

We're inviting design partners to test and shape Video Intelligence using real-world workloads.

Partners can deploy in our managed cloud or their own environment, evaluate performance against their own footage and queries, and collaborate directly with our engineering team to inform future development. Register your interest below.

Contributors

By Luke Ross, Dennis Zhao, Timothy Ang

Request access

  • Test it on your video library. Evaluate performance using your own content, queries, and use cases.
  • Work directly with our experts. Get hands-on support from Cohere’s AI search team.
  • Shape the product roadmap. Influence future capabilities based on your organization’s needs and experience.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight…
item.description: Full title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
item.content:encoded:
Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Published November 16, 2026

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

Run them with the tools you already use

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

How open-weight models are used

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

Routing powered by OpenRouter

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

zai-org/GLM-5.3            # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability
zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest    # highest throughput
zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest   # lowest price
zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita     # only Novita

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video and audio generation

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

See where your requests go

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Breaking change: custom provider keys

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

What's next

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

  • Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face.
  • More tasks routed through OpenRouter.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

item.title: [OpenRouter] OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face
item.content:encoded:
OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face

Sasha Blumenfeld ·11/16/2026

We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond. Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face. Chat models on Hugging Face Inference Providers now run through OpenRouter, with the same routing across providers that OpenRouter customers already rely on.

The integration also runs the other way. OpenRouter can now send a trace of each request to a Hugging Face Storage Bucket you own, so the prompts and responses from your real traffic sit next to the models and datasets you would use to evaluate or fine-tune on them. The setup guide has the steps.

What you get on Hugging Face

Many chat models on Hugging Face are served by more than one provider. OpenRouter’s provider routing now powers routing on Hugging Face Inference Providers, and it picks the provider for each request based on live price, speed, and reliability. You don’t have to set anything up, and your existing Hugging Face token and code keep working.

You also get automatic failover. If a provider slows down or starts failing, requests go to other providers until it recovers. If a provider returns an error, the request is retried on the next one inside the same call.

When we rebuilt this routing in October, a live experiment measured 46% fewer requests hitting a capacity error, 16.9% faster time to first token, and 16.3% higher throughput, for 6.0% higher cost per request. Everyone building on Hugging Face now gets the same routing.

You stay in control of the trade-off. Adding a suffix to the model ID, such as :fastest, :cheapest, or a provider name, tells OpenRouter what to prioritize, and requests work through OpenAI’s Chat Completions and Responses APIs or Anthropic’s Messages API. A conversation also stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache.

Each model page has a new Providers tab with live price, speed, and uptime for every provider. You can see your spend by provider and turn off any provider you don’t want to use.
