item.title: [Modular] Modular: Modular at LLVM Developers' Meeting 2026
item.content:encoded:
November 16, 2026

Modular at LLVM Developers' Meeting 2026

Michael Dunn-OConnor

Community

Modular recently spent three days at the 2026 LLVM Developers' Meeting in Santa Clara, California (October 26 to 28), where we ran a full-day MAX and Mojo workshop, gave a technical talk on device graphs, and talked with folks in the LLVM community in the hallways and at our booth. This was the first time we could share details about the entire Modular stack from end to end, with all of the source code available for attendees to follow along. We showed the internal architecture of the Mojo language, how we use MLIR across the stack, and how we layer Mojo with our graph compiler, among other topics. This post covers what we presented, what we heard, and what collaboration we see ahead.

Mojo and MAX workshop poster

Workshop: Mojo Internals Deep Dive and Roadmap

On Monday, October 26th, we ran "Mojo: Internals Deep Dive and Roadmap," an all-day session for compiler engineers familiar with LLVM and MLIR. The goal was to give that audience a working map of how Mojo is built, from the compiler and type system to GPU back-ends and the standard library. Despite the name, this was not just a session on Mojo. We built MAX on the foundation that Mojo provides, so we also covered how MAX targets new accelerator hardware, and how it compiles and optimizes computational graphs for complex AI models. The newly source-available MAX let us show, for the first time, how the entire Modular stack works together.

Mojo is built on MLIR (a subproject of LLVM), so this audience of active users and contributors had a unique perspective on the language, though many were new to Mojo and MAX. We were able to go much deeper into the internals of both Mojo and MAX than we typically do for a general audience. Unfortunately, LLVM workshops are not recorded, but the slides are included below.

What each talk covered

  • Mojo's place in the LLVM ecosystem. Billy Zhu, Lukas Hermann, and Weiwei Chen framed Mojo as the user-facing layer over MLIR for accelerators, where hardware specialization is performed by libraries that domain experts can write, not locked inside a compiler or a vendor binary. Mojo gives programmers the full power of direct MLIR and LLVM IR access, acting as a unified LLVM-style layer for AI.
  • Mojo compiler architecture overview. Billy Zhu and Weiwei Chen went deep into the unique MLIR-based design of the Mojo compiler. They discussed how the Mojo parser emits parametric MLIR directly, with no AST, and resolves declarations lazily. They also covered how the elaborator concretizes generic code asynchronously, and how the plugin system allows new backends to be added without forking the entire compiler.
  • Plugin architecture: separating the compiler and SDK from hardware-specific parts. Connor Gray showed how Modular is creating a portable and performant AI stack through programmable plugins. Anyone can extend the standard library and MAX accelerator library with optimized support for new hardware by implementing simple Mojo PluginHooks and MaxPluginHooks traits. These plugins are concise, with the backend for Qualcomm Cloud AI 100 only 263 lines. The full plugin architecture will enable plugins to bring the entire Modular stack to new hardware, a key technical enabler for the Modular hardware alliance.
  • Value ownership, lifetimes and origins: Mojo's memory safety model. Chris Lattner explained the benefits of Mojo's origins system: memory safety without a garbage collector, systems-level control, and an escape to unsafe APIs when needed. Generally, programmers don’t have to think about references until they define an API that returns one. The compiler checks lifetimes and destroys each value right after its last use, which gives smaller capture sets, more tail calls and copy-to-move optimization, and linear types that compose with the rest of the type system.
  • How Mojo supports non-LLVM back-ends (TPU and Trainium). Kolya Panchenko explained why TPU and Trainium are difficult hardware backends for a generalpurpose language. They expect typed, tiled, structured code, and Mojo has no memref type. The first milestone was a vector add written in Mojo that compiles to Mosaic MLIR for the TPU.
  • MAX graph compiler and the MLIR dialects behind kernel fusion. Feras Boulala walked an RMS-norm example through the whole MAX pipeline. Along the way, he showed the optimizations applied at each stage and features that set MAX apart for debugging a model, including Python stack traces and tracing.
  • How we write Mojo in Mojo. Joe Loser and Nathan Ward built an Int from scratch in MLIR, then showed how the types in the Mojo standard library are built the same way. A few leaf types wrap MLIR (like Bool, SIMD, and Pointer), then other types are built in Mojo using these leaves.
  • Case study: metaprogramming that abstracts away hardware specifics. Kern Handa described bringing up a 32-bit device behind a 64-bit host. The case study detailed three problems (a fixed C entry point, packing arguments into a flexible array, and serializing closures), each solved with Mojo library code. Kern demonstrated how bringing up an accelerator is mostly library work.

Technical talk: Moving Beyond Record & Replay

On Wednesday, October 28, Spenser Bauman from our Graph Execution team presented Moving Beyond Record & Replay, a case for building device graphs in a compiler, such as the one inside MAX, instead of capturing them at runtime. If you’re not familiar, both CUDA and HIP (as well as other accelerators) offer a means of sending a graph of operations to an accelerator, instead of sending each operation by itself.

As GPUs get faster, the cost of CPU-to-accelerator communication grows until it takes up much of the inference time. Device graphs address that by submitting a whole sequence of work to the device at once. MAX uses them, and so does every widely used serving stack. The usual way to build one is record and replay: capture a stream of commands at runtime, then replay it. CUDA and HIP both offer this.

Spenser laid out two problems with that approach:

  • Record and replay spreads complexity across the graph executor, async runtime, memory pools, kernels, and drivers.
  • It depends on a capture mode that not every vendor provides. Several accelerators expose device-graph or command-buffer construction APIs but have no record and replay equivalent, which puts them out of reach for a capture-based stack.

The alternative Modular is pursuing is to use a graph compiler to build those device graphs directly. Rather than capturing and then replaying a graph, the graph compiler within MAX already knows the fundamental structure of the final device graph. The graph compiler can construct the device graph and emit direct calls to the target's graph-construction APIs. The talk walked through four pieces of that design:

  • How kernels declare their device-graph capabilities.
  • The front-end IR that marks device-graph-capable regions.
  • The middle-end dialects and operations that model device graphs.
  • The Mojo-level APIs for working with them.

The approach is already working in practice. A production Gemma 4 model now runs end-to-end through device graph synthesis on one or more GPUs, and a single model can contain multiple device-graph regions. Building the graph directly is about 40% faster than recording it. DeviceGraphBuilder implementations exist for CUDA, HIP, and Qualcomm AI100, all behind one interface, so the same approach extends to new targets.

What comes next

The workshop closed with the Mojo roadmap and an invitation to contribute.

Roadmap. Denis Gurchenkov outlined the near-term priority of Mojo language features for kernel programming (enumerations and pattern matching, more compile-time metaprogramming, syntax for hardware concepts such as address spaces) and a longer-term goal for 2027 of reaching developers who write performant CPU code, with the necessary development of async/await, dynamic dispatch, threading, and networking. On the compiler side, the plan is to make the GPU and NPU backends source available, support pluggable MLIR and LLVM backends, enable a WASM backend, and to continue improving compilation speed. Tooling and community items include automatic Mojo and C interoperability, a debugger, a testing framework, a package manager built on pixi, and a Bazel-based build system.

Modular's open source journey. Brad Larson and Joe Loser traced three years of progressive open-sourcing of Mojo and MAX, starting with the Mojo standard library in March of 2024, all the way to open-sourcing Mojo and making MAX fully source-available just a few weeks ago. The whole Modular stack now builds from the public modular/modular repository (which now has over 30,000 GitHub stars!), a tremendously exciting milestone. We’ve also learned a lot of lessons during our process of open-sourcing Mojo and MAX, which we get into in this presentation.

With all of the source code for Mojo and MAX now publicly available, the team left attendees with one message: please clone the modular/modular repository, build Mojo and MAX from source, and experiment with extending the platform. Check out the contributor guides for Mojo as well as the newly added guide for MAX and see where and how you can upstream fixes and additions for both.

Modular (and Qualcomm) are proud long-time supporters of LLVM Foundation events, and this year was particularly special: we finally took everyone behind the curtains of our work, and are excited to see what the community will build.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] The Claude Tag guide for startups
item.content:encoded:
Startups frequently work at a fast pace with lean teams wearing many hats. In many ways, Claude Tag (beta) is suited for how startups work. You @Claude to a Slack channel where your context lives, add connectors, and have your team assign and steer tasks together.

For startup teams new to using Claude Tag, one of the most frequent questions is “which channels should I add Claude to first?” To help answer it, we spoke with eight high growth startups to see how Claude Tag works inside their teams.

Featuring insights from

We heard from leaders at companies with visions from reinventing law firms to building the next generation of resource planning software. Some had added Claude to nearly every channel while others had focused deeply on one or two specific use cases.

CompanyOn callThread to PRCompany brainSelf-serve dataRoutine reporting
Kikoff●●●●
NavigateAI●●●●
Campfire●●●
Flagler Health●●●
Moritz●●
Orderful●●●●
Valence●●●
Descript●●●

But everyone we spoke with shared an “aha!” moment where they realized a minutes-long Claude Tag conversation replaced days of work or uncovered insights that would otherwise have remained hidden.

The most common are contained in this guide, each with practical implementation details designed to help founders find and deploy the use cases that will move the needle for their team. Here are some examples of how the needle moved for the startups we spoke with:

21

minutes from Slack mention to open PR

134

pull requests merged from Slack threads

5

minutes for the daily end-of-shift update, down from 1 hour

<1

hour from client ask to no-code solution

2

days from Slack question to production

Days to hours

of recurring reporting prep

In this guide, we share the most common use cases, channels, and collective insights from leading startups for using Claude Tag.

Top channels to tag Claude

The eight startups we spoke with use Claude Tag across Slack, but a handful of channels came up again and again as the best places to start.

01 Claude on call

Example setups:

Channels

#on-call #alerts-ci #deploy-watch #support-escalations

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Sentry, dbt, PagerDuty, Linear, Datadog, Jira, Grafana, incident.io

Threads and routines

Incident response, morning incident digest, Monday on-call handoff, daily health summary, hourly incident recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: monitor alerts and immediately triage each one in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket. Query the data first, then theorize, and separate what you verified from what you inferred. If it's real, name the likely root cause with links, tag the owner, and open a draft PR only if the fix is contained. If no action is needed, say so. After each incident, add what you learned to [lessons file].

Triage channels are notoriously noisy. There are constant interruptions from Sentry errors, Datadog alerts, customer bug reports, and support requests making it difficult to find the signal from noise. It's usually the first task teams hand to Claude.

With Claude in the channel as a first responder, the first pass is often done before the on-call engineer opens their laptop. Claude reads each item as it lands, investigates the codebase and the tools it has access to, and shares what it found. If the fix is contained, it opens a draft PR; if not, it routes the issue to the right person with the investigation attached. In these setups, a person reviews each fix before it merges, and only genuinely new problems need someone to start the investigation themselves.

At Campfire, which builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams, an engineer tagged Claude on a report that some of its AI agent’s finished answers weren’t reaching users. Claude had a PR open 21 minutes later, and it merged that afternoon.

Kikoff: A first responder in every triage channel

Kikoff is a fintech startup that helps consumers build credit, solve liquidity needs, and achieve financial security. Claude Tag is the first responder in triage channels across the company, including:

  • #deploys: Claude decides what to watch after each release and flags anything it broke.
  • #alerts-ci: When a build fails, Claude finds out why and proposes a fix as a draft PR.
  • #alerts-sentry-backend: Claude takes the first pass on Sentry exceptions and crashes.
  • #dog-fooding: Claude investigates what employees flag while dogfooding and tags the right owner.
  • #support: Claude takes the first pass on support tickets.

Kikoff started with Claude contributing to the conversation only when mentioned, and the biggest wins came once the team let it jump in on its own. When sign-up broke, Claude traced it to a backend change, sized the impact, named the team that owned the fix, and opened a draft PR so the app would fail softly in the meantime.

Claude flags that sign-up is broken, traces it to a backend change, sizes the impact, names the team that owns the fix, and opens a draft PR so the app fails softly. A recreated conversation from Kikoff. Names and images have been modified. Used with permission from Kikoff.

“I’m always hyped when Claude catches an issue before a monitor or human does. One person can only personally manage so much context, Claude Tag helps us organize and own some context, and we manage the outcomes.”

Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff

NavigateAI: Fixing bugs with fragmented context

NavigateAI builds AI copilots for construction field teams. They run Claude Tag in about 90 channels for alert triage, bug bashes, quick feature building, and support escalations. Since June, Claude has opened about 223 PRs straight from Slack threads and 134 have merged with a median of two hours from open to merge.

Triage has been a particularly valuable use case for NavigateAI. Because Claude has so much context, it can find unintuitive root causes to issues that may have been missed at first glance.

“Our biggest ‘wow!’ moment with Claude Tag was when we were trying to debug a load issue, which seemed to be caused by a customer (since their calls were failing). A normal human response would be to continue chasing down that customer. But because Claude had access to so many other data sources, it actually found that it was from an uninstrumented internal cron job that was running during the same time.”

Mike Chen, head of engineering at NavigateAI

With Claude, mean time to resolve issues has improved. In one case, Claude had the root cause eight minutes after a Sentry alert fired, and the fix was merged 93 minutes after the alert.

“Fast-moving startups typically have to pick speed over structure. Claude Tag gives us both. It’s a brain that connects the dots across all our tools, so we get the structure without having to build it ourselves,” said Mike.

02 Thread to PR

Example setups:

Channels

#quick-wins #bug-bash #product-feedback #feature-requests #ux-papercuts #tech-debt #design-polish

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Figma, Sentry

Threads and routines

One request per thread, weekly backlog sweep, daily PR roundup, weekly shipped recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: when someone describes a bug or small feature, work on it in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first. If details are missing, ask for them or for a real example instead of guessing. If the change is small and contained, open a draft PR with a short summary of what changed and how you tested it. Never merge; a person reviews and approves. If it's too big or risky, say why and suggest a ticket.

Speed is one of a startup’s biggest advantages, but often small requests that delight users can get lost in the shuffle. The intelligence is often gathered by customer-facing teams, submitted in Slack, and, if it's not overlooked, eventually makes its way to Linear or Jira where it’s prioritized against hundreds of other tickets.

With Claude Tag, anyone can draft the PR, technical or not. Surface an idea in a thread, get live feedback from product, engineering, and GTM in the same place, and Claude turns the thread into a draft PR that reflects everyone’s input.

Many of the startups we spoke with used Claude Tag for the “light and delight” features or to remove papercuts that are quick to review but would otherwise not get prioritized.

Orderful: From Slack exchange to production feature in two days

Orderful is an EDI platform that connects companies with their trading partners, through an API or straight from the browser. Its customers trade standard documents with their partners through the platform.

One document type, the 753, wasn’t supported in Orderful’s web app. The request had sat in the backlog, and shipments for one large retailer were delayed.

When an account manager followed up in Slack, the PM tagged Claude in: “@Claude, you should build one.” Claude asked for real examples of the document so it could build to the actual format, then opened a draft PR adding 753 support.

Claude confirms a fix works on a real 753 transaction. Names and images have been changed. Used with permission from Orderful.

The next morning, Claude filed a ticket for the accompanying 754, the retailer’s response, and opened a second PR. Both were in production about two days after the Slack exchange.

“Something that took weeks or months before just took a Slack conversation,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful. “Light features with hard-to-prove value used to get stuck in the backlog. Now they have a way out.”

Valence: From feature request to rollout

Valence works with the world’s largest employers to connect enterprise talent and performance with Nadia, an AI coach. When a Valence engineer explained in Slack how to address an urgent product change requested by an important client, Claude didn’t just follow directions, it identified additional changes that needed to be made as the same configuration lived in two spots. Without Claude, the initial change would have been incomplete.

Claude calls out that a requested change is actually two changes. Used with permission from Valence.

“It didn’t just agree with the expert. It caught duplicated configuration, the kind of thing humans lose track of.”

Sameer Bansal, principal AI engineer at Valence

In another case, a client urgently asked for a customization. Claude checked the code and, working with an engineer, confirmed it could ship with no code change. In under an hour, a teammate had a solution ready for the client.

03 Company brain

Example setups:

Channels

#ask-anything #company-wiki #product-questions

Connectors

GitHub, Notion, Google Drive, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Granola, Metabase

Threads and routines

One question per thread, decision log updates, weekly stale doc check, repeat questions recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer questions from our code, docs and past threads, and link your sources. If sources disagree, check the code, give the current answer, and flag the stale doc. If you aren’t sure, say so and tag the owner. When a thread reaches a decision, record it in [docs location]. Anything going to a client needs a human check first.

At a startup, institutional knowledge often lives in people's heads, from the intricacies of product billing codes to where the onboarding docs are hosted.

For many of the startups we spoke with, Claude Tag has become the company brain. Claude answers with the source, and tags the owner when it isn't confident. It keeps that knowledge current too: when a thread reaches a decision, Claude can record it in your docs the same day and flag docs that have gone stale.

Example exchange.

Moritz: A live source of truth from intake to staffing

Moritz is an AI-native law firm that promises a same-day turnaround on contracts, against what Moritz cites as an industry standard of at least three weeks. Everything around the legal work, from intake and quoting to staffing and follow-up, lives in Slack, with a thread per matter and a channel per client.

Now everyone from the CEO to paralegals asks Claude first. Questions that took up to 30 minutes of searching in Slack get answered in under two. The end-of-shift update, now drafted from the day’s threads, went from about an hour of assembly to a five-minute edit.

That time goes back to legal work. Claude Tag handles the administrative work around a case, like follow-up questions, reminders, and status updates. It can’t access client documents or privileged conversations with Moritz’s lawyers.

“A firm working across 44 countries generates hundreds of one-off questions a month that no one will ever build a feature for. Claude Tag answers them from our own history in Slack. Every answer is a thread with links, so institutional memory compounds.”

Stefan Mandaric, co-founder and CTO at Moritz

Campfire: Customer experience on demand

One Slack channel in particular “exploded in popularity”: their CX (or customer experience) channel. Sales uses this channel “to validate certain functionality during prospect conversations,” rather than having to “ping 10 different people.”

This type of channel is particularly effective because sales can answer in the moment, while the customer is paying attention, and can operate more independently and confidently in early customer conversations.

“Claude Tag basically acts as our central knowledge base.”

Nancy Jin, AI engineering manager at Campfire

04 Self-serve data

Example setups:

Channels

#data-requests #ask-revops #metric-definitions

Connectors

dbt, GitHub, Metabase, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Notion

Threads and routines

One question per thread, weekly pre-standup readout, launch and experiment readouts, pipeline failure triage, new question triage

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer from our governed models and the definitions in [data skills repo]. If the data isn’t covered there, say it’s unvalidated instead of guessing. Lead with the answer, then give the number, what’s driving it, and any caveat. Check recent incidents, releases, and Slack discussions before explaining a change. If a metric’s definition is unclear, ask which one we mean. For anything important, share your plan or SQL before you run it. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and list any open data quality warnings at the end of your answer. If someone finds a mistake, draft a fix for a data team member to review. If a question comes up twice, suggest scheduling it.

At a fast-growing startup every function wants numbers, and the data team has to decide whose request comes first. With Claude Tag connected to your data, anyone can ask in plain English without waiting in the data team’s queue.

This is a use case we have adopted as well. In one of our data channels over a month, Claude Tag answered more than 75% of questions people posted, typically within a minute or two. It works from governed data and the same definitions analysts use, which live in a versioned repo that Claude re-reads in every conversation.

From Self-service data analytics in Slack: how Anthropic deploys Claude Tag for ad-hoc questions.

Descript: Answering ad-hoc data requests

Descript is an AI-powered video editing platform. Claude Tag is now the first line of support for data requests and initial analyses. Product, growth, RevOps, and finance ask questions in Slack and get answers grounded in Descript’s dbt models.

“I used to write complicated SQL and refresh the numbers by hand every week or month. Now I’ve replaced several data-team dashboards with my own Claude artifacts, and I no longer refresh them by hand.”

Daisy Zhang, head of growth marketing at Descript

Daisy’s recurring reporting prep went from days to hours.

The growth team, for example, asks why lifecycle subscriptions dropped, whether paid search is losing last-touch credit to other channels, or how long a self-serve account takes to become an enterprise opportunity. The data team tracks the artifacts Claude generates to see which data assets matter most across teams, and spends its own time on strategic questions and on building the context that makes self-serve work.

“The promise of business intelligence has always been self-serve for business users. I’d never seen it actually realized until we had Claude Tag set up with immense context for our data.”

Jen Huhn, monetization PM at Descript

Orderful: From question to dashboard

At Orderful, self-serve analytics spans conversational analytics and full data builds: anyone can go from a question in Slack to a dashboard merged to production. The key is a semantic layer that encodes agreed definitions and metrics, so every answer and every build uses the same definitions.

“We trust the output because a semantic layer constrains the SQL, CI gates the builds, and there’s a process for agreeing on definitions. Without those, you get confident-looking wrong answers. Once those guardrails were in place, connecting Claude Tag took under 30 minutes. Now teammates build together in shared Slack threads instead of solo sessions.”

Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful

05 Reporting and handoffs

Example setups:

Channels

#sales-pipeline #customer-handoffs #standup-summary #qbr-prep

Connectors

Notion, Google Drive, Gong, Salesforce, Gainsight

Threads and routines

End-of-day status draft, pre-QBR brief, deal handoff

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: draft each recurring report from our threads, docs, and data, and link your sources. Lead with what changed and what needs a decision. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and flag anything missing instead of filling the gap. Post the draft in its own thread for [owner] to edit. Nothing goes out until a person approves it. If a report keeps getting the same edits, suggest updating these instructions.

Many of the examples we’ve covered are reactive: something happens, Claude responds. Routine reporting is work Claude owns on a schedule, the way a teammate owns a recurring deliverable.

Example of using Routines in Claude Tag.

You describe the outcome once; Claude runs it every time and posts the result where the team already works.

Valence: Deal reviews and handoffs

Valence is setting Claude up to brief the team before every quarterly business review, with customer health, open deals, blockers, and next steps. They are also working to make the handoff from sales to customer success when a deal closes more seamless. Claude saves the team time by helping to aggregate details across their engagement and often finds key items they may have missed.

“When a deal closes, Tag builds the handoff from the deal history, calls and contract: who’s who, what was promised, what’s customized, and what’s still open. Customer success then reviews it before their kickoff,” said Sameer.

06 Getting started checklist

The checklist below pulls together these startup teams’ best practices so you can apply them to your own workflows.

Before launch

Check the prerequisites.

Claude Tag is in public beta on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, and isn’t available on Free, Pro, or Max. You’ll need a Claude organization Owner and a Slack workspace admin to connect the two. An admin must also turn on Routines, and Team plans need usage credits before Claude responds.

Set up Claude’s access with a bundle.

In channels, Claude works under its own agent identity, with service accounts rather than anyone’s personal login. Group the connectors, repos, and instructions it needs in a bundle, and attach them org-wide, per workspace, or per channel. That sets what Claude can reach in each place, and everyone in a channel gets the same access. Start narrow: only what the first channel’s job needs.

Experiment in a private channel.

Nearly half the startups we spoke with started their Claude Tag journey by having a small cross-functional team experiment in a private channel. “Start private with a mix of roles, then move to a group channel,” said Sameer.

Determine the boundaries.

By default, anyone in your Slack workspace can use Claude, even without a Claude account. You can restrict access to your org and limit search to channels Claude is in. On Enterprise, you can also restrict access to specific roles or chosen channels.

Set clear expectations for what Claude can do and can never do. Several teams we spoke with let Claude open draft PRs, but people review and merge. For Orderful, Claude Code, not Tag, handles “infrastructure changes, audits, sensitive data.” For a “hard call,” such as “a PR that touches more than one service,” Claude gets a second opinion. Moritz doesn’t give Claude Tag access to client documents or privileged conversations with its lawyers.

Start your security review early.

The usual questions are data retention and what Claude can reach, and the security and data lifecycle pages answer both. Claude Tag isn’t available to orgs with zero data retention turned on, a customer-managed encryption (CMEK) policy, or the HIPAA configuration, and it isn’t covered by our Business Associate Agreement, so check that before you plan a rollout.

Set a budget and alerts.

Claude Tag bills by usage, so an early conversation avoids surprises as adoption grows. You can set spend limits overall and per channel, choose the model per channel, and attribute costs by user using the Enterprise Analytics API. Orderful runs an org-wide cap with alerts at 75% and 90%. “We have extreme ownership on the channel costs. The owner justifies that ‘yes, this spend is reasonable for the output / outcomes,’” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff. Use your first channel’s actual costs to size the next one.

Deployment

Pick one clear task in a channel your team already uses, like on-call alerts or bug triage.

“We experiment on certain teams, see what works, then once confident we’ve worked out the kinks, we push the idea out to other teams to add to their own similar channels as well. We want to avoid trust breaking experiences with folks with lower tolerance to AI mistakes,” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff.

Prime your experts and culture bearers.

Have the people your team already trusts use Claude first, and in the open.

“Going back and forth with Claude in the open has been productive and fun. Several people in sales and customer success have watched experts [interact with Claude Tag], then started asking Claude themselves, and got value fast,” said Sameer Bansal, principal AI engineer at Valence.

Tune the noise.

Multiple startups told us they needed to adjust Claude’s chattiness. Too chatty is one risk.

“Conversation in ad hoc requests can sometimes get noisy. We’ve been trying to tune down the responsiveness here and also be more principled on what we use Claude on ad hoc requests for,” said Mike Chen, head of engineering at NavigateAI.

Too little chattiness is also a risk, however. In busy channels, “You either have to @ every time or it won’t do much,” said Will Hu, cofounder at Flagler Health. And “if no one is watching a channel closely or interacts with it, it will sit idle.”

Have teammates connect their own accounts.

The admin bundles from setup are what Claude can reach for everyone in a channel. Personal connectors work differently: Claude acts with the permissions of the person asking, so it can pull from their docs, inbox, or CRM once they approve it (an Owner adds the connector for the org first, and on Enterprise an admin manages personal connectors). The answer still posts in the channel, so choose “Allow with review” for anything sensitive.

Write channel instructions like you’re onboarding a new hire:

what to check first, when to open a PR, when to ask, and that “no action needed” is a valid answer.

Give Claude feedback in the channel, not in DMs.

Correct it in the thread. It remembers per channel, and teammates learn how to work with it by watching. For a lasting fix, ask Claude to update its memory for this channel.

Two Valence employees thank a colleague after watching them work through a question with Claude in the open. Used with permission from Valence.

Not sure where to go next? Tag Claude and ask what it has learned about your org and which use cases it would expand to.

Moritz’s co-founder and CTO, Stefan Mandaric, asked Claude to recommend use cases for each team. Fifteen minutes later, it had read the firm’s Slack channels, Linear issues, Notion SOPs, Drive, and Metabase dashboards, and published 25. “18 of 25 worked with no further setup. That became our rollout plan.”

Last word: what we learned from the wow moments

The wow moments weren’t always about speed. Often, Claude found something no one had asked it to look for. Sometimes the surprise was restraint. And sometimes the surprise was the unexpected exchanges. “Eventually you get used to Claude jumping in on jokes, and you soon appreciate that it’s an easy audience and the first one to laugh,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful.

Recreated Orderful conversation in Slack. Used with permission from Orderful.

We hope you found this guide useful. Special thanks to Campfire, Descript, Flagler Health, Kikoff, Moritz, NavigateAI, Orderful and Valence for sharing their experiences and insights.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Building always-on agents
item.content:encoded:
Over the past few months, we’ve seen a resurgence of always-on agents.

Always-on agents are stateful and proactive, meaning they manage context across sessions and take actions without direct supervision. Underneath, they run on the same core loop as other agents. The difference is the surrounding architecture, which is built from primitives that control when the agents wake up, what carries over between runs, and how their work reaches the user.

The resurgence is largely due to recent model advancements, which have made always-on agents more practical to run. First, the latest models have better judgment: they’re more reliable at understanding user intent and knowing when to check in. Second, intelligence is becoming cheaper, with long-horizon tasks benefiting the most. For example, on one long-horizon coding benchmark, Opus 5.5 cost 78% less per solved task than Opus 5, compared with 40% less on typical workloads.

Customers have started to ask us how to integrate this type of experience into their own products. Some companies want to make their existing agents more proactive, while others are looking to build them from the ground up.

This post breaks down the primitives behind always-on agents and walks through how they fit together.

The cycle behind the always-on agent

An always-on agent is not actually “always on.” This is just a description of the user experience.

In reality, the agent spends most of its time asleep, waking up periodically to do work. Each stretch of work is called a run: the agent receives an event, completes its task, and then saves information about what happened. A run works inside a session, which is the transcript of messages and tool calls. Once the run is finished, the agent goes back to sleep, and the cycle repeats indefinitely.

The core primitives

The surrounding architecture of an always-on agent has five core primitives: an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions, and an outbox. Let’s take a look at each.

Event inbox

Most AI agents only run when the user sends a message. In contrast, always-on agents can be triggered by many types of events, including webhooks, scheduled tasks, and background jobs.

One tempting approach is to have each event source call the agent directly, but that has a few failure modes. For example, two events arriving at the same time can start competing runs, and a crash can lose an event entirely.

This is where the event inbox comes in. Instead of calling the agent, every source sends an event to an inbox, where a worker picks it up.

The simplest version has three components:

  • A durable list of events, usually a database table;
  • A handler, usually an HTTP endpoint, that writes events to the list; and
  • A worker, usually a background service, that reads from the list.

The inbox should track the status of each event, and events can be deduplicated based on unique identifiers from the source. A relational database works well for the inbox, with every event appended as a new row. We recommend starting with one inbox per user, but you can split this further if you need more parallelism.

When a new event comes in, the handler writes the event to the inbox and wakes the worker. The worker reads whatever is pending and starts a run. Events that continue earlier work, such as a reply from the user, resume an existing session, while everything else starts a new session.

From there, the worker passes the events to the agent loop, waits for the run to finish, and marks the corresponding events as done. The implementation details can get tricky, so here are a few best practices:

  • The handler should acknowledge events quickly. Some sources, such as webhook providers, treat slow responses as failures. The handler can still run lightweight checks, but any deeper verification, such as checking for prompt injection, should be done during the run.
  • The inbox should be the source of truth. When the worker is woken up, it should pull the latest events from the inbox first. That way, if the worker dies mid-run, a new one can pick up the same event and retry.
  • An inbox should only have one active worker at a time. This prevents two runs from duplicating work or overwriting each other. When a new event shows up mid-run, you can either push it to the next run, fold it into the current run, or interrupt and restart.
  • The worker should batch pending events together. For example, if the user sends several messages in a row, the worker can merge them into a single run, so the agent only needs to reply once.

Timers

Together with the event inbox, timers let always-on agents be proactive. Timers generally fall into one of two categories: follow-ups or schedules. A follow-up is a deadline that the agent sets for itself, such as checking in on a reply. A schedule, on the other hand, is a recurring task that happens on a known cadence, such as a daily newsletter.

Timers live in their own durable store, usually another database table, separate from the inbox. The inbox should only hold events that are ready to be worked on. A follow-up and a schedule can share a similar schema, but a schedule needs to track its recurrence as well.

A timer doesn’t initiate a run on its own. Instead, a scheduler, usually a background service, polls the store at a fixed interval and fires anything that’s due. On each pass, the scheduler:

  • Scans the store and finds timers that are due.
  • Updates each timer based on its category.A follow-up should be marked as done.A schedule should get its due time updated to the next occurrence.
  • Adds an event to the inbox and wakes the worker.

For the scheduler, you can either build your own service or use a durable execution engine.

Memory

Always-on agents work across many disjointed runs and rely on memory to maintain continuity.

Similar to the event inbox and timers, memory should have its own store. In our products, such as Claude Code’s auto memory and the Messages API’s memory tool, this is implemented as a directory of files. For an always-on agent, the directories should map to durable storage, usually a database or an object store. This way memories outlive the worker.

As a rule of thumb, memory should only hold what the agent can’t look up again. If something already lives in another system, such as an issue tracker, you should save a pointer instead. Here is a breakdown of the types of memory an always-on agent should store:

  • User instructions: Any instructions from the user about agent behavior should be saved in their own file and loaded at the start of every run. The user won’t always be around to steer the agent, so the instructions have to carry over between runs.
  • User notes: The agent should save what it’s learned about the user, such as their role, their preferences, or any corrections they’ve given. You can start with one file and move to several small files as the notes grow. In the latter case, only an index is loaded at the start of each run, but the agent can pull the individual files into context when it needs more details.
  • Past messages: The agent should keep track of what it’s already told the user so nothing is repeated. It can either store this in a separate file that’s loaded at the start of each run, or have the worker load the agent’s last few messages with the user.
  • Task progress: For each ongoing task, the agent should keep a progress file that covers what’s been done and what’s left. Any new run can then read that file and pick up where the previous run left off. Similar to user notes, only an index is loaded at the start of each run, but the agent can pull the individual files into context when it needs more details.

The diagram below shows one example setup.

All of the above describes memory that’s saved during a run. You can also add dreaming, which reviews past sessions to curate memories. Dreaming can replace outdated entries and find patterns that only show up across many runs. If you’re interested in learning more, our post on agent memory covers this in more detail.

Inside the context window

Before doing any work, the agent loads the system prompt, tool definitions, and memory files. This initial context “overhead” is included in every run, so we recommend keeping it lean and using prompt caching to lower costs.

A new session starts only with this context overhead and the events that triggered the run. An existing session, on the other hand, brings back the messages and tool calls from its earlier runs.

If a session becomes too long, you can either compact the older messages or start a new session. Both approaches lose detail, so anything that needs to persist should be saved to memory along the way.

Permissions

Permissions are where always-on agents carry the most risk. A run holds the user’s access and, by design, operates unattended. For each tool call, the agent needs to decide whether to proceed on its own, block it, or wait for approval.

The components for permissions are the same ones other agents use:

  • Credential store: Always-on agents often need sensitive user credentials like passwords or access tokens to be useful. The recommended pattern is a proxy outside the agent’s environment that adds credentials to outgoing requests. The agent sends requests without credentials, and the proxy injects the real credentials before forwarding.
  • Auto mode: An always-on agent should be able to work without constant user input. We’ve already tackled a version of this problem with auto mode in Claude Code. Auto mode uses classifiers to review higher-risk actions and block the ones they identify as dangerous so Claude can find a safer approach. User review, however, is still necessary for the most important decisions.
  • Deferred tool calls: In Claude Code, a hook can defer a tool call and wait for additional input from the user. The same pattern applies to always-on agents, which may need clarification or approval before taking certain actions. When a call is deferred, the run ends and the session is saved mid-call. The request is shown to the user (e.g., through an interactive card built with MCP Apps), and their answer comes back as an event in the inbox. That event starts a new run, which resumes the saved session with the user’s input. While the deferred call waits for a response, the worker can pick up other events, so the agent isn’t blocked.

Outbox

With most AI agents, the response is streamed to the user as it’s generated, so they can follow along as Claude reasons through the problem, calls tools, and writes its answer.

Always-on agents, on the other hand, do most of their work in the background. The user gets the outcome and a few details, rather than the entire step-by-step breakdown.

A run can end in one of three ways:

  • The agent sends a message to the outbox,
  • The agent decides that nothing needs to be sent, or
  • The agent uses a deferred tool call to request permission or additional input.

Most always-on agents can get by with a “send” tool that delivers the message directly to the user. You only need a formal outbox when you want to pace your agent’s messages or allow your agent to recover from errors.

The outbox is a separate table of outgoing messages, analogous to the event inbox. There’s also a dispatcher, usually a background service, that’s analogous to the worker. The dispatcher reads the pending messages, decides what to deliver, and sends those to the user. A request from a deferred tool call can either go through the outbox or be shown directly in the interface.

Beyond delivery, it’s important to tune how many messages the agent sends. An agent that sends too many becomes noisy, while an agent that doesn’t send enough misses things that the user needs to know. We recommend building evals to find the right balance. In practice, it’s better for the agent to start quiet and then earn more of the user’s attention over time.

How everything fits together

Here is how the five primitives fit together:

Every run starts with an event from the inbox, whether it’s a user message, a webhook, or a timer. When the worker picks up an event, it kicks off a run and wakes the agent in a new or existing session. The agent reads its memory to get a baseline, works within its permissions to take actions, and then updates its memory with anything it has learned. Once the run is finished, the agent pushes a row to the outbox, and the dispatcher delivers the message to the user.

Together, these form a cycle. A run can set a timer that wakes the agent again later, and when the user replies to a message, their answer comes back as an event in the inbox. Each run is brief, but the cycle keeps going indefinitely, and that’s what makes the agent feel like it’s always on.

Acknowledgements

Written by William Hu. Special thanks to Rodrigo Olivares and Michael Segner for their contributions.

item.description: Full title: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem
item.content:encoded:
llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

Team Article

Published November 13, 2026

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

During the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

Releases

ReleaseLibraryPublic header(s)
llama.cpp v1.0.0 - LLM inference in C/C++libllamallama.cpp/include/
ggml v1.0.0 - Tensor library for machine learninglibggmlggml/include/

Semantic version update rules

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

Change typeBump
MAJORBreaking change to the public C API in ./include
MINORBackward-compatible feature, backend updates, model support, or API addition
PATCHBug fix with no API change

Distribution

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

ChannelPlatforms
Pre-release artifactsLinux, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS
DockerLinux
DebianLinux
HomebrewmacOS, Linux
conda-forgeWindows, macOS, Linux
MacPortsmacOS
WingetWindows
XCFrameworkiOS, macOS

Development

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

Backend and model coverage

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

Thanks

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

Additional resources

  • llama.cpp examples
  • ggml-org at Hugging Face
  • ggml-org at Github
  • Check out Llama desktop apps for MacOS and Windows, shipped with love by the team behind llama.cpp and Hugging Face.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
item.content:encoded:
Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

Enterprise + Article

Published November 13, 2026

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

What makes a robot asset SimReady?

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

  • Profile: a group of features for a use case, such as a robot body.
  • Features: capabilities needed for the use case, such as joints that can be controlled.
  • Requirements: checks on the settings needed for each feature, such as a joint’s drive settings.

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

What comes with the asset, and what do you add?

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

What should you check before running a pick-and-place task?

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

  • Joint settings: Review the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings.
  • Movement: Test a small arm movement and open and close the gripper.
  • Contact: Confirm that the can rests on the work surface without falling through it.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

Build a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Required Software:

  • Install Isaac Sim 6.2, the version used for this example, and check its system requirements.
  • Set up an agent of your choice that can use the Isaac Sim skills. Follow the Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent.
  • Install the Hugging Face CLI only if you choose the command-line asset download option.
  • Use the USD Search endpoint.

Step 1: Download the robot arm, gripper, and beverage can assets

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

~/ASSETS/hf/src/simready-assets-c7fa7615/Robotiq_2F_140/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_140.usda

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

What does asset validation tell you?

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

Step 2: Assemble the robot and compose the scene for pick and place

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

./isaac-sim.sh --enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

Sample prompt used in this example:

Assemble the robot arm <local path to Simready ur17g robot usd>
with the gripper <local path to downloded simready Robotiq_2F_140 gripper usd>
using the Robot Assembly tutorial in Isaac Sim
https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/robot_setup/assemble_robots.html.

Validate the assembly on completion.

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Step 3: Test the controls and run pick-and-place

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Sample prompt used in this example:

Run pick and place with the assembled robot and soda can
<path to soda can USD from SimReady library> in Isaac Sim.

Ensure you do a contact based grasp for picking up the can and validate
the accuracy/placement error for the pick and place as well.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

Simulation assumptions:

  • Fixed setup: The can starts at a known position, with an anchored robot and clear, flat workspace. No vision was used and collision checks were limited.
  • Simplified can: Deformation and liquid motion are not modeled, so this example does not test crushing.
  • Scripted grasp and motion: A horizontal grasp uses a 2 N·m drive-effort cap chosen through simulation tests, not calibrated to fingertip forces or recommended by the manufacturer. Contact and friction hold the beverage can as the arm follows fixed waypoints without replanning. For hardware gripping-force specifications, see the Robotiq product sheet.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your next simulation with SimReady Assets

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

Discover assets

  • Find robots and objects: Browse SimReady Central on Hugging Face.
  • Check what an asset supports: Review the profiles and requirements in SimReady Foundation alongside the asset’s validation reports.

Build a pick-and-place scene

  • Set up the simulator: Follow the Isaac Sim installation guide for the version used in this example.
  • Connect your agent: Follow the Isaac Sim Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent.
  • Assemble the robot: Follow the Robot Assembler tutorial if you prefer to connect the arm and gripper manually.

Prepare and contribute content

  • Start from CAD: Follow the 5 Steps to Create SimReady Assets for Robotics to prepare your own robotics assets.
  • Validate and submit assets: Follow the SimReady Central submission guide to make your assets available to other developers.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

Happy building!

item.title: [Hugging Face] XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
item.content:encoded:
XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Enterprise Article

Published November 13, 2026

📄 Paper | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

Building XYBench

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

Evaluating how an answer helps

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

  • Pragmatic solution—records whether a model’s response includes solutions to the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X), checking each separately.
  • Pragmatic emphasis—measures whether a model’s answer focuses on the stated request (Y), focuses on the intended request (X), or balances the two.
  • Misconception identification—measures whether a model’s response steers the user toward the underlying goal (X) while discouraging or avoiding the mistaken approach (Y).

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

What the experiments show

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

What this means for evaluation

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Reranking in RAG: How to Fix Bad Retrieval with a Reranker
item.content:encoded:
Reranking in RAG: How to Fix Bad Retrieval with a Reranker

OpenRouter ·11/13/2026

When a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) app gives wrong answers even though the right information is in your documents, retrieval is often the cause. Vector search is great at finding chunks on the right topic, but it often falls for near misses, like pulling the bucket limit for the Enterprise plan when the user asked about the Growth plan. Reranking in RAG fixes this by taking your vector search’s top 30 candidates and passing them through a dedicated cross-encoder model that re-scores each chunk directly against the question.

On a 274-question benchmark, standard vector search with google/gemini-embedding-2 landed the exact right chunk at the top 81% of the time. Adding voyageai/rerank-3-lite to rerank the top 30 pushed that to 97% for roughly $0.10 per 1,000 queries. Keep in mind this was tested on a small synthetic dataset, so your real-world gains will depend on your documents, but the workflow below will help you measure your own baseline.

TL;DR
Retrieve about 30 candidates, rerank them, and send the top 3 to the LLM.
voyageai/rerank-3-lite and voyageai/rerank-3 were the most accurate dedicated rerank models and the cheapest of all 11 rerankers, at $0.10 and $0.26 per 1,000 queries.
An LLM reranker (openai/gpt-6-luna) put the right chunk first for 99.6% of questions, but each call took 4.0 seconds against 1.3 for a rerank model.
The cheap voyageai/voyage-4-lite plus voyageai/rerank-3-lite reached 96.7% precision@1, against 81.0% for the more expensive google/gemini-embedding-2 alone.
Set input_type on embedding calls. Leaving it out costs 7 to 12 points of precision@1.
cohere/rerank-v3.5 reads only the first 4,096 tokens (4K) of a document and gives no error.

Why does RAG retrieve the wrong chunks?

Standard vector search struggles because embedding models compress an entire chunk into a single vector before seeing the user’s question. If a 130-word chunk explains bucket limits, the specific plan name is only one or two words out of that entire block. As a result, the vectors for the Starter, Growth, Scale, and Enterprise plans cluster right on top of each other in vector space, and the retriever can easily rank the wrong plan first.

To test retrieval accuracy without relying on subjective scoring, we built a controlled dataset for a fictional storage service named Fernbank. The corpus contains 274 chunks spanning documentation, error codes, SDK guides, changelog entries, and noise, including unanswered forum posts and support tickets designed to trap naive keyword and vector matches. We generated each chunk from a fixed set of facts with anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 and checked it with a script. A separate model, openai/gpt-6.1-sol, wrote the questions. Because every question maps to one correct chunk, we can score retrieval without judgment calls.

In the full test set, the question was “How many buckets can I create in a single Fernbank account on the Growth plan?”. google/gemini-embedding-2 ranked the Starter, Enterprise, and Scale plan chunks 1, 2, and 3. An unanswered forum post ranked fourth, and the actual Growth plan answer sat at fifth. If your RAG pipeline only sends its top three candidates to the LLM, the model never even sees the right document.

A reranker fixes this by using a cross-encoder architecture. Rather than evaluating documents in isolation, it processes the user’s question alongside each candidate chunk. Running a cross-encoder across thousands of documents is too slow for real-time queries, so a vector search serves as a fast retriever, narrowing the field to a shortlist before the reranker sorts it.

How to add a reranker to your RAG pipeline

You don’t need to replace your existing embedding search. Keep it as the first retrieval stage, increase the number of candidates it returns, and add a reranking call before passing the final results to your LLM.

Retrieve 30 chunks with embeddings, rerank them, and send the top 3 to the LLM.

The following Python example uses our embeddings and rerank APIs. It retrieves candidate chunks using cosine similarity, reranks them with voyageai/rerank-3-lite, and returns the three highest-ranked results.

You’ll need an OPENROUTER_API_KEY environment variable, along with numpy and requests installed.

Python

import os
 
import numpy as np
import requests
 
API = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}
 
def embed(texts, input_type, model="google/gemini-embedding-2"):
    r = requests.post(f"{API}/embeddings", headers=HEADERS, timeout=120,
                      json={"model": model, "input": texts,
                            "input_type": input_type})
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = sorted(r.json()["data"], key=lambda d: d["index"])
    v = np.array([d["embedding"] for d in data])
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)
 
def retrieve(question, chunks, chunk_vectors, n=30):
    sims = chunk_vectors @ embed([question], "search_query")[0]
    return [(sims[i], chunks[i]) for i in np.argsort(-sims)[:n]]
 
def rerank(question, candidates, top_n=3, model="voyageai/rerank-3-lite"):
    r = requests.post(f"{API}/rerank", headers=HEADERS, timeout=120,
                      json={"model": model, "query": question,
                            "documents": candidates, "top_n": top_n})
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
    ranked = [(res["relevance_score"], candidates[res["index"]])
              for res in data["results"]]
    return ranked, data.get("usage", {}).get("cost")
 
# Your knowledge base, already split into chunks
chunks = [
    "Starter plan limits: an account on the Starter plan can create up to "
    "10 buckets.",
    "Scale plan limits: accounts on the Scale plan can hold up to "
    "2,500 buckets.",
    "Enterprise plan limits: Enterprise accounts can create up to "
    "40,000 buckets.",
    "Growth plan limits: an account on the Growth plan can hold up to "
    "150 buckets.",
    "Q: What's the bucket cap on the Growth plan? Reply: I think it "
    "changed recently, check the docs.",
    "Growth plan object size: a single object on the Growth plan can be "
    "up to 50 GB.",
]
chunk_vectors = embed(chunks, "search_document")
 
question = ("How many buckets can I create in a single account "
            "on the Growth plan?")
retrieved = retrieve(question, chunks, chunk_vectors)
print("Vector search:")
for sim, text in retrieved:
    print(f"  {sim:.3f} {text[:60]}")
 
ranked, cost = rerank(question, [text for _, text in retrieved])
print(f"Reranked (${cost:.7f}):")
for score, text in ranked:
    print(f"  {score:.3f} {text[:60]}")

  0.741 Scale plan limits: accounts on the Scale plan can hold up to

  0.717 Growth plan object size: a single object on the Growth plan
